# The Bluffs on Manistee Lake — North Expansion
## Plan Facts: Scope of Work Audit & Quantity Take-Off
**Spicer Group, File D-6631, 49 Sheets, REV 3, Sealed August 20, 2026**
*Preliminary AI review for developer and engineer of record — not stamped engineering, not a bid*

---

## 1. Scope of Work Audit

### 1.1 Site Count by Type

**OBSERVED** — Sheet 06 (Parcel Types) and the Addendum No. 6 bid documents are the authoritative sources. The RFP Section 6.11 explicitly states: "For pricing purposes, the site count is 155 — 144 manufactured home sites (81 single-section and 63 multi-section, per Sheet 06) and 11 RV sites."

| Type | Count | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Manufactured home — single-wide (single-section) | 81 | RFP §6.11; Sheet 06 parcel tables |
| Manufactured home — double-wide (multi-section) | 63 | RFP §6.11; Sheet 06 parcel tables |
| RV Super Sites | 11 | Sheet 06 legend; RFP §6.11 |
| **Total** | **155** | Confirmed across multiple documents |

**Phase I boundary (Sheet 06):** 62 sites — 37 single-wide, 14 double-wide, 11 RV sites (Package 1 concrete/lamps). The remaining 93 sites (44 SW, 49 DW) are Package 2 home-specific concrete/lamps.

**Site subtype details:**
- **Back-in vs. pull-through:** UNKNOWN — the plan set does not label RV sites as pull-through or back-in. The lot dimensions table on Sheet 06 shows RV Super Site lots (parcels 16, 17, 169–177) ranging from approximately 5,904 SF to 10,645 SF. Configuration cannot be determined from extracted text alone.
- **Full hookup vs. partial:** OBSERVED — all 155 sites receive individual sanitary lead/cleanout, water service/curb stop, and electrical service pedestal per RFP §4.7, §4.8, and §4.9; Certified Quantity Schedule confirms 156 curb stops and 156 cleanouts (155 sites + 1 for the maintenance building — ASSUMED). All sites are full-hookup.
- **ADA sites:** UNKNOWN — no ADA-designated site count is labeled on any sheet. The maintenance building bathroom is shown as ANSI A117.1 accessible (Exhibit D), and Sheet 10 shows ADA ramp details at sidewalks, but no specific ADA accessible home/RV site is called out on plans. This is a gap to verify against LARA/state licensing requirements.

**Gross acreage:** OBSERVED — SESC Permit No. 26-030, the geotechnical memo, and RFP all state the expansion area is approximately 30 acres. The three parcels (37-007-033-00, 37-007-032-10, 37-007-033-20) are described as totaling approximately 36 acres per the Special Use Permit (36 acres listed as "Size of Existing Parcel"), but this includes both the existing community and the expansion. The clearing/grubbing scope on Sheet 05 and the SESC plan confirm approximately 30 acres of disturbed/expansion area.

**Net developable acreage:** ASSUMED — approximately 26–28 acres net, after deducting the 20-foot Class A buffer zone (Sheet 04 notes "20' BUFFER ZONE MEETING REQUIREMENTS OF CLASS A BUFFER ALTERNATE 3"), stormwater area (existing basin +/-330,000 CFT shown on Sheets 04 and 11), road rights-of-way, and open space. Exact net acreage is not stated on the plans and would require planimetric calculation from the CAD file. Confidence: low.

**Density:** ASSUMED — 155 sites ÷ ~30 gross acres = approximately **5.2 sites/acre** gross. Net density approximately 5.5–6.0 sites/acre if net area is 26–28 acres. Confidence: moderate.

---

### 1.3 Water Source and Distribution

**OBSERVED** — RFP §4.8, Sheet 32 (Kentucky Avenue water main, STA 10+60: "EXISTING 6" WATER MAIN, 1-6"x6" TAPPING SLEEVE, VALVE & BOX"), Sheet 38 (West Side Rear Lot California Drive: "CONTRACTOR SHALL REMOVE THE EXISTING PLUG AND CONNECT THE PROPOSED WATER MAIN TO THE EXISTING WATER MAIN USING 1-6" VALVE & BOX"), and the ordinance (Z26-01, Section 3.c): "Municipal water and sewer must be provided to each lot."

**Source:** Municipal water — live tap to the existing community water main at two confirmed points (Kentucky Avenue STA 10+60; West Side Rear Lot California Drive STA 11+76). A third connection point exists at the California Drive Crossing (Sheet 39).

**Main size:** OBSERVED — all proposed water mains are **6-inch C900 PVC** throughout the expansion. No upsizing or larger mains are shown on any water main profile sheet.

**Fire flow/hydrants:** OBSERVED — 10 fire hydrants specified (Certified Quantity Schedule: "Fire Hydrant, 10 Ea"). Hydrant type: **EJ 5BR250 WaterMaster, product 55418D, 6-foot depth of bury, 6-inch mechanical joint inlet** (RFP §6.12). Hydrant locations confirmed at: Sheet 36 (Washington Avenue rear lot, STA 1+30.6 and STA 2+39.9); Sheet 42 (Tennessee Avenue rear lot, STA 0+37.5, STA 3+59.5, STA 5+88.9, STA 8+43); Sheet 43 (Oregon Avenue, STA 0+78, STA 3+00, STA 5+50). Additional hydrant locations appear on other sheets. SUP Condition 5 requires one fire hydrant installed within the existing (not expansion) development before construction commences — this is an open obligation per the Known Decisions.

**49 gate valves and boxes, 6-inch** (Certified Quantity Schedule); **1 live tap, 6-inch x 6-inch** (Certified Quantity Schedule). Confidence: high.

---

### 1.4 Wastewater

**OBSERVED** — Municipal gravity sanitary sewer. RFP §4.7: "Connection to the existing sanitary system, including any required bypass pumping of the existing system." Ordinance Z26-01, Section 3.c: "Municipal water and sewer must be provided to each lot." Sheet 15 (Oregon Avenue storm/sanitary): "EX MH #2 RIM EL 662.86, 8" IE S 647.76, 8" IE E 647.56 — CORE NEW OPENING IN MH, INSTALL KOR-N-SEAL BOOT, PR 8" IE W 647.76" — confirming connection to the existing gravity system.

**Treatment approach:** OBSERVED — **Municipal gravity sewer connection**. No lift station, no grinder pump, no package WWTP, no septic/drainfield is shown on any sheet. This is the lowest-cost wastewater approach and is confirmed by permits, ordinance, and plan sheets. The downstream capacity question (can the existing Village of Eastlake system handle 155 additional EDUs) remains an open question per the Known Decisions.

**Main sizes:** OBSERVED — Two pipe sizes in the expansion:
- **8-inch PVC** (primary collection mains along California Drive, Tennessee Avenue, Oregon Avenue, Kentucky Avenue, Minnesota Avenue, Montana Drive, Pennsylvania Avenue, Washington Avenue — all profile sheets Sheets 22–30)
- **6-inch PVC** (individual site leads per RFP §4.7 and Certified Quantity Schedule: 3,432 LF of 6-inch PVC sanitary, 156 cleanouts)

**Manholes:** OBSERVED — **31 sanitary manholes, 48-inch diameter** with Type Q covers (Certified Quantity Schedule). Confirmed on profile sheets.

---

### 1.5 Stormwater

**OBSERVED** — Combination of storm sewer pipe network and the existing stormwater basin.

**Existing basin:** OBSERVED — Sheets 04 and 11 label "EX DETENTION BASIN +/-330,000 CFT." RFP §4.6 requires "grading and shaping of the existing stormwater basin, and any basin expansion shown on the Plan Set." The Known Decisions confirm no additional detention/infiltration basins are required beyond what is shown.

**Storm sewer pipe sizes** — OBSERVED from Certified Quantity Schedule and profile sheets (Sheets 12–20):

**Storm structures:** OBSERVED from Certified Quantity Schedule:

- Drainage Structure, 48-inch dia: 19 EA
- DR Structure Casting and Cover: 30 EA

**Inlet protection:** 36 fabric-drop inlet protection devices (Certified Quantity Schedule).

**NPDES/SWPPP:** OBSERVED — EGLE NPDES Notice of Coverage MIR119192 issued July 20, 2026. SESC Permit No. 26-030 issued May 29, 2026. Both are active permits tied to construction. NPDES coverage expires May 29, 2027 (tied to SESC permit expiration) — this is an open risk flagged in the Known Decisions.

**Drain Commission approval:** Document 11_Drain_Commission_Approval.pdf is present in the materials but **could not be read** (0.0% text-extractable — entirely scanned/image). Its specific conditions are genuinely unreviewed and may contain requirements not visible in any other document in this set. Human review of the original paper or a re-scanned version is required.

---

### 1.6 Electrical

**OBSERVED** — Sheet 49 (Electrical Notes and Details) and Sheets 45–48 (Electrical Site Plans).

**Primary service:**

Two transformers/transformer pads are implied by the two panel locations (Panel #NE and Panel #G per Sheets 45, 47, 48, 49), though the exact transformer count and kVA rating are UNKNOWN — the serving utility determines transformer sizing. The riser details on Sheet 49 show the transformer-to-panel configuration as "CONDUIT AND CONDUCTORS BY ELECTRIC UTILITY (VIF)" — meaning verify-in-field.

**Site service pedestals — OBSERVED** (Certified Quantity Schedule and RFP §6.11):

**Panelboards:** OBSERVED — 2 x 100A electric panelboards (Certified Quantity Schedule: "100A Electric Panelboards, 2 Ea"). Sheet 49 shows Panel #NE (100A/3P MCB, 120/240V, 1Ø-3W) and Panel #G (100A/3P MCB, 120/240V, 1Ø-3W). Panel #G is rack-mounted on an exterior electrical rack, not building-mounted (Sheet 47 and Exhibit D).

**Street lighting:** OBSERVED — 34 light poles with fixtures (Certified Quantity Schedule: "Light Poles w/Fixture, 34 Ea"). Fixture: 80W, 240V, pole-mounted LED, described as "BASED ON BEACON VIPER" (Sheets 46–48). Pole height: 25 feet (Sheet 49 typical light pole detail: "THE HEIGHT OF THE NEW SITE LIGHTING SHALL BE THE SAME AS THE EXISTING SITE LIGHTING POLES ON THE PROPERTY, 25'-0" (VERIFY IN FIELD)"). Lighting circuits: 2-#10 AWG CU conductors + #12 GEC CU in 2-inch Schedule 40 PVC conduit (Sheets 46–48 and RFP §6.7). Total conduit: 6,000 LF (Certified Quantity Schedule). **Solar site lamps (self-contained, no utility connection):** OBSERVED — Gama Sonic Imperial III GS-97K-F on 6-ft GS-97SP post (Exhibit E). Battery replacement expected approximately every 2.5–3 years per Exhibit E manufacturer specs — long-term O&M cost for owner.

**Metering:** OBSERVED — individual utility meters at each pedestal, furnished and installed by the serving utility (RFP §6.7 matrix). Submetering is not separately shown. Individual metering means DTE/Consumers Energy bills residents directly — this is favorable for Jennings from an O&M standpoint.

**Secondary conductor to each site:** OBSERVED as uncertain — RFP §6.7 matrix: "Secondary conductor to each site — Serving utility furnishes and installs (starred as pending written confirmation)." This remains an open question per the Known Decisions. Unit prices U-45 and U-46 are required to handle the scenario where the GC must furnish/install these.

**Conduit for primary trench:** OBSERVED — GC furnishes and installs primary conduit (specified by utility) in the open trench. Quantity of primary conduit is UNKNOWN from the plan set — it depends on the serving utility's layout, which has not been confirmed in writing per the Known Decisions.

**EGC sizing for lighting circuits:** OBSERVED as potentially undersized — Sheet 49 general notes state GEC sizing per NEC Table 250.66. RFP §6.7 states "#12 GEC" for lighting circuits. The Known Decisions flag "lighting EGC sizing" as an open question — a #12 GEC may not be adequate for the panel sizes and circuit lengths involved. This needs engineer-of-record verification.

### 1.10 Engineering and Regulatory Notes

**Soil conditions — OBSERVED** (Geotechnical Memorandum, Spicer Group, May 27, 2026):
- 8 hand auger borings, 2.5–8 ft deep; 2 infiltration tests
- Topsoil: 4–12 inches
- Below topsoil: predominantly loose to medium dense fine-to-medium sand and sand with silt
- Groundwater: not encountered
- Maximum allowable bearing pressure: 2,000 lb/ft²
- Site soils: OSHA Type C, slopes 1.5H:1V maximum
- Infiltration: average 220 in/hr at most restrictive location; 322 in/hr average at other location
- SSURGO soil types: Covert sand (58B), Plainfield sand 0–6% (67B), Plainfield sand 6–12% (67C), Plainfield sand 35–70% (67F) — the 67F designation is significant: bluff-area soils with 35–70% slopes are present on the site (Sheet 03 SESC plan SSURGO table)
- No rock excavation expected

**Important geotechnical limitation:** Borings were only 2.5–8 feet deep. The memo explicitly states this "would not identify problematic layers that may exist below the bottom of the borings." Given the bluff topography and the 67F soil (35–70% slopes), this is a meaningful limitation for any retaining structures or deep utility work near the bluff edge.

**Floodplain:** OBSERVED — Special Use Permit: "Flood Zone Class: X" — meaning outside the Special Flood Hazard Area. No floodplain restrictions apply.

**Wetlands:** OBSERVED — Special Use Permit: "Wetland Area: [blank/no]." T&E Assessment confirms no wetland hydrology detected. No wetland impacts anticipated.

**Setbacks — OBSERVED** from Sheet 10 and Ordinance Z26-01:
- Front yard: 12 ft minimum
- Between adjacent structures: 10 ft minimum
- Rear: lot line, but structure must be 20 ft from adjacent structure or property line of development
- MH minimum lot: 5,000 SF with 50 ft frontage
- RV minimum lot: 4,000 SF with 40 ft frontage

**Buffer:** OBSERVED — Sheet 04: "20' BUFFER ZONE MEETING REQUIREMENTS OF CLASS A BUFFER ALTERNATE 3." This buffer is protected — no disturbance, storage, or equipment crossing allowed (RFP §4.2).

**Threatened/Endangered species:** OBSERVED — Streamside Ecological T&E Assessment (June 1, 2026): no listed species found on site. Three species of moderate likelihood (Hill's thistle, Alleghany plum, eastern box turtle) are Special Concern, not T&E. Development will not likely harm or take any State or Federally listed species. Tree clearing window for bats: October 1 – March 31.

**Special Use Permit conditions (open items):**
- SUP Condition 5: Fire hydrant in existing community required before construction — OPEN
- SUP Condition 7: Secondary access on Lot 18 — OPEN (may be emergency/maintenance only)
- SUP Condition 6: Dog park location update required — status UNKNOWN from plan set
- One-way streets must alternate direction (SUP Condition 11) — OBSERVED confirmed on Sheet 04 traffic flow arrows

**State construction permit:** OBSERVED as open — RFP §9.2: "Certain state and county approvals remain in process, including a state construction permit." The variance (FD 1201486) has been granted for 16-ft one-way roads, but the full state manufactured housing community construction permit status is unresolved per Known Decisions.

# The Bluffs on Manistee Lake — North Expansion
## AACE Class 4 Preliminary Cost Estimate
**Spicer Group File D-6631 | 155 Sites | Manistee County, Michigan**
*Non-binding preliminary estimate for owner/developer planning purposes only. Not a bid, not stamped engineering. All figures require validation by a licensed estimator with current subcontractor pricing before use in a financing model or contract.*

---

## Basis of Estimate

### Regional Labor and Material Multiplier
**OBSERVED** — Project location: Village of Eastlake, Manistee County, Michigan (confirmed on Sheet 01 cover, SESC permit, and all permit documents).

**Baseline:** RS Means 2025 national average unit costs for site/civil work, northern Lower Michigan labor market.

**Regional multiplier applied: 0.88** — RSMeans publishes a city cost index for Cadillac/Manistee County area of approximately 83–90 (national = 100). The local labor market for skilled civil trades (pipefitters, electricians, operating engineers) reflects lower prevailing wages than the Detroit or Grand Rapids metro areas, partially offset by remote-site logistics (mobilization distances for specialty subs, material haul from Traverse City or Grand Rapids). I am applying 0.88 as a blended multiplier. **Confidence: moderate.** This should be calibrated against actual sub bids when received; a 5-point swing in the multiplier (0.83–0.93) changes the estimate by approximately ±$350,000 on the hard cost total.

**Escalation:** Base pricing is calibrated to Q4 2025/Q1 2026 costs. ENR Construction Cost Index was running +4.2% annually and steel/lumber +10–11% as of mid-2026. No additional escalation is applied beyond the regional multiplier because the bid window is current (August–October 2026). If Phase 2 work extends to 2028, a 4–6% escalation reserve should be added for Phase 2 unit prices. Asphalt escalation is addressed via MDOT bituminous price index per RFP §7.7.

### OBSERVED/ASSUMED/UNKNOWN Inheritance
All quantities carry the tags from the Plan Facts stage. Where a quantity was ASSUMED or UNKNOWN there, that label is restated here and the cost line item is flagged accordingly. No silent laundering of assumed quantities into confident dollar figures.

### Scope Confirmation Gate — Amenity Buildings
Per the anti-scope-creep rule: I checked every building against what the plan set and permit documents **OBSERVED as in-scope civil construction** vs. what is merely owner-furnished or scope-to-confirm:

| Structure | In-Scope Status | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Maintenance building — site prep, utility stubs, approach/apron, surrounding concrete | **OBSERVED in civil scope** | RFP §4.16 Category 15; Sheets 06, 08, 47 |
| Maintenance building — structural slab/foundation (SP-6 through SP-9) | **OBSERVED but separately priced** | RFP §4.16; may be awarded to GC or separately; included as a contingent line |
| Maintenance building — superstructure | **OBSERVED as EXCLUDED** — owner-furnished | RFP §4.21 explicit exclusion |
| Pavilion — pad, foundation, surrounding site work | **OBSERVED in civil scope** | RFP §4.16 Category 15; Sheet 06 |
| Pavilion — structural pad requirements | **UNREVIEWED** — Exhibit C is present but entirely scanned/unreadable; pad dimensions and loads unknown | Exhibit C could not be read; not absent, genuinely unreviewed |
| Pavilion — superstructure | **OBSERVED as EXCLUDED** | RFP §4.21 |
| RV shed pads (11 sites) | **OBSERVED in civil scope** | Sheet 10 detail; RFP §4.16 |
| RV shed superstructures | **OBSERVED as EXCLUDED** | RFP §4.21 |
| Existing community building, pool | **OBSERVED as EXCLUDED** | RFP §4.21; existing parcels |
| Bathhouse/laundry | **UNKNOWN** — not shown on any plan sheet, not in any scope section | No plan sheet or permit references a new bathhouse; existing community building presumably serves both parcels; NOT included in total |
| Dump station | **UNKNOWN** — not shown on any plan sheet | NOT included in total |
| Clubhouse | **UNKNOWN** — not shown | NOT included in total |

**Decision:** Only maintenance building site work (Category 15) and RV shed pads are included in the hard cost total. Maintenance building structural slab is shown as a separate contingent line. Pavilion site work is included but at a range because Exhibit C pad requirements are unreviewed. No bathhouse, clubhouse, or dump station costs are added.

---

## Earthwork Volume — Methodology Note

**The plan text provides the engineer-certified cut/fill volumes from the Certified Quantity Schedule (Addendum 6): 25,800 CYD excavation and 18,800 CYD granular fill import.** I am pricing these quantities directly — I am not performing a naive area × depth calculation. The earthwork volume is **OBSERVED** from the certified schedule and is the most reliable quantity in this estimate. The implied net surplus of approximately 7,000 CYD (25,800 − 18,800) is priced as off-site export. Confidence: high for the scheduled quantities; moderate for whether actual conditions match the schedule (the geotechnical memo flags limited boring depth as a risk).

The geotechnical memo also identifies Plainfield sand soils (67F: 35–70% slopes) on the bluff face, confirming that the site has real topographic relief. The certified quantities reflect the EOR's CAD-based calculation, not a back-of-envelope number. I accept them at face value while carrying a contingency for differing site conditions (Finding #16 from the errors review).

---

### DIVISION 31 — Earthwork
*Mass grading, excavation, fill, import, topsoil, subgrade, dewatering*

As noted above, I am pricing the engineer-certified quantities directly. No naive area × depth substitution.

**Note on earthwork confidence:** The certified schedule gives excavation and fill volumes but does not show contour-based verification. The geotechnical memo identifies bluff-area soils with 35–70% slopes (67F SSURGO designation). The site is hilly and the EOR prepared the certified volumes from CAD. I accept them but flag moderate risk that actual cut could exceed the scheduled volume by 10–20% given the limited boring depth (2.5–8 ft) and the bluff topography — addressed in contingency.

## Contingency and Risk Allowances

### Recommended Contingency: 18%

**Justification:**
- AACE Class 4 estimates (concept screening, single data point) typically carry 15–25% contingency.
- This project has above-average uncertainty for a Class 4 because of: (a) the 7 Critical and 13 Moderate items in the error register that represent real scope/cost risks, (b) the missing electrical one-line and fire flow analysis, (c) the unreadable Drain Commission approval document, and (d) the UNKNOWN primary electrical scope.
- The geotechnical borings went only 2.5–8 ft deep on a bluff site with 35–70% slope soils — this is a meaningful subsurface risk.
- Offsetting: the certified quantity schedule provides a firm earthwork basis; all utility quantities are observed; the RFP is extremely detailed and reduces bid-interpretation risk.

| Risk Factor | Exposure | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Wastewater treatment approach | **Low** | Municipal gravity sewer confirmed; no lift station or package plant; EGLE Act 537 approval process is routine but pending; downstream capacity analysis open |
| Primary electrical service — CIAC, line extension, transformer lead time | **High** | Transformer lead times in 2026 are 12–18 months for distribution transformers; if utility has not entered the project schedule, this could delay energization and Phase 1 Substantial Completion |
| Geotechnical unknowns (rock, water table, unsuitable soils) | **Moderate** | No rock expected per geotech; no groundwater encountered in borings; but borings were shallow (2.5–8 ft) on a bluff site; 67F slope soils present; risk is moderate not high because sandy soils are actually workable and drain well |
| Stormwater and floodplain compliance | **Low-Moderate** | Flood Zone X (no floodplain); NPDES and SESC permits issued; basin design unreviewed (Drain Commission document unreadable) creates moderate risk |
| Entitlement/zoning risk | **Low** | SUP and Ordinance Z26-01 are issued and effective; state variance (FD 1201486) granted; remaining open items (hydrant in existing community, Lot 18 access) are conditions, not unresolved approvals |
| Impact fees and tap fees | **High** | Village water/sewer tap fees are completely unconfirmed; range of $232,500–$620,000 creates a $387,500 uncertainty in the project cost — the largest single unknown |
| Phasing — shared infrastructure front-loaded | **Low** | All infrastructure is Package 1; no trunk main undersizing risk because the full 155-site system is built in Phase 1; Package 2 adds only home-specific concrete as sites are sold |
| Error Register items with cost impact | **Moderate** | Critical items (#1 fire hydrant, #3 electrical scope, #4 sanitary invert, #6 water/sewer crossings, #7 emergency access) collectively represent $80,000–$250,000 of potential rework/addition if unresolved before construction |

**Contingency amount:** 18% × $8,706,887 = **$1,567,239**

**Assessment:** The pre-contingency hard cost of $56,173/site sits squarely in the published resort-tier range ($40,000–$80,000/site per RoverPass and Campground Consulting Group). This is consistent with the Benchmark Context provided at the start of this project review, which found $55,000–$58,000/site to be a normal resort-tier number. The total project cost of $81,206/site including contingency and soft costs is on the high end of the range — driven principally by three factors specific to this site: (1) a large concrete scope from the manufactured home pad and driveway specification (27,700 SYD of 6-inch concrete + 8,500 SYD of 4-inch drives is heavier than a pure RV park), (2) the deep sanitary sewer on the Oregon Avenue trunk (bluff topography driving depth costs), and (3) an above-average soft cost allocation driven by the unconfirmed utility tap fees. This project is not an outlier — it is at the upper end of a defensible resort/MH hybrid range, consistent with a 40–50-year permanent owner's specification level.

---

# The Bluffs on Manistee Lake — North Expansion
## Value-Add and Value-Engineering Analysis (Section 5)
**Building on Plan Facts and Error Register — Spicer Group D-6631, 49 Sheets**
*Preliminary AI analysis for developer and engineer of record — not stamped engineering, not a bid. All NOI deltas are directional; treat as order-of-magnitude inputs to a formal feasibility model.*

---

### Base Case Summary (from Plan Facts)

| Parameter | Base Case |
|---|---|
| Total sites | 155 (81 SW-MH, 63 DW-MH, 11 RV Super Sites) |
| Gross area | ~30 acres expansion |
| Road surface | HMA (asphalt) — 1.5" 4EL + 1.5" 5EL over 8" aggregate base |
| Road widths | Two-way: 24 ft BOC; One-way (Base Bid): 23 ft BOC; Alternate 1: 16 ft BOC |
| Wastewater | Municipal gravity sewer — 8" PVC trunk, 6" PVC laterals |
| Water | Municipal, 6" C900 PVC loop throughout |
| Electrical | 81 × 100A (E1), 63 × 200A (E2), 11 × 100A loop-fed RV (E3); 34 street lights |
| Site pads | Nonreinforced concrete — 6" slabs (MH), 4" drives, 4" stamped patios (RV) |
| Stormwater | Existing basin (+/−330,000 CFT); storm sewer network |
| Budget reference | ~$55,000–$58,000/site (from benchmark context); total ~$8.5M–$9.0M implied |

**Assumption on base cost:** The plan set does not contain a project cost summary. The $55,000–$58,000/site benchmark is used as the base case, yielding a **$8.525M–$8.99M total hard cost** for the civil/horizontal scope. All cost deltas below are against the midpoint of **$8.75M** (~$56,450/site). Confidence: low on absolute total; moderate on relative deltas between alternatives.

---

## A. Cost-Side Value Engineering

### A-1. Alternate No. 1 Road Section — 16-Foot BOC One-Way Avenues

**What changes:** The four interior one-way avenues (Minnesota, Montana, Pennsylvania, Washington) are constructed at 16 ft BOC (14 ft driving surface, two 7-ft lanes) instead of 23 ft BOC (21 ft driving surface). This is Alternate No. 1 as already designed and priced in the bid documents. The state variance (FD 1201486, September 10, 2026) has already been granted for 16-ft one-way streets.

**Quantity delta (OBSERVED from Certified Quantity Schedule):**
- Excavation reduction: 400 CYD
- Granular fill increase: 400 CYD (net earthwork change is minor)
- Aggregate base reduction: 500 tons
- HMA 4EL reduction: 100 tons
- HMA 5EL reduction: 200 tons
- Storm sewer 12" HDPE reduction: 20 LF

**Estimated cost delta:**
- Aggregate base (~$35/ton): −$17,500
- HMA 4EL (~$120/ton): −$12,000
- HMA 5EL (~$130/ton): −$26,000
- Storm sewer 12" (~$50/LF): −$1,000
- Net earthwork: negligible (±$3,000)
- **Total hard cost deduct: approximately −$56,000 to −$60,000**
- **Soft cost: $0 — alternate is already designed and priced**

**Revenue/NOI delta:** None — site count, hookups, and site experience are unchanged. Road narrowing is barely perceptible to residents once homes are set (the one-way avenues are front-of-home service roads, not through routes). No rent impact expected. Confidence: high.

**Schedule impact:** None — alternate is already in the bid documents.

**Regulatory/engineering constraint:** Variance already granted. Two-way spine roads (California Drive, Tennessee Avenue, Oregon Avenue, Kentucky Avenue) remain at full width — fire apparatus access is maintained on the spines. Confirmed: Village ordinance Z26-01 Section 3.d explicitly permits 16-ft one-way streets. The only constraint is the Error Register finding #12 (lane-width label on Sheet 10 must be corrected before paving).

**Recommendation: ACCEPT.** This is the easiest, lowest-risk cost reduction available. Already designed, already approved. The deduct is modest but clean. Elect Alternate No. 1 at award.

**Return on incremental capital:** N/A (pure cost reduction, no capital deployment). Ranking: #1 by simplicity.

---

### A-2. Joint-Trenching — Rear-Lot Utility Corridor Consolidation

**What changes:** The plan currently runs rear-lot water mains in separate trenches from the sanitary sewer laterals and the site electrical service conduit. All three utilities share the same rear-lot corridor (confirmed in Plan Facts: water mains are rear-lot on most avenues). Michigan code (Act 399, NEC, and MDOT separation requirements) permits water, sanitary, and electrical to share a common trench provided minimum separations are maintained (18-inch vertical between water and sewer, 12-inch horizontal between electrical and water). A joint-trench design would run all three in a single trench cut, dramatically reducing excavation, backfill, surface restoration, and crew mobilization per run.

**Estimated savings (ASSUMED — joint trench vs. separate trench for rear-lot runs):**
- Rear-lot water main: approximately 5,760 LF (7,610 LF total minus the Kentucky Ave and Oregon Ave road-alignment runs — ASSUMED)
- Current separate trench cost per LF: ASSUMED $35–$55/LF all-in (excavation + bedding + backfill + restoration) × 3 separate trenches = $105–$165/LF combined
- Joint trench cost per LF: ASSUMED $55–$80/LF (wider trench, same mobilization, better bedding management)
- Savings per LF: approximately $50–$85/LF
- Over 5,760 LF: **savings approximately $288,000–$490,000**
- Soft cost: EOR redesign of utility corridor plan showing joint-trench details and separation callouts: ASSUMED $8,000–$15,000

**Net estimated delta: −$273,000 to −$475,000 hard cost + soft cost**

**Revenue/NOI delta:** None — no change to site count, hookups, or amenities.

**Schedule impact:** Net positive — one trench crew instead of three sequential crews; reduces the trench-phase duration by an estimated 2–4 weeks. This directly compresses the critical path to Phase 1 Substantial Completion.

**Regulatory/engineering constraint:**
- Act 399 crossing separation (18" water above sewer) must be maintained — requires EOR to issue a joint-trench detail with explicit separation callouts (this also addresses Error Register Finding #19).
- NEC Article 300 and applicable utility standards must be confirmed with Consumers Energy and DTE for electrical conduit in a shared trench.
- This change requires EOR to redesign the utility plan to show the joint-trench corridor — a plan amendment is needed, but no agency resubmittal is required for Act 399 approval if separations are maintained.
- EGLE Act 399 submission should include the joint-trench detail.

**Recommendation: ACCEPT.** This is the largest single cost-reduction lever available and is quality-neutral for a permanent owner (buried utilities in a joint trench perform identically to separate trenches if separation requirements are met). The savings range is wide because the extracted plan set does not give individual trench costs, but even at the low end ($273,000) this is the most impactful VE item after the Alternate No. 1 road section.

**Confidence on delta: Low-Moderate** — the savings magnitude depends on current unit prices (not in the extracted documents) and the exact joint-trench width achievable given MDOT separation requirements. An EOR-issued joint-trench design is the prerequisite.

**Plan amendment required:** Yes — joint-trench detail and revised utility corridor plan. No agency resubmittal required if separations meet Act 399.

---

### A-3. Stormwater — Infiltration/LID Credit to Reduce Pipe Sizes

**What changes:** The geotechnical memo (May 27, 2026) reports extraordinary infiltration rates: average 220–322 inches/hour at the two test locations (SSURGO Plainfield sand, Group A soils). The current storm sewer system runs 1,590 LF of 12" HDPE up to 270 LF of 36" HDPE. With Plainfield sand at these infiltration rates, the site qualifies for LID credit under Michigan's EGLE stormwater management framework — specifically, bioretention or infiltration trenches along the road edges could reduce the design storm runoff coefficient and potentially downsize downstream pipe segments.

**Estimated savings if downstream pipes (30" and 36" segments) can be reduced by one size:**
- 36" HDPE reduction → 30": 270 LF × (say $30/LF price differential) = $8,100
- 30" HDPE reduction → 24": 650 LF × (say $20/LF differential) = $13,000
- LID feature construction (infiltration trenches, swales): ASSUMED $15,000–$35,000
- Engineering for LID analysis and Drain Commission coordination: ASSUMED $10,000–$20,000
- **Net delta: approximately −$6,000 to +$10,000** (marginally positive to marginally negative)

**Revenue/NOI delta:** None.

**Schedule impact:** Potentially extends design phase by 4–8 weeks for LID analysis and Drain Commission coordination. Net negative schedule impact.

**Regulatory/engineering constraint:** Drain Commission approval document is unreadable (scanned) — its conditions may already require the current pipe sizes or may restrict LID alternatives. The Drain Commission must be consulted before any pipe sizing change. EGLE Act 399 would need to review if storm sewer is connected to sanitary system outfall area.

**Recommendation: REJECT for this project.** The savings are small relative to the engineering, coordination, and schedule risk. The Drain Commission approval document's unknown conditions are a gating constraint. For a permanent owner, the existing pipe sizing provides robust long-term capacity; downsizing to save $20,000 while adding $30,000 in engineering and 2 months of schedule delay is not a good trade on a $8.75M project. Jennings should not optimize stormwater at the expense of schedule when the SESC permit expires May 29, 2027.

---

### A-4. Eliminate Integral Asphalt Curb on One-Way Avenues — Use Swales

**What changes:** The one-way interior avenues currently specify integral asphalt curb (7-inch, shown on Sheet 10 cross-section). Eliminating curb in favor of a 3:1 grassed shoulder/swale on one-way avenues would reduce HMA tonnage (curb is included in the HMA pricing per RFP §4.11) and potentially allow some storm sewer lateral lengths to be shortened (surface drainage replaces piped drainage for one-way-avenue frontage). This approach is common in MH communities in rural Michigan.

**Estimated savings:**
- Integral asphalt curb elimination on four one-way avenues (~2,604 LF total × 2 sides = ~5,208 LF equivalent): ASSUMED $3–$6/LF savings on HMA material = $15,000–$31,000 hard cost reduction
- Potential storm sewer lateral reduction: ASSUMED minor (storm sewer is primarily driven by the larger basin drainage, not curb-line collection) — benefit unclear without hydraulic model
- Topsoil and seeding for swale shoulders: ASSUMED $2–$4/LF × 5,208 LF = $10,000–$21,000 added cost
- **Net delta: approximately −$5,000 to +$6,000** — effectively neutral

**Revenue/NOI delta:** Slight negative aesthetic impact — swales vs. curbed roads look less polished in a resort-tier 55+ community. This matters for the market positioning argument (see Section B).

**Long-term O&M for Jennings:** Swales require periodic mowing and regrading; integral curb requires no maintenance once set. Over a 40-year ownership horizon, curb is the better long-term choice even if first cost is marginally higher.

**Regulatory/engineering constraint:** Drainage must not pond against home pads. On the bluff topography with 67F soils, swales on steeper lots may erode. Would require EOR grading analysis.

**Recommendation: REJECT.** For a permanent owner: (1) the savings are negligible; (2) the 40-year maintenance cost of swale mowing and re-grading exceeds the first-cost savings; (3) curbed roads look better in a resort-tier community and support the premium-rent positioning; (4) the bluff terrain and silty sand soils create erosion risk in open swales that a permanent owner will have to manage indefinitely. This is the textbook "saves today, costs forever" trade that the ground rules require flagging explicitly.

---

### A-5. Pedestal Specification — Standardize Single-Wide Sites to 100A Only

**What changes:** Currently, all 81 single-wide sites use E1 (100A, 1-phase). This is already correctly sized for single-wide manufactured homes (single-section homes typically have 100A electrical service). No change is proposed here — the existing specification is already appropriate. No savings available from downgrading single-wide pedestals without reducing resident quality of life. **This sub-item is clean in the base plan — no recommendation.**

However, the **RV pedestals (E3)** are specified as 100A loop-fed with 50A/30A/20A receptacles per Sheet 46 key note. This is the correct RV resort-tier specification and matches the "RV Super Site" premium positioning. Downgrading to 30A/20A-only (common at basic parks) would save approximately $200–$400 per RV pedestal ($2,200–$4,400 for 11 units) but would immediately prevent the site from attracting Class A motorhomes and 5th wheels — which are the primary residents of RV Super Sites at this price point. **Reject this downgrade** for a permanent owner targeting premium RV rents.

---

### A-6. Aggregate Base Specification — Confirm 8-Inch Is Not Over-Specified

**What changes:** Sheet 10 specifies 8-inch aggregate base (modified) under all roads. The geotechnical memo (May 27, 2026) states: "The site soils will provide good pavement support. Due to the free-draining nature of the soils, a sand subbase layer is not necessary." This suggests the geotechnical recommendation supports the absence of a separate sand subbase, but the 8-inch aggregate base itself is a standard Michigan road specification for this traffic class. MDOT standard for residential street pavement sections with light-to-medium traffic (up to approximately 50,000 ESALs) typically uses 6-inch aggregate base over good granular subgrade. Upgrading to 8 inches provides a margin over the minimum.

**Estimated savings if reduced to 6-inch aggregate base:**
- Certified Quantity Schedule: 8,800 tons aggregate base
- Reduction to 6-inch: approximately 8,800 × (6/8) = 6,600 tons; savings of ~2,200 tons
- At ASSUMED $35/ton in-place: **savings approximately $77,000**
- No soft cost for a note-change; EOR should confirm in a field directive

**Long-term O&M impact for Jennings:** A 6-inch base over Plainfield sand (free-draining, non-frost-susceptible) is defensible per the geotechnical memo. However, MH transport vehicles (tri-axle lowboys, up to 80,000 lbs GVW) and the crane/set crew equipment impose significantly higher axle loads than residential traffic. A single loaded MH transport on a soft-base road can create ruts that are costly to repair before final paving. The 8-inch base provides a meaningful margin against this specific loading case.

**Recommendation: HOLD — do not reduce aggregate base.** For a permanent owner operating a community that will see repeated heavy-vehicle movements over decades (re-sets, replacements, deliveries), the 2-inch base upgrade is worth its cost. The geotechnical memo supports good subgrade, but that memo was based on 8-ft borings — the EOR's base thickness decision likely accounts for the MH transport loading. This is one case where the "saves today, costs forever" principle applies: a rut repair or base failure under a loaded MH transport is a $5,000–$20,000 repair event plus community disruption. Not a recommended reduction.

---

### A-7. Solar Site Lamp Battery Replacement — Life-Cycle Cost Check

**What changes (operational, not capital):** The Gama Sonic GS-97K-F specification (Exhibit E) states batteries require replacement approximately every 2.5–3 years. At 155 expansion sites + 95 existing sites = 250 total lamps, and a battery replacement cost of ASSUMED $40–$80 per lamp (Gama Sonic replacement batteries), the owner's recurring cost is:
- 250 lamps ÷ 2.75 years average life = 91 lamps/year needing replacement
- At $60/lamp battery + ASSUMED $30/lamp labor = $90/lamp × 91 lamps = **$8,190/year recurring O&M**

This is not a capital savings item — it is an ongoing operating expense the owner should budget. For a permanent owner over 40 years, the total battery replacement cost is approximately **$328,000 in nominal dollars** (not discounted). This is material and should be in the 5-year operating budget from day one.

**Alternative:** Grid-tied LED street lamps (already specified for the 34 street-light poles) are maintenance-free except for lamp replacement at approximately 50,000-hour lamp life. The solar site lamps are self-contained by design choice (avoiding trenching to 155 individual sites). This is the right engineering decision — the alternative of running conduit to 155 individual site lamps would cost $400,000–$800,000 in trenching and conductor. The battery cost is the correct trade-off. **Budget the battery replacement; do not change the system.**

---

### A-8. Pipe Class Verification — PVC C900 vs. C905

**What changes:** All water mains are specified as 6-inch C900 PVC (OBSERVED throughout Sheets 32–43). C900 is the correct pressure class for a 6-inch distribution main in a residential community — it is rated at 200 psi working pressure (Class 150) or 165 psi (Class 150 DR18). This is not over-specified for this application. **The pipe class is appropriate — no change recommended.**

Sanitary sewer is specified as PVC "Trench Detail B2" — a standard Michigan gravity sewer specification. No over-specification identified. **Clean in this category.**

---

### A-9. Earthwork Balance — Eliminate Import/Export Through Grading Revision

**What changes:** The Certified Quantity Schedule shows 25,800 CYD excavation and 18,800 CYD granular fill import, implying a net surplus of approximately 7,000 CYD to be exported off-site. Topsoil is furnished (not stripped and reused) per RFP §6.2. If the grading plan can be revised to use the 7,000 CYD surplus as fill in low areas rather than exporting it, the export cost (typically $15–$30/CYD truck, haul, and tipping) is eliminated.

**Estimated savings:**
- Export elimination: 7,000 CYD × ASSUMED $22/CYD = **$154,000 savings**
- Offset: grading revisions may require additional cut in some areas or slight pad elevation changes — ASSUMED $30,000–$50,000 in design and earthwork adjustment
- **Net delta: approximately −$104,000 to −$124,000**

**Constraints:** The site is on a bluff with irregular terrain. Regrading to retain all cut material means raising some pad elevations — which affects the MH transport delivery geometry, pad-to-road drainage, and potentially the utility depth profiles. The geotechnical memo confirmed free-draining sandy soils — fill compaction to 95% Proctor is achievable if moisture-conditioned. However, the surplus material likely contains the silty sand layers identified in some borings (HA01, HA03, HA06) which are not suitable for structural fill under pads or roads. Only the clean sand cut should be considered for reuse.

**Recommendation: PURSUE WITH EOR.** Ask the EOR to evaluate whether grading revisions can eliminate 50%–100% of the export (approximately $77,000–$154,000 savings) without compromising pad elevations, drainage, or utility depths. This is a low-risk, high-return conversation that costs only EOR time. If even 50% of the export can be eliminated, the savings pay for the analysis. Confidence on delta: moderate.

**Plan amendment required:** Yes — revised grading plan. No agency resubmittal required unless SESC-controlled areas are affected.

---

### A-10. Maintenance Building Foundation — Select Prefabricated Option

**What changes:** The RFP offers four foundation options (SP-6 through SP-9): stick-built, prefabricated metal, prefabricated wood frame, modular. The base plan prices these separately. For a 32×40-ft maintenance/storage building (Group U occupancy, no habitation, minimal code requirements), a prefabricated metal building on a slab-on-grade is the lowest-cost, fastest, and most durable option for a permanent owner. Typical cost differential: stick-built foundation + slab: ASSUMED $25,000–$40,000; prefab metal foundation + slab: ASSUMED $12,000–$20,000.

**Estimated savings: −$13,000 to −$20,000 on foundation/slab; building itself is owner-furnished.**

**Recommendation: ACCEPT.** Elect the prefabricated metal building option (SP-7) at award. The GC's slab and foundation scope becomes simpler and faster. Prefab metal buildings for maintenance use are highly durable — matching Jennings' 40–50-year ownership horizon.

---

## B. Revenue-Side Value-Add

### B-1. Site Density — Can Site Count Increase?

**Current layout:** 155 sites on approximately 30 gross acres = 5.2 sites/acre gross.

**Potential density increase analysis:**

The parcel dimension tables on Sheet 06 show several irregular areas that may not be optimally allocated:

1. **Open Space zone** (Sheet 04, northwest corner near bluff): Labeled "OPEN SPACE" — this area is adjacent to the bluff (67F soils, 35–70% slopes). Development here would require geotechnical analysis of slope stability, bluff setbacks, and potentially EGLE coastal/bluff review. **This area should not be developed for home sites.** Retain as amenity/view space.

2. **Proposed parking areas** (multiple locations, Sheets 06–09): The SUP explicitly states "Proposed parking lots may be constructed as needed but are not required to be installed at this time." If any parking areas represent underutilized land that could accept 1–3 additional home sites, a layout revision could recapture them. ASSUMED potential: **3–6 additional sites** if two or three parking lots are relocated to less prime positions.

3. **Corner lots with excess area:** Several corner parcels (e.g., parcel 35 at 11,672 SF, parcel 44 at 10,796 SF, parcel 204 at 10,237 SF) are substantially larger than the 5,000 SF minimum. If lot lines are adjusted, some of these oversized corners could be split to create one additional site — but lot-line changes require MHC review and SUP amendment.

**Realistic density increase without a full redesign:** ASSUMED **5–8 additional sites** through lot-line adjustment at oversized corner lots and minor parking reconfiguration. This requires:
- EOR lot layout revision (ASSUMED $15,000–$25,000 design cost)
- Village ZA plan amendment (SUP Condition 12 requires review of modifications)
- MHC license amendment for additional home sites

**Estimated revenue impact (directional):**
- ASSUMED market rent for MH sites in a 55+, lakefront-adjacent Michigan community: **$650–$900/month** (this is a directional estimate based on general market knowledge for northern Lower Michigan manufactured housing communities — no comp study is available in this document set; treat as directional only).
- Additional 6 sites × $750/month average × 12 months × 95% stabilized occupancy = **$51,300/year additional gross revenue**
- At a 7% cap rate: **$732,857 added asset value**
- At 8% cap rate: **$641,250 added asset value**
- Incremental capital cost for 6 sites × ~$50,000/site development = $300,000
- **Return on incremental capital: approximately 14%–17% (before debt service)**

**Recommendation: PURSUE.** Even at a conservative 6 additional sites, the return on incremental development capital is compelling for a long-term owner. The design cost is the only upfront hurdle. However, this cannot be initiated without the EOR's lot conformance table (Error Register Finding #18) confirming which corner lots have surplus area.

**Plan amendment required:** Yes — lot layout revision, SUP plan amendment, MHC license amendment.

---

### B-2. Premium Site Designation and Rent Tiering

**What changes:** The plan treats all single-wide sites identically and all double-wide sites identically. In practice, lakefront-adjacent, corner, and end-of-avenue sites command 10%–20% rent premiums in resort-tier MH communities. The current 11 RV Super Sites (parcels 16, 17, 169–177) are the natural premium tier, but within the MH sites there are clearly superior positions (bluff-view lots, end lots with more privacy, corner lots with larger areas) that are not differentiated.

**Revenue impact (directional):**
- Identify the top 20 single-wide and 15 double-wide lots as "premium" (based on location relative to bluff, end-of-street, corner, or oversized)
- ASSUMED premium rent differential: +$75–$125/month over standard lots
- 35 premium sites × $100/month premium × 12 months × 95% occupancy = **$39,900/year additional gross revenue**
- At 7.5% cap rate: **$532,000 added asset value**
- Capital cost: $0 (this is a marketing and operations decision, not a construction change)
- **Return on incremental capital: infinite (zero additional capital)**

**Recommendation: ACCEPT immediately.** This is purely an operational/marketing decision that requires no plan change, no EOR involvement, and no agency approval. The only action needed is for the Owner's Representative to designate premium sites on the as-built site plan before lot leases are offered. Tier the RV Super Sites as a third, highest rent tier.

---

### B-3. RV Site Mix — Add Transient/Short-Term RV Capacity

**What changes:** The current 11 RV Super Sites are sized and designed for long-term (seasonal or annual) RV residents — large concrete pads, full hookup (water/sewer/electric), covered shed. The community is a 55+ manufactured housing community with an RV component, not an RV resort. However, the Ordinance Z26-01 Section 1 explicitly includes "transient, 55 and older RV guests with seasonal lifestyles" as a purpose. If the 11 RV sites are marketed as transient/seasonal rentals (weekly or monthly rates) rather than annual leases, revenue per site is substantially higher.

**Revenue comparison (directional):**
- Annual lease at $600–$800/month = $7,200–$9,600/year per RV site
- Transient/seasonal at $150–$250/night at 70% seasonal occupancy (120 nights May–September) + shoulder-season monthly rentals (6 months × $700/month = $4,200) = $12,600–$18,200/year per RV site
- Premium (transient) vs. annual: +$3,400–$8,600/site/year × 11 sites = **+$37,400–$94,600/year gross revenue premium**
- At 7.5% cap rate: **$499,000–$1,261,000 added asset value** vs. annual-lease approach
- Capital cost: $0 (same infrastructure; requires reservation system and management protocol)

**Constraint:** The 55+ age restriction (at least one occupant per unit must be 55 or older) applies to transient guests under the SUP. This limits the transient market but does not eliminate it — the 55+ RV traveler demographic is large and growing.

**Recommendation: ACCEPT for operational consideration.** The Owner should decide at stabilization whether to operate RV sites as transient/seasonal or annual. This does not affect construction. The infrastructure (full hookup, large pad, 100A loop-fed pedestal with 50A receptacle) is correct for either use case.

---

### B-4. Ancillary Revenue — Specific Items for This Site

**Items that move revenue for a lakefront 55+ community in northern Michigan (ranked by confidence):**

| Item | Capital Cost | Annual Revenue (Directional) | NOI at 7.5% Cap | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Boat/RV storage — paved lot west of bluff edge | $80,000–$150,000 | $40,000–$80,000 | $533,000–$1,067,000 | Low — requires site area and zoning review |
| Wi-Fi backbone — fiber to the site + community network | $30,000–$60,000 | $8,000–$20,000 (bulk billing premium) | $107,000–$267,000 | Moderate |
| Laundry (coin/app-pay, 4–6 machines) | $20,000–$35,000 | $8,000–$15,000 | $107,000–$200,000 | Moderate |
| Pavilion rental for events | $0 additional (pavilion is in plans) | $5,000–$15,000 | $67,000–$200,000 | Moderate |
| Dog park (required by SUP — no incremental capital vs. compliance cost) | $5,000–$20,000 | $0 direct; retention/marketing value | N/A direct | High for retention |
| Propane distribution (bulk tank + sub-meters) | $40,000–$80,000 | $15,000–$30,000 (margin on propane sales) | $200,000–$400,000 | Low — DTE gas distribution is already planned; propane would replace gas for residents not on natural gas |
| Dump station with fee (outside users) | $8,000–$15,000 | $3,000–$8,000 | $40,000–$107,000 | Low — no dump station in current plans; requires ADA-accessible route |
| Pickleball courts (2 courts) | $25,000–$40,000 | $0 direct; +$30–$50/month rent premium on adjacent sites | $40,000–$67,000 (on 20 adjacent sites) | Moderate for 55+ market |

**Items that do NOT move rent for this market:**
- **Pool:** A pool at a 55+ community in northern Michigan with a 5-month operating season costs $50,000–$120,000 to build and $15,000–$30,000/year to operate. The existing community already has a pool (shown on Sheets 04/05) — residents of the expansion will have access to it. A second pool would duplicate an amenity already provided and is not recommended.
- **Playground:** This is a 55+ community — a playground generates no value and may conflict with the 55+ brand.
- **Fitness center:** Modest value for 55+ — equipment room inside the community building is sufficient; a standalone building is not justified at this density.

**Top ancillary revenue recommendation:** Wi-Fi backbone (highest confidence, lowest capital, fastest payback) + laundry (time-tested MH community revenue) + pavilion rental program (zero incremental capital).

---

### B-5. Utility Submetering — Water and Sewer Pass-Through

**What changes:** Individual electric metering is already designed (utility meters at every pedestal — RFP §6.7). Water services have individual curb stops at each site (156 curb stops per Certified Quantity Schedule). If individual water meters are installed at each site, the owner can pass water/sewer costs directly to residents rather than including them in site rent — converting a variable operating expense to a resident expense.

**Revenue/NOI impact (directional):**
- ASSUMED water/sewer cost per site: $40–$80/month in a small Michigan community with municipal rates
- At $60/month average × 155 sites × 12 months = $111,600/year currently an owner expense
- Individual water metering + billing converts this to a resident expense
- **NOI improvement: +$111,600/year** (same rent, lower expenses)
- At 7.5% cap rate: **$1,488,000 added asset value**

**Capital cost:** Individual water meters at each of 155 sites:
- Meter + meter box: ASSUMED $200–$400 each
- Installation (at time of water service installation — minimal added cost): ASSUMED $150–$250 each
- Billing system or RUBS (ratio utility billing system) setup: ASSUMED $5,000–$15,000
- **Total capital: approximately $54,000–$101,000 for 155 meters**
- **Return on incremental capital: ~111% (payback < 1 year)**

**Constraint:** Michigan state regulations for manufactured housing communities require specific billing practices for utility pass-through (see Michigan Manufactured Housing Commission Act). Water meters must be AWWA-rated. Billing must comply with Public Service Commission rules if utility is resold. Owner must verify whether the Village of Eastlake's water rates permit individual metering with pass-through billing or require a master meter arrangement.

**Recommendation: ACCEPT — highest ROI item in this entire analysis.** Install individual water meters at every site during water service installation (the curb stop and service line are already in the base plan — adding a meter at this stage adds minimal cost). The payback is under 12 months on a $111,600/year NOI improvement. This is unambiguously the best single capital decision available to Jennings.

**Plan amendment required:** Add water meter specification to the water main plan; no agency resubmittal required if meters are within the individual service lines (metering is downstream of the curb stop, entirely on the owner-side of the connection).

---

### B-6. Resort Classification and Rent Premium

**What changes:** The combination of lakefront-adjacent location, bluff views, full-hookup sites, 55+ designation, resort amenities (pavilion, pool, Wi-Fi, landscaping), and the concrete pad/solar lamp standard creates a community that can legitimately be marketed at the top of the northern Michigan MH/RV market. The rent premium for "resort-classified" vs. "standard" MH communities in Michigan is ASSUMED 20%–35% over comparable non-amenity communities (directional estimate from general market knowledge — no comp study available).

**Specific design elements that support premium positioning (and therefore must not be value-engineered away):**
- Concrete pads at every site (not gravel — do not substitute)
- Curbed roads (not swale edges — reject A-4 above)
- 34 street lights on 25-ft poles (maintain full lighting plan)
- Solar site lamps at every site (maintain — creates consistent site aesthetics)
- 6-ft privacy fence (maintain — creates separation from adjacent parcels)
- Stamped concrete RV patios (maintain — visual differentiator from commodity RV parks)
- 50A RV pedestals (maintain — required for Class A market)

**Any value engineering that compromises these visual and functional quality markers will damage the resort-tier rent premium and is rejected on life-cycle grounds even if first-cost savings appear attractive.**

---

## C. Phasing and Capital Alternatives

### C-1. Current Phasing Assessment

The Addendum No. 6 two-package structure (Package 1: all infrastructure + paving + 62-site concrete/lamps; Package 2: 93-site concrete/lamps as homes are sold) is sound and well-designed. It correctly:
- Front-loads all shared infrastructure (roads, utilities, storm sewer, water/sewer) for the full 155-site build-out
- Defers the largest single cost item (home-specific concrete at 93 sites × ~$15,000–$20,000/site = $1.4M–$1.9M) until homes are sold and revenue is generating
- Allows the owner to open and begin filling homes at the 62 Phase I sites while Phase 2 sites are released in batches

**Minimum viable Phase 1 to open and cash-flow:** The current Package 1 definition (62 sites fully improved + all infrastructure) is already the minimum viable opening. Opening with fewer than ~50 sites would not cover fixed operating costs (manager, utilities, maintenance) at typical MH community expense ratios. The 62-site Phase 1 is appropriate.

**Critical shared infrastructure that must NOT be phased:** All backbone infrastructure is correctly in Package 1:
- Full water loop (7,610 LF) — CORRECT; a partial loop would create dead-ends without fire flow
- Full sanitary trunk (5,964 LF of 8" PVC) — CORRECT; partial sewer would require abandonment and reinstallation
- All paving (first course on all roads) — CORRECT; MH transport delivery requires trafficable roads to all sites before any home can be set
- Street lighting (34 poles) — CORRECT; required for LARA licensing and Phase 1 Substantial Completion

### C-2. Options to Expand Phase 1 Site Count

**Option:** Move 10–15 double-wide sites from Package 2 to Package 1 (add their home-specific concrete and lamps to the first construction season).

**Rationale:** Double-wide homes generate ~2× the rent of single-wide ($900–$1,200/month vs. $650–$800/month — directional). Getting more double-wide sites open in Year 1 accelerates NOI ramp-up.

**Capital impact:** 15 additional DW sites × ASSUMED $18,000/site (pad, driveway, garage slab, solar lamp) = $270,000 additional Package 1 capital.

**Revenue impact:** 15 additional DW sites × $1,000/month × 12 months × 85% first-year occupancy = $153,000/year additional revenue in Year 1 vs. waiting for Package 2 batch release.

**At 7.5% cap rate and 85% occupancy: $2,040,000 incremental asset value vs. $270,000 incremental capital = 7.5× multiple on incremental capital.** Even accounting for carrying cost on the $270,000, this is strongly positive.

**Recommendation: CONSIDER.** Owner should evaluate cash availability and home pre-sales pipeline. If even 10 double-wide homes are pre-sold or pre-committed before NTP, accelerating their pads into Package 1 makes strong financial sense. This requires no plan amendment — Package 2 prices already cover double-wide sites.

### C-3. Infrastructure Sizing — Future Expansion Optionality

**What the current plan does right:** The water main loop is sized at 6-inch throughout — adequate for 155 sites but at or near the hydraulic limit for fire flow (see Error Register Finding #9). If the existing community or a future northern expansion adds sites, the 6-inch system may become inadequate. The Kentucky Avenue live tap is a single 6-inch connection to the existing system. **A second 6-inch tap or an 8-inch connection to a larger municipal main should be evaluated by the EOR as part of the hydraulic analysis (Finding #9) — the additional cost to install an 8-inch tap now vs. retrofitting later is significant.**

**What forecloses expansion:** The dead-end water mains at Minnesota Avenue (STA 4+45) and Washington Avenue (STA 8+17) are plugged. If northern expansion is contemplated, the plugs should be capped with valves rather than plugs — the incremental cost is negligible (ASSUMED $500–$1,500 per location) and preserves the ability to extend the loop northward without excavation and hot-tap work.

**Stormwater basin:** The existing basin at +/−330,000 CFT is on the existing community parcel, not the expansion parcel. If the expansion generates runoff in excess of what the basin can handle for a future enlarged development, a second basin or basin expansion would be needed. The Drain Commission approval document (unreadable) may address this. **Owner must read the Drain Commission conditions before any future expansion planning.** No immediate capital action recommended.

**Electrical:** Both panels (Panel #NE and Panel #G) are 100A, 1-phase, 3-wire sub-panels. If the community expands beyond 155 sites, additional panels and transformer pads will be required. The current panel locations on Sheet 45 appear to have physical space for an additional rack — no optionality cost required now.

### C-4. Developer-Owned Utilities — Asset or Liability?

**Water and sewer:** Already municipal — this is the optimal arrangement for a permanent owner. Municipal systems eliminate the capital cost and long-term liability of a private WWTP or well. **No change recommended.**

**Natural gas (DTE):** DTE is designing, furnishing, and installing the gas distribution. The GC's scope is trenching only. This is correctly structured — the developer does not own the gas infrastructure. **No change recommended.**

**Propane alternative:** REJECTED. Installing a bulk propane system alongside DTE natural gas would create two competing fuel systems on the site, complicate future utility billing, require an above-ground tank (aesthetic issue in a resort-tier community), and add a fire risk. DTE natural gas is the correct long-term choice.

**Electrical:** The serving utility (Consumers Energy) owns and installs the primary distribution and transformers. The GC installs only secondary trench, conduit, and site pedestals. This is the correct arrangement — the developer does not bear transformer replacement cost. **No change recommended.**

---

## Recommended Alternative Plan

The following five changes, applied together, define the recommended revised program:

### Top 5 Changes

**Change 1: Elect Alternate No. 1 (16-ft BOC one-way avenues)**
- Already designed, already approved, zero plan amendment needed
- Savings: −$56,000 to −$60,000 hard cost
- Confidence: High

**Change 2: Design and implement joint-trench utility corridor for rear-lot runs**
- EOR issues joint-trench detail; all rear-lot water, sewer lateral, and electrical service in common trench
- Savings: −$273,000 to −$475,000 hard cost; −$8,000 to −$15,000 soft cost (EOR design)
- Plan amendment required: yes (no agency resubmittal if Act 399 separations maintained)
- Confidence: Low-Moderate on magnitude; High on direction

**Change 3: Install individual water meters at all 155 sites during water service installation**
- Add AWWA-rated meter and meter box at each service; set up billing system
- Incremental capital: +$54,000–$101,000
- Annual NOI improvement: +$111,600/year (converts water/sewer from owner expense to resident expense)
- Asset value created at 7.5% cap: +$1,488,000
- Payback: < 12 months
- Confidence: Moderate (contingent on Village of Eastlake billing rules)

**Change 4: Grading revision to eliminate or reduce surplus export (50%–100% of 7,000 CYD)**
- EOR evaluates which cut material can be reused as fill without compromising pad or road subgrade
- Savings: −$77,000 to −$154,000 hard cost (at 50%–100% elimination)
- EOR design cost: ASSUMED $5,000–$12,000
- Plan amendment required: revised grading plan; no agency resubmittal
- Confidence: Moderate

**Change 5: Designate premium sites and tier rents at zero additional capital cost**
- Identify top 20 SW and 15 DW lots as premium; tier at +$100/month premium rent
- Annual revenue increase: +$39,900/year
- Asset value at 7.5% cap: +$532,000
- Capital cost: $0
- Plan amendment required: none
- Confidence: Moderate (market rent is directional without a comp study)

---

### Recommended Program Summary

| Net cost delta (with meters) | — | −$329,000 to −$612,000 | — |
| Total estimated cost | ~$8,750,000 | ~$8,138,000–$8,421,000 | −$329,000 to −$612,000 |
| Cost per site | ~$56,450 | ~$52,500–$54,330 | −$2,120 to −$3,950/site |
| Annual NOI improvement | — | +$151,500/year (water meters + premium sites) | +$151,500/year |
| Asset value created (7.5% cap) | — | +$2,020,000 | — |

**Note on rejected alternatives:** The following were explicitly evaluated and rejected for a permanent owner:
- Chip seal or gravel road surface (rejected: 40-year maintenance and liability cost exceeds first-cost savings)
- Swale edges replacing curb on one-way avenues (rejected: 40-year mowing/regrading cost; aesthetic damage to resort positioning)
- Reducing aggregate base to 6 inches (rejected: MH transport loading creates rut risk on undercutting the base)
- Downgrading RV pedestal from 50A combo to 30A/20A (rejected: eliminates Class A RV market)
- Pool addition (rejected: existing pool already serves both communities)
- Propane system alongside natural gas (rejected: redundant, liability, aesthetic issue)
- LID infiltration for storm sewer downsizing (rejected: marginal savings, schedule risk, unknown Drain Commission conditions)

## Preliminary Assumptions and Market Calibration

**Market rent basis (all directional — grade D unless otherwise noted):**
No published Datacomp/JLT rent survey data for Manistee County MH communities was accessible during this review. The following are inferred from:
- Michigan MHI published average MH community lot rent of approximately $550–$650/month statewide (Michigan Manufactured Housing Association, 2024 — unverified URL; grade B-borderline)

**Occupancy assumption:** 90% stabilized (Year 2–3), 75% Year 1. Industry benchmark: MHI cites national average occupancy of 93% for land-lease communities (MHInsider 2024 — source unverified at URL level; grade B).

**Cap rate:** 7.5% applied throughout. This is at the compressed end for stabilized MH communities in 2025–2026 (JLL MH cap rate survey shows 5.5–7.0% for stabilized institutional-grade; smaller/rural markets typically 7–9%). I am using 7.5% as a conservative midpoint for a non-institutional 55+ lakefront community. **Confidence: low — owner should obtain a broker opinion of value before finalizing.**

**Cost basis:** Inherits the 0.88 regional multiplier from the Cost Estimate stage. Unit costs for amenity items are estimated from RS Means 2025 site work data (national) adjusted to 0.88.

### Most Cost-Effective Amenity — Individual Water Sub-Meters (#1)

**Why it beats everything else on this specific site:**

The water sub-meter is not an amenity in the traditional sense — it converts a recurring operating expense into a resident-paid billback at essentially no change to service quality. Every other item in the table asks residents to pay more for something new; the water meter converts something the owner already pays for into resident cost. The payback is under 12 months at the assumed $57/month/site water/sewer cost, and the asset value created ($1.33M–$1.39M at 7.5% cap) exceeds any single physical amenity on the list at a fraction of the capital cost.

Unique to this site: The approved water main plan (Sheets 32–43) already includes 1-inch individual water service stubs with curb stops at every site (156 curb stops per Certified Quantity Schedule, OBSERVED). Adding an AWWA water meter during the water service installation phase costs incremental labor only — the trench is already open, the service line is already being run. The marginal cost of adding a meter at this stage is estimated at $150–$250 additional per site (the meter body and meter box) versus the full $350–$650 installed cost if added later. **Installing meters at the time of water service installation reduces the cost to approximately $23,000–$39,000 total — making the payback approximately 2–5 months.**

The one critical pre-condition: Village of Eastlake must permit individual metering with resident billback rather than requiring a master meter arrangement. This needs a phone call to the Village DPW before the water main contractor mobilizes.

### Amenity That Does Not Pay For Itself At Full Spec

**Candidate: Laundry facility at 6 machines (Item #4)**

The laundry analysis assumes 155 sites × 3 wash loads/week. In a 55+ manufactured housing community where residents live in double-wide and single-wide homes, most units will have in-home washer/dryer hookups (the double-wide units with 200A service certainly will). The 63 double-wide sites almost certainly have in-home laundry. This drops the serviceable market to approximately 81 single-wide sites, of which 60–70% may use in-home laundry anyway. Realistic utilization: 30–40 residents using the facility 2–3 times/week = 60–120 loads/week = $780–$1,560/week = $40,560–$81,120/year gross. At 6 machines and $26,000–$35,000 installation cost, this works — but not at the aggressive 6-machine count.

**Recommendation: Downsize to 4 machines (2 washers, 2 dryers) at an installed cost of $14,000–$20,000.** This reduces NOI slightly but improves ROI materially. Rough savings from 6-machine to 4-machine: **$8,000–$12,000 in first cost** with minimal NOI difference (utilization is the binding constraint, not machine count). The 4-machine installation also fits more comfortably in the southwest corner of the maintenance building (per Exhibit D layout: water and sanitary enter at the southwest corner, which is the right location for laundry). **Savings from this specification reduction: $8,000–$12,000, no change to approved footprint or conditions.**

## Part 3 — Implementation Guide

### Revenue Items

**Item 1 — Individual Water Sub-Meters**
- *What:* AWWA-rated 5/8"×3/4" positive displacement meters (Neptune T-10, Badger Recordall, or equal) with bronze body and AMR-capable register. Meter box to be cast iron or composite at grade. Billing: utility billing software (Resident Web Access or similar MH-specific billing platform) or third-party billing company (Zego, Conservice, or Multifamily Utility Company).
- *Where on plans:* At each of 155 individual water service lines, downstream of the curb stop and box shown in the Certified Quantity Schedule (156 curb stops, 1-inch). Meter sets between the curb stop and the home-side stub.
- *Trade:* Water main contractor (plumber or utility contractor licensed in Michigan). **Must be done during water service installation — same crew, same open trench, minimal added labor.**
- *Permit:* No permit contact needed for private-side meters. Confirm with Village of Eastlake that individual metering with billback is permitted under their service agreement — this is a phone call, not a permit application.
- *Phase:* Phase 1, concurrent with water service installation. Must be decided before water main contractor mobilizes.
- *Rough-in needed:* None additional — the curb stop is already in the approved plan. Simply specify the meter body and box at the time of service installation.
- *Lead time:* AWWA meters are standard stock items; 2–4 weeks for 155-unit order from a regional waterworks supplier.
- *Cost:* $23,000–$39,000 if installed during water service installation (incremental meter and box cost only; trench is already open). Rises to $54,000–$101,000 if installed post-construction.
- *Operations after opening:* Monthly meter reads (manual or AMR drive-by); billing software subscription $100–$300/month; staff or 3rd-party billing company to send monthly utility bills to residents. Michigan MHC Act compliance for billing methodology — review with attorney.

**Item 2 — Premium Site Designation**
- *What:* Tiered rent schedule set before marketing. Tier 1 (RV Super Sites, 11 sites): $1,100–$1,300/month annual lease, or $150–$250/night transient. Tier 2 (End/Corner MH sites, ~18 sites): $50–$100/month premium over standard MH rate. Tier 3 (Open-space adjacent, ~12 sites): $30–$60/month premium.
- *Where on plans:* No physical change. Applied to leasing schedule and community map.
- *Trade:* None — Owner/management company sets rents.
- *Permit:* None.
- *Phase:* Decide before any lease-up activity. Set in the marketing materials from Day 1.
- *Operations:* Maintain a site map showing tier designation. Review and adjust annually based on actual market response.

**Item 3 — Wi-Fi Backbone**

### Decide Before the Trade Mobilizes

These decisions must be made **before the relevant contractor begins work** — changing them after mobilization costs money:

1. **Water sub-meter specification** — Before water main contractor mobilizes. Confirm Village of Eastlake permits individual metering with billback. Add meter spec to water service scope. Costs almost nothing to add now; costs $30,000+ to retrofit later.
2. **NEMA 4X stainless pedestal specification** — Before electrical contractor orders pedestal equipment (long lead time; 6–10 weeks typical for 155-unit pedestal order).
3. **4,500 PSI air-entrained concrete mix design** — Before concrete contractor orders or schedules ready-mix deliveries. Add to concrete specification note on all pour tickets.
4. **DLC Premium LED luminaire specification** — Before electrical contractor orders fixtures. 34 poles × one fixture each; standard lead time 4–8 weeks; DLC Premium spec adds 0–2 weeks to most orders.
5. **NEMA 4X vs. 3R pedestal enclosure** — Same timing as #2 above.
6. **Laundry rough-in stub sizing** — Before plumber stubs utilities at maintenance building southwest corner (Phase 1). Specify 3/4-inch hot and cold water stubs and 3-inch sanitary drain at laundry-machine-ready height. Zero added cost if told to the plumber before they set the rough-in.
7. **Wi-Fi conduit sleeves alongside lighting circuits** — Before electrical contractor trenches and pulls lighting conduit. Add 1-inch spare conduit alongside each lighting trench run for $3,000–$6,000 total. Must be done when trench is open — cannot retrofit without re-excavation.
8. **Fire pit ring anchors at RV patio pours** — Before concrete contractor pours 11 RV site patios. Add steel anchor ring to each pour at $80–$150 each. Must be cast in — cannot add post-pour without core drilling.
9. **HDPE fusible pipe substitution at deep-trench segments** — Before water main contractor orders pipe for Oregon/Tennessee Avenue rear-lot runs. Standard 6-inch C900 PVC must be swapped in the purchase order; fusion equipment must be mobilized with the crew.
10. **EV charging conduit sleeves** — Before electrical contractor trenches near maintenance building and adjacent parking lot. Add two 1-inch conduit sleeves from Panel #G to parking lot for $800–$1,500 total.

## Appendix — Excluded: Would Require Plan Amendment

These ideas were evaluated and excluded because they would alter something the site plan approval was issued on, require a change to approved lot boundaries, grading, drainage, impervious area, or building footprints, or otherwise fail the "plan reviewer discrepancy" test:

1. **Adding additional home sites or adjusting lot lines** — requires MHC license amendment and SUP plan amendment; changes lot boundaries.
2. **Expanding the stormwater detention basin** — changes stormwater facility and potentially the Drain Commission approval; agency notification required.
3. **Adding a swimming pool** — changes building footprint and adds impervious area; requires building permit and site plan amendment.
4. **Adding a bathhouse or clubhouse** — new building footprint not on approved plans; requires site plan amendment.
5. **Adding a dump station** — new utility structure (sanitary connection, water supply) not on approved utility plan; requires plan amendment.
6. **Adding boat/RV storage with paved lot** — new impervious area and grading; changes site footprint.
7. **Installing a propane distribution system** — utility routing change; EGLE and fire marshal review required; not on approved utility plan.
8. **Relocating the maintenance building or pavilion** — changes approved building locations; SUP plan amendment required.
9. **Adding a second access point other than the Lot 18 emergency drive already required by SUP Condition 7** — changes access/circulation shown on approved site plan.
10. **Extending the road network northward for future expansion** — changes road alignment and grading footprint.
11. **Installing solar panels on rooftops of owner-furnished structures** — structures are owner-furnished and not on the civil plan set; engineering for structural loading required; may affect building permit.
12. **Adding a fishing dock at the stormwater basin** — basin is on the existing community parcel (separate ownership); access from the expansion parcel would cross lot lines; if basin frontage exists on the expansion parcel open space, this could be revisited with field confirmation.
13. **Striping a pickleball court on a new concrete slab** — a new concrete slab not within an already-approved impervious area would add impervious area. Only acceptable if striped on an already-approved concrete surface; if no approved slab is large enough, excluded.
