items.description: The electrical responsibility matrix (RFP §6.7) has three starred items pending written utility confirmation: (a) serving utility sets the transformer, (b) serving utility furnishes secondary conductor to each site, (c) serving utility installs secondary conductor to each site. No written confirmation from Consumers Energy or DTE is present in the project record. If the utility requires the GC to furnish or install secondary conductors (each potentially 50–200 LF per site × 155 sites = 7,750–31,000 LF of conductor), the electrical bid is missing a substantial cost item and the installed sequence conflicts with paving (road crossings must be conduit-sleeved before paving).
items.consequence: Bid is incomplete and uncompetitive. If utility shifts responsibility to GC after award, GC will file a change order for conductor and conduit. If road-crossing conduits are not installed before paving, asphalt must be saw-cut and patched at every site service crossing — a rework cost of $500–$2,000 per crossing × 155 sites.
items.correction: Before NTP, Owner/Owner's Representative must obtain written confirmation from Consumers Energy stating exactly what the utility will and will not furnish and install. If the utility requires GC-furnished/installed secondary, an addendum must issue pricing at U-45 and U-46 before contract execution. All road-crossing conduits for secondary service must be installed and inspected before the HMA first course — this sequencing must be on the CPM schedule regardless of how responsibility is assigned.
items.resolves: Owner's Representative to obtain utility written confirmation; EOR to amend responsibility matrix by addendum if needed
items.permit: Agency notification unavoidable if scope shifts secondary installation to GC — state electrical inspection covers secondary from utility meter to pedestal
items.documentation: Written utility confirmation letter; addendum if scope changes; inspection hold point before first-course paving
items.rom: If GC bears secondary: $150,000–$400,000 additional depending on run lengths; 2–4 week conduit installation before paving adds to critical path

items.description: Oregon Avenue sanitary sewer trunk (Sheet 25) shows manhole OA1 at STA 6+85 with invert 8" W. INV 649.95 and 8" N. INV 649.85. The rim is 664.70 — giving approximately 14.75 ft of cover. At STA 9+00 (where Sheet 15 storm sewer begins profiling Oregon Avenue), the existing sanitary MH #2 is shown with 8" IE S 647.76 / 8" IE E 647.56 (rim 662.86). The new 8" W connection to that existing MH is called at 8" IE W 647.76. The sanitary profile sheets (Sheets 25 and 30) show the trunk continuing west from OA1 at progressively deeper inverts (WA1 at STA 0+81 has invert at 652.6 — shallower than OA1 at 649.85), meaning flow direction from OA1 westward to OA1/WA branch is from the deeper OA1 toward the shallower WA1. This implies the Oregon Avenue–Washington Avenue sanitary junction flows from 649.85 to 652.6 — uphill by approximately 2.75 ft — which is hydraulically impossible for a gravity system.
items.consequence: Sewage will not flow. Entire northwest quadrant (Washington Avenue, Pennsylvania Avenue sites 169–212 range) cannot drain to the existing system. Sewage backup during operations.
items.correction: EOR must issue a corrected sanitary profile for the Oregon/Washington connection junction. One or more of the following must change: (a) confirm whether OA1 is a junction structure receiving flow from Washington Avenue branch at a different invert than shown, or (b) confirm the Washington Avenue main flows east to OA1 rather than west; the flow direction arrows or missing label on Sheet 30 must be verified against the CAD file. Do not install any sanitary pipe in the Oregon/Washington area until EOR issues a corrected profile with confirmed flow arrows and continuous downhill gradient to the existing MH #2 connection.
items.resolves: Engineer of record — requires CAD file review and corrected profile
items.permit: EOR letter required — corrected profile must be re-stamped; if EGLE-approved sanitary design is amended, EGLE notification may be required
items.documentation: RFI to EOR immediately; construction hold on sanitary in Oregon/Washington quadrant; updated profile stamped by EOR before installation
items.rom: Rerouting or depth change: $20,000–$80,000 depending on extent; 2–4 week design delay; could affect Phase 1 schedule if sanitary is on critical path

items.description: RFP §6.7 specifies lighting circuit conduit as "2-inch Schedule 40 PVC with 2-#10 CU and #12 GEC." Sheet 49 general note 14 states: "ELECTRICAL CONTRACTOR SHALL FIELD VERIFY ALL EXISTING ELECTRODE GROUNDING CONDUCTORS (EGC) AND COORDINATE WITH THE ENGINEER." NEC 250.122 sizes equipment grounding conductors based on the overcurrent protective device rating for the circuit — a #12 EGC is only appropriate for circuits protected at 20A or less. Street lighting circuits fed from 100A panelboards with branch circuits larger than 20A require a larger EGC. The plans do not show the OCPD rating for each lighting branch circuit, making the #12 GEC callout unverifiable and potentially non-compliant.
items.consequence: NEC 250.122 violation. AHJ (state electrical inspector) will reject the installation. Field correction after conduit is buried = excavation and re-pull.
items.correction: Electrical contractor must calculate EGC size per NEC Table 250.122 for each lighting branch circuit based on the actual OCPD rating shown in the panel schedule (which is not in the plan set — see Finding #2). Do not pull conductors until the panel schedule and OCPD ratings are confirmed by EOR. If OCPD is 20A or less, #12 EGC is acceptable; if 30A or larger, minimum #10 EGC is required per Table 250.122. Size conduit accordingly — a #10 EGC replaces the #12 and fits in 2-inch conduit.
items.resolves: Engineer of record must issue panel schedule and confirm OCPD ratings; electrical contractor verifies EGC per NEC 250.122
items.permit: EOR letter required — panel schedule is a missing design document; no agency resubmittal if correction is contained to EGC sizing within approved conduit
items.documentation: RFI to EOR for panel schedule; inspection hold point before conduit backfill
items.rom: $0 if #10 EGC fits in 2-inch conduit (no conduit upsizing needed); $5,000–$15,000 if conduit must be upsized and re-trenched

items.description: Water main crossings over or under sanitary sewer and storm sewer are shown at multiple locations (Sheet 39 explicitly shows crossings of 18" STM SWR INV 657.53 and 8" SAN SWR INV 658.34 in the same profile). Michigan Act 399 (safe drinking water) and MDOT/EGLE standards require a minimum 18-inch vertical separation between water main and sewer crossings, with the water main above the sewer. Sheet 39 shows water main flowing at approximately FL 660.1–660.5 and the storm sewer at INV 657.53 (approximately 2.6 ft below the water main centerline) and sanitary at INV 658.34 (approximately 2.1 ft below WM centerline). These separations appear to meet the 18-inch minimum. However, the plan sheets do not explicitly call out separation distances at any crossing, and Sheet 42 (East Rear Lot Tennessee Ave) shows water main and sanitary crossing at multiple stations (STM SWR INV 655.99 and SAN SWR INV 652.00 called at two stations, with WM flow lines at 654.6–658.0) where the water main may be below the storm sewer at some stations — this cannot be fully resolved from extracted text alone.
items.consequence: Where water main is less than 18 inches above sewer at any crossing, Act 399 approval will require special construction (sleeving, encasement). If built without required separation and not caught at inspection, contamination risk exists; also a EGLE compliance failure.
items.correction: EOR must provide a crossing schedule table listing every water/sewer crossing station, the pipe materials, the top-of-pipe elevation of each, and the clear vertical separation. For any crossing with less than 18-inch separation, specify: (a) 20-foot minimum horizontal separation or (b) HDPE water main with no joints within 10 feet of crossing. Install all water-main/sewer crossings before aggregate base — inspections must verify separation before backfill.
items.resolves: Engineer of record — crossing schedule is a missing design document
items.permit: EOR letter required; if crossings fail Act 399 minimums, EGLE Act 399 water main approval may require amendment — agency notification
items.documentation: RFI to EOR for crossing schedule; inspection hold point at every crossing before backfill
items.rom: $0 if separations confirm acceptable; $2,000–$8,000 per non-conforming crossing for sleeving/encasement; potentially 10–15 crossings at risk

items.description: SUP Condition 7 requires "a secondary vehicular access point on Lot 18 to allow for additional ingress and egress" — may be emergency/maintenance only, gated. Lot 18 is shown on Sheet 06 (parcel area 7,911 SF) and Sheets 07/08 show the maintenance building area at Lot 18 with an "EMERGENCY ACCESS DRIVE" labeled on Exhibit D. Sheet 04 shows the maintenance garage with emergency drive, but no plan sheet shows the gate, lock, or fire department key provision required by SUP Condition 7. The access drive width, surface type, and turning radius are not dimensioned on any sheet. Sheet 08 shows an access drive stub at the maintenance building but its connection to 3rd Street or Oregon Avenue is not shown with dimensions.
items.consequence: SUP condition not fully addressed. Fire department may not accept Phase 1 Substantial Completion (hydrant acceptance per RFP §4.15) if emergency access at Lot 18 is not installed and fire department key/code is not provided.
items.correction: EOR must issue a detail or plan revision showing: (a) the Lot 18 emergency access drive alignment, width (minimum 12 ft for emergency vehicle access — verify with Village fire marshal), surface type, and connection to 3rd Street or the internal road network; (b) gate or barrier design with fire department Knox lock or key; (c) signage per IFC 503. GC to include access drive in site prep scope. Confirm with Village fire marshal before paving.
items.resolves: Engineer of record for access drive detail; Owner for fire department coordination
items.permit: Agency notification unavoidable — SUP condition requires compliance before occupancy; fire marshal acceptance is required
items.documentation: Revised site plan submitted to Village ZA; fire marshal acceptance letter; inspection hold point before Phase 1 Substantial Completion
items.rom: Access drive design and construction: $8,000–$25,000 depending on length and surface; gate: $3,000–$8,000
items.blocks_label: Blocks Substantial Completion -- fire dept may not accept Phase 1 without the SUP Condition 7 access point

items.description: All sanitary sewer mains are shown at a uniform slope of 0.40% (8-inch PVC) throughout the system — confirmed on every profile sheet (Sheets 22–30). MDOT standard and Michigan Act 537 (sanitary sewer design) requires minimum self-cleansing velocity of 2.0 ft/s in sanitary sewers, which requires 0.40% minimum slope in an 8-inch PVC pipe at full-flow (Manning's n = 0.013). At 0.40% and an 8-inch pipe, the self-cleansing velocity is approximately 1.95–2.05 ft/s at full flow — marginally compliant. However, sanitary laterals are sized at 6-inch PVC. The 6-inch lateral slope is not shown on any profile sheet; the Certified Quantity Schedule confirms 3,432 LF at unspecified slope. 6-inch laterals require a minimum slope of 1/8 inch per foot (1.04%) per the detail on Sheet 31. If laterals are installed at less than 1.04% — which is likely given the deep trunk inverts (12–17 ft cover on Oregon Avenue) and shallow pad elevations — self-cleansing velocity is not achieved.
items.consequence: Chronic solids accumulation in flat or under-sloped 6-inch laterals. Blockages and backups at individual sites. Annual jetting costs; potential sewage backup into homes — owner liability. Long-term O&M burden on a 40–50 year asset.
items.correction: EOR must provide a lateral profile or at minimum a slope table for all 155 sanitary laterals, confirming each achieves 1.04% minimum slope. For deep-trunk areas (Oregon Avenue, approximately 14–17 ft deep), the lateral will require either a riser construction (per Sheet 31 detail, correctly shown) or a revised horizontal run. GC/excavator must verify lateral slope from cleanout elevation to main invert using as-staked grades before installation. Do not backfill laterals until slope is confirmed by field measurement.
items.resolves: Engineer of record for lateral slope table; GC and excavating sub for field verification of each lateral
items.permit: EOR letter required — lateral slope table is a missing design document; no agency resubmittal if slopes meet Act 537 minimums
items.documentation: RFI to EOR for lateral slope table; inspection hold point on lateral installation before backfill for deep-trunk areas
items.rom: $0 if designed correctly; rework cost if laterals must be re-graded: $500–$1,500 per lateral; 155 sites at risk

items.location: Sheets 32–43; all water main profile sheets
items.description: Water main is entirely 6-inch C900 PVC throughout the expansion (7,610 LF total). NFPA 13D/NFPA 291 and Michigan Act 399 guidance for fire flow: 6-inch mains can support fire flow but only if pressure and flow at the hydrant can be maintained above 20 psi residual while delivering the required fire flow. No hydraulic model, fire flow calculation, or hydrant flow test result is included in the 49-sheet set or any legible supporting document. The system serves 155 sites with 10 hydrants. The existing system is a 6-inch supply from the existing community. At 7,610 LF of 6-inch main off a single 6-inch tap, head loss under fire flow conditions (typically 1,000–1,500 GPM for a community this size) may drop residual pressure below the required minimum.
items.consequence: If fire flow is inadequate, EGLE Act 399 water main approval cannot be obtained, the Village will not accept the system, and fire department acceptance (required for Phase 1 Substantial Completion per RFP §4.15) will fail. Owner may be required to upsize portions of the main before the system is accepted.
items.correction: Before any water main installation, EOR must complete and submit a hydraulic network analysis (pipe flow model) demonstrating that 1,000 GPM fire flow at any hydrant can be maintained with minimum 20 psi residual pressure at all other points in the system. If the model shows deficiency, upsizing to 8-inch main on one or more trunk segments will be required. GC/water contractor should not begin water main installation until EOR's hydraulic analysis is accepted by EGLE under Act 399.
items.resolves: Engineer of record for hydraulic model; Owner for EGLE Act 399 submission
items.permit: Agency notification unavoidable — EGLE Act 399 approval requires hydraulic analysis; if main must be upsized, plan revision and re-approval required
items.documentation: RFI to EOR for hydraulic analysis; EGLE Act 399 submission and approval before water main installation
items.rom: $0 if model confirms adequacy; upsizing selected segments to 8-inch: $15,000–$60,000 in material cost differential + design fee

items.description: The Certified Quantity Schedule lists 10 fire hydrants. Sheet 42 (East Rear Lot Tennessee Ave) shows 4 hydrant locations (at STA 0+37.5, 3+59.5, 5+88.9, 8+43). Sheet 43 (Oregon Ave) shows 3 hydrant locations (STA 0+78, 3+00, 5+50). Sheet 36 (Washington Ave rear lot) shows 1 hydrant (STA 1+30.6). Sheet 39 (California Drive Crossing) shows 1 hydrant (STA 1+41). Total from profile sheets: 9 hydrants. Certified Quantity Schedule states 10. The 10th hydrant location is not confirmed in any readable profile sheet text.
items.consequence: One hydrant is unlocated in the plan text as extracted. If the 10th hydrant location is ambiguous, the fire marshal may identify a gap in coverage during acceptance inspection, requiring a field relocation that conflicts with installed utilities.
items.correction: EOR must provide a hydrant location table listing all 10 hydrant stations, the associated water main sheet, and the coverage radius (NFPA 1 recommends 500-ft maximum distance between hydrants in residential settings). The water contractor must field-verify all 10 locations against the table before trenching.
items.resolves: Engineer of record for hydrant location table
items.permit: Within approved plans if all 10 are shown on the plan sheets (extraction may have missed one); EOR letter required if one hydrant was inadvertently omitted
items.documentation: RFI to EOR for hydrant location table; photo log of each hydrant installation
items.rom: $0 if hydrant is already designed; additional hydrant if genuinely missing: $8,000–$15,000

items.description: Sheet 49 electrical note 16 states: "E.C. SHALL PROGRAM THE WIRELESS DIGITAL NETWORK LIGHTING CONTROLS PER THE OWNER'S SPECIFICATIONS TO COMPLY w/ THE ENERGY CODE (BASED ON IECC 2021). FIXTURE AND CONTROLS SHALL INCLUDE PHOTOCELL CONTROL, TIMER CONTROL, AND LIGHTING SETBACK." No control specification, wireless network system specification, or wiring diagram for the lighting control system appears anywhere in the 49-sheet set. The 34 light poles are shown with a panel reference (PNE or PG) and circuit numbers, but no control wiring is detailed.
items.consequence: Electrical contractor cannot price or install a compliant lighting control system without a specification. IECC 2021 compliance for outdoor lighting requires automatic shutoff controls — if not installed, the system will fail state energy code inspection. Programming without an owner's specification leaves the Owner without a defined and repeatable control baseline, creating operational ambiguity across dozens of luminaires.
items.correction: EOR must issue a lighting controls specification including: (a) wireless network brand/model or approved equal, (b) photocell setpoint, (c) timer schedule, (d) dimming setback level and hours, (e) wiring or communication diagram from each pole to the wireless network gateway. Electrical contractor must submit a controls submittals package for EOR approval before installing fixtures.
items.resolves: Engineer of record for controls specification
items.permit: EOR letter required — specification is a missing design document; state energy code (IECC 2021) compliance is required for occupancy
items.documentation: RFI to EOR for controls specification; submittals review before fixture installation
items.rom: Lighting controls system: $15,000–$40,000 depending on system; typically included in fixture cost if specified correctly

items.description: Sheet 10 shows the typical one-way road cross-section (Base Bid 23 ft BOC) with "7' LANE / 7' LANE" and integral asphalt curb. The Michigan Manufactured Housing Commission variance (FD 1201486, dated September 10, 2026) grants a variance for 16-foot one-way streets "rather than the required twenty-one (21) feet wide two-lane streets." The variance document uses the phrase "sixteen (16) foot wide one-way streets" as the approved width. The Base Bid 23 ft BOC section provides a 21-ft driving surface (two 10.5-ft lanes, not two 7-ft lanes as the detail labels them). This labeling discrepancy — "7' LANE / 7' LANE" when the driving surface math gives 10.5 ft lanes — is internally inconsistent on Sheet 10. Additionally, the Alternate No. 1 (16 ft BOC) plan set detail shows two 7-ft lanes; the label "7' LANE / 7' LANE" on the BASE BID section appears to be a copy error from the Alternate No. 1 detail.
items.consequence: Concrete contractor or paving sub may form or strike off the one-way road at 14 ft (7+7) instead of 21 ft (10.5+10.5), resulting in an undersized road that does not meet the Base Bid specification or the state standard.
items.correction: EOR must issue a corrected Sheet 10 clearly distinguishing the Base Bid cross-section (two 10.5-ft lanes, 21-ft driving surface, 23-ft BOC) from the Alternate No. 1 cross-section (two 7-ft lanes, 14-ft driving surface, 16-ft BOC). Paving contractor and concrete sub must be shown the corrected detail at the pre-construction meeting. Verify road width with a tape before paving any one-way section — minimum 21 ft to edge of integral curb for the Base Bid.
items.resolves: Engineer of record for corrected detail
items.permit: EOR letter required — corrected sealed detail needed before paving
items.documentation: Field change order issuing corrected cross-section; inspection hold point measuring road width before HMA first course
items.rom: $0 for correction; paving a 14-ft road instead of 21-ft and correcting: $20,000–$60,000 per avenue segment

items.description: Sheet 04 notes that one-way streets must alternate direction per SUP Condition 11 (confirmed in SUP document: "The one-way streets shown on the site plan must alternate direction for each street"). Sheet 04 shows traffic flow arrows. The Site Overall and electrical plans show "ONE WAY" and "DO NOT ENTER" signs at entries to each one-way avenue. However, the plan set does not include a signing and pavement marking plan as a standalone sheet. The sign schedule references MDOT Standard Highway Signs R6-1R, R5-1, R-1, and D3-1, but no sign layout plan, post spacing, or mounting height detail is provided. Pavement markings are shown only as a quantity (1,000 LF at 4-inch white waterborne).
items.consequence: SUP Condition 11 compliance cannot be field-verified without a signing plan showing which direction each avenue flows and where each sign is located. Incorrect sign installation could result in two-way traffic on a one-way road — a safety hazard. Missing signage at Phase 1 Substantial Completion delays certificate of occupancy.
items.correction: EOR must issue a signing and pavement marking plan showing: (a) each one-way avenue's direction of flow, (b) location of every R6-1R, R5-1, R-1, and D3-1 sign with distance from intersection, (c) pavement marking layout for stop bars and any edge lines. GC/signage sub must install per that plan. SUP Condition 11 compliance (alternating direction) should be verified by Owner before sign installation.
items.resolves: Engineer of record for signing plan
items.permit: Within approved plans if SUP directions are already established; EOR letter required if a signing plan must be separately sealed
items.documentation: RFI to EOR for signing plan; photo log of each installed sign; ZA confirmation of SUP compliance
items.rom: Signing plan: $2,000–$5,000 design; signs and posts: included in bid Category 16

items.description: Sheet 14 (Tennessee Avenue storm sewer profile) shows a callout labeled "TM CB#5025" with elevation "64.67" and "NV 660 97" near the Montana Drive/Tennessee Avenue intersection. "TM" is not defined in the Sheet 02 abbreviation list or any legend in the 49-sheet set. The elevation "64.67" appears truncated (likely 664.67) and "NV 660 97" is unclear (possibly invert 660.97 but the decimal placement is uncertain from extraction). This structure is located near the junction of Tennessee Avenue storm sewer and Montana Drive storm sewer.
items.consequence: If "TM CB#5025" is an existing structure that the proposed storm sewer must connect to, and its rim/invert elevations are uncertain, the proposed pipe slope and invert at the connection point may be incorrect. Misread elevations at a junction structure cause pipe slope errors that can result in ponding or reverse-flow conditions.
items.correction: EOR must clarify: (a) what "TM" designates, (b) the correct rim elevation (confirm as 664.67 or otherwise), (c) the correct invert elevation (confirm as 660.97 or otherwise), and (d) whether this is an existing structure to be connected or a proposed structure. GC/storm sewer sub must field-verify the actual rim and invert of any structure at this location before setting pipe grades in this area.
items.resolves: Engineer of record clarification
items.permit: Within approved plans if clarification confirms no conflict; EOR letter required if elevations differ from plan values
items.documentation: RFI to EOR; field survey of existing structure before storm sewer installation in this area
items.rom: $0 if confirmed; $2,000–$8,000 if pipe slope must be reset

items.description: The SESC Plan (Sheet 03) and SSURGO table identify "Plainfield sand, 35 to 70 percent slopes" (MUSYM 67F) as present on site. The geotechnical memo (Spicer Group, May 27, 2026) confirms borings were limited to 2.5–8 ft depth and explicitly states this "would not identify problematic layers that may exist below the bottom of the borings." The storm sewer profiles show pipes ranging from 12-inch to 36-inch HDPE discharged toward the existing stormwater basin. None of the storm sewer profiles show the basin outlet structure details, emergency spillway elevation, or outfall protection (riprap or energy dissipator). Sheet 04 labels the basin as "+/-330,000 CFT" but no detention routing calculation, outlet structure design, or Drain Commission-approved capacity documentation is readable in this set (Drain Commission approval document is present but entirely unreadable — scanned image only).
items.consequence: If the basin outlet structure is inadequately designed or the emergency spillway is absent, a storm event exceeding design capacity could overtop the basin and erode the bluff face — a geotechnical failure risk given the 35–70% slope soils adjacent to Manistee Lake. The Drain Commission approval document may contain conditions on the outlet structure that are unknown at this time.
items.correction: Before any grading near the existing basin, EOR must provide: (a) a readable copy or human transcription of the Drain Commission approval conditions, (b) the outlet control structure design (weir elevation, orifice size, emergency spillway elevation), (c) the detention routing calculations showing basin volume, peak inflow, and peak outflow for the design storm, (d) riprap or energy dissipator detail at the outfall. Owner must obtain and read the Drain Commission approval document.
items.resolves: Engineer of record for basin and outlet design; Owner for Drain Commission document retrieval
items.permit: Agency notification unavoidable — Drain Commission approval document contains binding conditions; construction must comply with those conditions even though they are currently unreadable
items.documentation: Drain Commission approval document retrieved and reviewed before grading; RFI to EOR for outlet structure detail; inspection hold point before basin grading
items.rom: Outlet structure design: $5,000–$15,000 if not already in EOR's file; riprap: $3,000–$10,000; no excavation cost if done in original earthwork scope

items.location: Sheet 10 / Road cross-sections; Sheet 03 / SESC soils; Geotechnical memo
items.description: The geotechnical memo specifies imported granular fill must meet "MDOT Class II granular material." Sheet 10 road cross-section notes "NATIVE GRANULAR MATERIAL COMPACTED TO 95% MAXIMUM DRY DENSITY" below the aggregate base. The geotechnical memo states on-site soils are "loose to medium dense sand and sand with silt" and identifies some borings with silt layers that would not be suitable as subgrade without moisture conditioning. The distinction between which site soils are acceptable as native subgrade vs. which require removal and replacement with imported Class II is not drawn on any plan sheet or in the road cross-section detail. No moisture sensitivity threshold or silt content limit is given in the plan set.
items.consequence: Pavement subgrade prepared with silty sand that is not moisture-conditioned to optimum density will fail proof-roll, require remediation after the GC has already moved on to another area, and create persistent pavement failures (rutting, cracking) under MH transport and heavy-truck loading. Long-term pavement performance issue for a permanent owner.
items.correction: EOR must issue a subgrade specification or earthwork specification addendum that defines: (a) maximum fines content for native material to be used as compacted subgrade, (b) moisture conditioning requirements, (c) proof-roll procedure (loaded tandem axle, maximum deflection criteria), (d) trigger for undercut and replacement. GC/excavator must proof-roll all subgrade before aggregate base is placed; EOR or independent testing lab must be present for proof-roll.
items.resolves: Engineer of record for subgrade specification
items.permit: EOR letter required — earthwork specification is a missing design document
items.documentation: RFI to EOR; compaction test reports for every 500 LF of road; inspection hold point before aggregate base placement
items.rom: $0 if soil conditions are as expected; undercut and replacement beyond the 50-CYD allowance: $25–$60/CYD at U-03 unit price; potentially 500–2,000 CYD at risk

items.description: The electrical site plan sheets (46–48) show lighting circuit runs labeled with panel and circuit references (e.g., "SL1 PNE-06,08" and "SL1 PG-05,07\*"). The asterisk on "PG-05,07\*" is not defined in any legend or note on Sheets 46–48 or Sheet 49. Additionally, the circuit pairs shown (e.g., PNE-06,08 — two circuits to one fixture) imply a two-circuit arrangement for each street light, but Sheet 49 does not show a panel schedule confirming the circuit assignments or the OCPD ratings. Without a panel schedule, the electrical contractor cannot wire or label the circuits correctly, which is required by NEC 408.4.
items.consequence: Electrical contractor installs circuits without confirmed OCPD ratings or circuit labeling. Inspector will not approve. Rewiring after conduit is buried is extremely costly. Undefined asterisk may indicate a design condition (e.g., circuits fed from a different phase or a GFCI breaker) that the installer does not know about.
items.correction: EOR must issue: (a) panel schedules for Panel #NE and Panel #G showing every circuit number, OCPD rating, load, and connected luminaire; (b) definition of the asterisk on PG-05,07\*; (c) wiring diagram confirming the two-circuit arrangement at each pole is intentional (switching arrangement or phase arrangement). Electrical contractor must receive and review the panel schedule before any conduit is installed.
items.resolves: Engineer of record for panel schedule and asterisk definition
items.permit: EOR letter required — panel schedule is a missing design document required for electrical permit
items.documentation: RFI to EOR; submittals of panel schedule before conduit installation
items.rom: $0 for corrected documents; rework if circuits are wired incorrectly and must be re-pulled: $5,000–$20,000

items.description: Sheet 10 shows typical lot layouts for single-wide, double-wide (horizontal and vertical), and RV sites with setbacks and garage/pad configurations. The parcel dimension sheets (07–09) show lot frontages ranging from approximately 50 to 60 ft for single-wide sites and 50 to 60 ft for double-wide sites on the interior avenues. However, the typical double-wide home lot diagram on Sheet 10 shows a "24'×26' GARAGE" adjacent to the home. On lots with 50.8 ft frontage (the majority of double-wide lots per Sheet 06 tables), placing a 24-ft-wide garage plus the minimum 10-ft side setback to the adjacent structure on both sides leaves only 50.8 − 10 − 10 = 30.8 ft for the garage width — compatible. However, the typical vertical double-wide layout (SP-2B) orients the home perpendicular to the road; on lots with depth of approximately 113–114 ft, the home + 20-ft rear setback + 12-ft front setback = 32 ft minimum consumed by setbacks, leaving approximately 81 ft for home placement. No sheet verifies that all 63 double-wide lots can physically accommodate both a double-wide home and an attached garage within setbacks on every specific lot. Irregular corner lots (e.g., parcels 35, 44, 103, 204) have reduced areas (as low as 5,839 SF for parcel 201) — below the 5,000 SF MH minimum if a garage is counted as part of the home structure requiring full setbacks.
items.consequence: A home or garage placed on a lot that cannot meet setbacks will fail licensing inspection under the Michigan Mobile Home Commission Act. Owner cannot place homes on non-conforming lots. Revenue-producing sites reduced.
items.correction: EOR must provide a lot-by-lot conformance table for all 155 sites confirming that each lot meets: (a) minimum 5,000 SF (MH) or 4,000 SF (RV); (b) 50-ft minimum frontage (MH) or 40-ft (RV); (c) 12-ft front setback; (d) 10-ft side setback to adjacent structure; (e) 20-ft rear setback to adjacent structure. Flag any non-conforming lots before home purchase commitments are made.
items.resolves: Engineer of record for conformance table
items.permit: Agency notification unavoidable — LARA/Michigan Manufactured Housing Commission licensing requires minimum lot size compliance; non-conforming lots cannot be licensed
items.documentation: RFI to EOR for conformance table before home installation commitments
items.rom: $0 if all lots comply; loss of revenue if any site is non-licensable; potential site reconfiguration

items.description: The storm sewer profiles (Sheets 12–20) include plan view for each road, showing sanitary, storm, and water main in proximity. Sheet 15 (Oregon Avenue) shows the existing sanitary MH #2 noted with "CORE NEW OPENING IN MH / INSTALL KOR-N-SEAL BOOT." Sheets 12–20 do not include a horizontal utility conflict diagram or minimum separation callouts between storm and sanitary at crossing or parallel locations. Standard practice requires 10-ft minimum horizontal separation between water main and sanitary sewer, and 3-ft minimum horizontal separation between storm and sanitary where they run parallel. Where the rear-lot water main (east and west sides of California Drive, shown on Sheets 37–41) runs parallel to the sanitary on the same rear-lot easement, separation is not dimensioned.
items.consequence: Parallel utilities installed too close together compromise future maintenance access (excavating one may undermine the other) and can violate Act 399 and EGLE sanitary separation requirements. Conflicts discovered in the trench cause costly field reroutes and schedule delays.
items.correction: EOR must issue a utility corridor plan or a note on the overall utility plan (Sheet 11) specifying minimum horizontal separations for all parallel utility runs. GC/utility contractor must verify separation before trenching by staking all utilities simultaneously. Where rear-lot water main and rear-lot sanitary run within the same corridor, horizontal offset must be confirmed to meet a minimum of 10 ft (water to sanitary) unless sleeving or other Act 399 provisions are applied.
items.resolves: Engineer of record for separation callouts
items.permit: EOR letter required; if Act 399 minimums cannot be met, EGLE Act 399 approval amendment required — agency notification
items.documentation: RFI to EOR; utility staking verification before trenching; inspection hold point before backfill at parallel runs
items.rom: $0 if plan shows adequate separation; rerouting: $5,000–$20,000 per conflict

items.description: Sheet 45 (Electrical Site Plan Overall) shows Panel #G in the southwest area near the maintenance building. Exhibit D (Maintenance Building) specifies: "100A, 120/240V, 1-PHASE, FROM PANEL #G ON THE EXTERIOR RACK" and "PANEL IS RACK-MOUNTED, NOT BUILDING-MOUNTED." Sheet 47 confirms the rack location. Exhibit C (Pavilion prints and pad requirements) was provided but could not be read (entirely scanned — 0% text-extractable). The pavilion electrical requirements, pad dimensions, and structural loads are genuinely unreviewed — not absent from the project record, but unknown from this review. If the pavilion requires a separate electrical circuit or a dedicated panel connection, that connection is not shown on any electrical sheet.
items.consequence: If the pavilion requires electrical service (lighting, outlets, audio, HVAC) and that service is not in the GC's electrical scope, the pavilion will be unserviced at opening. If it is in scope but not shown, it is missing from the bid and will be a change order.
items.correction: Owner must obtain a human-readable version of Exhibit C (re-scan or original digital file) and transmit the pavilion electrical and structural requirements to the EOR before pavilion site work begins. EOR must issue an addendum or field change showing any pavilion electrical connection. GC must not pour the pavilion slab until conduit stub locations are confirmed.
items.resolves: Engineer of record after Exhibit C is read; Owner for document retrieval
items.permit: Within approved plans if pavilion has no electrical service; EOR letter required if electrical connection must be added
items.documentation: Exhibit C retrieval memo; RFI to EOR for pavilion electrical; inspection hold point before pavilion slab pour
items.rom: Pavilion electrical stub: $1,000–$5,000 if added; slab rework if conduit missed: $3,000–$8,000

items.description: The electrical site plans show E1 (100A, 1-phase) pedestals at all 81 single-wide MH sites and E2 (200A, 1-phase) pedestals at all 63 double-wide sites. Michigan and national practice for MH communities typically provisions 200A service at all sites capable of accepting a double-wide home, which is consistent with E2. However, the plans do not show the secondary conductor size from the utility transformer to each pedestal. For E2 pedestals (200A), the secondary run from transformer to pedestal at distances over 150–200 ft creates voltage drop that may exceed NEC 210.19 recommendations (maximum 3% voltage drop on branch circuits, 5% total to point of use). The rear-lot transformer placement is not confirmed in any plan sheet — transformer locations are pending utility confirmation.
items.consequence: If secondary runs exceed voltage drop limits, residents experience low voltage events damaging appliances and HVAC equipment — a warranty and resident relations issue. At long secondary runs (>200 ft), voltage drop requires conductor upsizing from the utility-standard size, which the GC cannot confirm until the utility commits to its transformer layout.
items.correction: Once the serving utility commits to transformer locations in writing, electrical contractor must calculate voltage drop for the longest secondary run to any E2 pedestal (200A). If voltage drop exceeds 3% on the secondary, request utility to upsize secondary conductor or reposition transformer. Do not accept utility standard conductor sizing without a voltage drop check. Document voltage drop calculations and retain for EOR review.
items.resolves: Electrical contractor and serving utility, with EOR review
items.permit: Potential — depends on transformer placement and utility-standard conductor size; within approved plans if utility confirms compliance
items.documentation: RFI to EOR once utility transformer layout is confirmed; voltage drop calculations retained
items.rom: $0 if utility positions transformers adequately; conductor upsizing: $10,000–$30,000 if long runs require it

items.location: Sheet 10; all parcel dimension sheets; known site geometry
items.description: Sheet 10 shows the typical RV Super Site with a concrete pad, concrete patio (350 SF minimum per Ordinance Z26-01 Section 3.b), and a "4" CONC SLAB FOR 8'×10' SHED." RFP §4.13 and the Certified Quantity Schedule confirm 800 SYD of stamped 4-inch concrete for RV patios (800 SYD ÷ 11 sites = approximately 72.7 SYD = 654 SF per site — substantially larger than the 350 SF minimum). The concrete layout and dimensions for each RV site are not detailed individually on any sheet. The Certified Quantity Schedule RFP note states: "RV/SP-4 concrete split" remains an open question per the Known Decisions. The 1,100 SYD of 4-inch driveway for RV sites in the Certified Quantity Schedule (1,100 ÷ 11 = 100 SYD = 900 SF per site) plus the 800 SYD patio (72.7 SYD = 654 SF per site) gives approximately 1,554 SF of concrete per RV site — a reasonable RV super site footprint but unconfirmed against individual lot dimensions.
items.consequence: Concrete contractor cannot accurately form and pour RV pads without dimensioned layout drawings for each of the 11 sites. Over-poured concrete is waste; under-poured fails the 350 SF minimum patio requirement per the ordinance, and the site cannot be licensed.
items.correction: EOR must issue dimensioned RV site concrete layouts for each of the 11 sites (parcels 16, 17, 169–177) showing pad footprint, patio footprint, shed slab location, and total concrete square footage — confirming that each site meets the 350 SF patio minimum. Concrete sub must form per those layouts.
items.resolves: Engineer of record for RV site layouts
items.permit: Potential — if existing quantities and Sheet 10 typical layout are sufficient, no EOR action needed; if specific layouts differ from the typical, EOR letter required
items.documentation: RFI to EOR for individual RV site concrete layouts; inspection hold point before RV slab pours
items.rom: $0 if typical layout applies uniformly; layout design: $2,000–$5,000

items.description: No cleanout spacing is shown or specified for the 8-inch sanitary trunk mains. The 156 cleanouts confirmed in the Certified Quantity Schedule are identified as "Sanitary Sewer Cleanout, 6 inch" — these are the individual site lateral cleanouts, not trunk line cleanouts. Michigan Act 537 and standard practice do not require cleanouts on 8-inch or larger gravity mains (manholes serve this function), and 31 manholes are provided. However, the maximum manhole spacing on the sanitary trunk should not exceed 400 ft (MDOT standard) without directional change justification. The profiles show several manhole spacings that may approach or exceed this limit — for example, on Oregon Avenue (Sheet 25), OA2 at STA 12+29 to OA3 at STA 13+32 is 103 LF (acceptable), but OA1 at STA 6+85 to OA2 at STA 12+29 is 544 LF — which exceeds the 400-ft standard maximum without a directional change or drop manhole between them.
items.consequence: A 544-ft manhole-free run on a relatively deep trunk (approximately 15 ft cover) with no intermediate access point makes televising and cleaning operations extremely difficult. If the pipe develops a defect or blockage, access requires excavation. Long-term O&M cost for a permanent owner.
items.correction: EOR must confirm manhole spacing on the Oregon Avenue trunk between STA 6+85 and STA 12+29. If the spacing exceeds 400 ft without a justifying directional change, add an intermediate manhole at approximately STA 9+50. Confirm all other trunk runs have manhole spacing ≤ 400 ft or have a documented reason for exceeding this.
items.resolves: Engineer of record for confirmation
items.permit: Potential — depends on whether the spacing exceeds local review agency's standard; EOR letter required if additional manhole is added
items.documentation: RFI to EOR for manhole spacing confirmation
items.rom: Additional manhole if required: $5,000–$10,000 including installation

items.description: No ADA-designated home or RV sites are labeled on any plan sheet. No ADA accessible route connecting all sites to common amenities (pavilion, mailboxes, parking, community building) is shown as a continuous accessible path. Exhibit C (pavilion) is unreadable. The Fair Housing Act and the Americans with Disabilities Act require manufactured housing communities to provide accessible routes and a minimum number of accessible sites. The specific site count required depends on the total number of sites and applicable state/local standards. The SUP and Ordinance Z26-01 do not specify ADA site requirements.
items.consequence: LARA state licensing may require ADA-compliant sites before the community can be licensed. Fair Housing Act complaints are possible if no accessible sites are provided. Correcting pad grades, ramp connections, and route surfacing after construction is substantially more expensive than designing them in.
items.correction: Owner must obtain legal advice on Fair Housing Act applicability to this community (55+ designation may affect but not eliminate ADA obligations). EOR must identify: (a) the required number of accessible MH and RV sites, (b) accessible route width and surface requirements connecting those sites to all common amenities, (c) any accessible parking requirements. At a minimum, the accessible route shown in concrete sidewalk (9,321 SF per the Certified Quantity Schedule) must be confirmed as forming a continuous, compliant path. Do not pour pads at identified accessible sites until grades are confirmed compliant.
items.resolves: Engineer of record for ADA site identification; Owner for legal review
items.permit: Potential — confirmed if applicable; agency notification unavoidable if LARA requires ADA sites as a licensing condition
items.documentation: RFI to EOR and Owner for ADA analysis before site-specific concrete work; inspection hold at accessible site pads
items.rom: ADA site upgrades if not already designed: $2,000–$8,000 per accessible site; route corrections: $5,000–$20,000

items.description: The Special Use Permit (Condition 6) requires: "The updated location of the dog park, wholly contained within the subject property, shall be reflected on a revised site plan and submitted to the Zoning Administrator." No dog park is shown on any of the 49 plan sheets reviewed. The SESC plan (Sheet 03) and Site Overall (Sheet 04) do not label a dog park location.
items.consequence: SUP condition is not satisfied on the submitted plan set. The Village Zoning Administrator may withhold a certificate of compliance or require a plan revision before occupancy.
items.correction: Owner must identify the dog park location, prepare a revised site plan showing it within the property boundary, and submit to the Village ZA before construction reaches final completion. EOR should incorporate the dog park on the as-built site plan. GC need not construct the dog park (it is not in the bid scope as described) but should avoid grading or utility conflicts with the chosen location.
items.resolves: Owner for SUP compliance; EOR for site plan revision
items.permit: Agency notification unavoidable — this is an open SUP condition requiring a plan submittal to the Village
items.documentation: Revised site plan submitted to Village ZA; ZA acceptance letter
items.rom: Dog park design and construction (fencing, surfacing): $5,000–$20,000; plan revision: $1,000–$3,000
items.blocks_label: Blocks occupancy -- Village may withhold the certificate of compliance without the SUP Condition 6 dog-park plan

items.description: SESC Permit No. 26-030 and NPDES Notice of Coverage MIR119192 both expire May 29, 2027. The RFP envisions Phase 1 Substantial Completion (all infrastructure, first-course paving) in the 2026 season with Phase 2 (final course, restoration, closeout) in 2027. If Phase 2 restoration and final stabilization are not complete by May 29, 2027, the SESC permit expires and the site will have unprotected, unstabilized disturbed areas. A permit renewal requires submission of a renewed SESC permit and renewed NOC through EGLE's MiEnviro Portal.
items.consequence: Expired SESC permit while disturbed areas remain unstabilized is a Part 91 violation. EGLE can issue a notice of violation and assess fines. Stabilization work cannot legally continue without a valid permit.
items.correction: Owner and GC must build the CPM schedule such that final topsoil respread, seeding, and mulching on all disturbed areas is completed no later than May 1, 2027 — allowing 4 weeks of establishment before the permit expires. If the schedule shows Phase 2 paving extending into summer 2027, the Owner must proactively file an NOC renewal and SESC permit extension before May 29, 2027. The renewal is available and can be submitted via MiEnviro Portal per the EGLE NOC letter. Do not wait for the permit to expire — file the renewal at least 60 days in advance.
items.resolves: Owner for permit renewal; GC for schedule management
items.permit: Agency notification unavoidable — permit renewal requires EGLE and Manistee County SESC agency filings before expiration
items.documentation: NOC renewal submitted to EGLE; SESC permit extension filed with Manistee County; GC CPM schedule milestone for permit expiration date
items.rom: Permit renewal fees: minimal; fine risk if expired: $2,500–$10,000 per day under Part 91; schedule impact if work stops: potentially significant

items.description: Sheet 49 riser diagrams for both Panel #NE and Panel #G show "CONDUIT AND CONDUCTORS BY ELECTRIC UTILITY (VIF)" with "VIF" not defined in any legend, glossary, or abbreviation list in the plan set or supporting documents. Without knowing what VIF requires or allows, the GC cannot determine what — if anything — the electrical contractor must install at the conduit runs shown in the riser diagram before the utility arrives. If VIF means the utility installs its own conduit, the GC needs to know the trench location and depth requirements to coordinate with other utility trenching.
items.consequence: GC cannot price or schedule the primary conduit scope without knowing what VIF means. If the undefined label creates a scope gap between GC and utility, primary conduit may be omitted and the utility will not install without a prepared trench — causing schedule delay.
items.correction: Owner/Owner's Representative must request a written definition of VIF from the engineer of record and from the serving utility immediately. Do not begin electrical primary trench coordination with Consumers Energy or DTE until VIF scope is defined in writing. Once defined, issue a clarifying addendum or RFI response to all bidders/GC.
items.resolves: Engineer of record for definition; Owner's Representative for utility coordination
items.permit: Potential — within approved plans once defined; no agency action unless scope changes
items.documentation: RFI to EOR for VIF definition; written utility confirmation of primary conduit responsibility
items.rom: $0 if utility provides conduit; $10,000–$50,000 if GC must furnish and install primary conduit not currently in bid

items.description: The water main system has two confirmed connection points to the existing system (Kentucky Avenue live tap at STA 10+60, Sheet 32; West Rear Lot California Drive connection at STA 11+76, Sheet 38). The system appears to form a loop through the rear-lot mains. However, the west end of the Minnesota Avenue rear-lot main (Sheet 33: "4+45 — 6"×6" TEE, 1-6" PLUG") and the west end of the Washington Avenue rear lot main (Sheet 36: "8+17 — 6"×6" TEE, 1-6" PLUG") terminate in dead ends with plugs. Dead-end mains require flushing hydrants or blow-off assemblies to maintain water quality (AWWA C651, Act 399). No flushing hydrant is shown at these dead ends.
items.consequence: Dead-end water mains accumulate sediment and stagnant water. Without flushing provisions, bacteriological sampling may fail at commissioning, and the system will not pass Act 399 acceptance. Chronic water quality complaints from residents at end-of-line sites. Long-term O&M issue for a permanent owner.
items.correction: EOR must add a flushing hydrant or 2-inch blow-off assembly at each dead-end plug location (at minimum: Minnesota Avenue rear lot STA 4+45 and Washington Avenue rear lot STA 8+17). If any additional dead ends exist that are not shown in extracted text, apply the same requirement. Water main contractor must not plug any dead-end without installing a flushing provision. Include flushing in the Act 399 acceptance test protocol.
items.resolves: Engineer of record for flushing hydrant locations
items.permit: EOR letter required — design change needed; EGLE Act 399 approval should confirm flushing provisions are acceptable
items.documentation: RFI to EOR for dead-end flushing provisions; include in Act 399 submission to EGLE; inspection hold point at dead-end installations
items.rom: Blow-off assembly per location: $1,500–$3,500; full fire hydrant at dead end: $8,000–$12,000; 2 locations minimum

items.description: Lighting circuit references on Sheets 46 and 47 include "PG-05,07\*" with an asterisk. The asterisk is not defined in any legend, note, or schedule on Sheets 46, 47, or 49. Additionally, the Sheets 46 and 47 legends show "PROPOSED UTILITY METER LOCATION" as a symbol but the locations of utility meters at each E1 and E2 pedestal are shown only as key-note callouts (E1 and E2), not as individual meter symbols at every site. The serving utility's meter locations must be field-verified and coordinated (per the E1 and E2 key notes). Without a confirmed meter location policy from the utility, the GC cannot confirm pedestal setback from property line, conduit stub height, and meter socket orientation.
items.consequence: Asterisk creates scope ambiguity that may result in incorrect circuit installation. Unconfirmed meter locations mean pedestals could be installed in the wrong position relative to the road edge or property line, requiring relocation before the utility will set meters — a cost and schedule impact.
items.correction: EOR must define the asterisk in the next plan revision or addendum. Owner's Representative must obtain written meter placement standards from Consumers Energy (or DTE for the applicable service area) before pedestal installation begins. Electrical contractor must confirm pedestal position, meter socket height, and conduit stub orientation with the utility before concrete pier pours.
items.resolves: Engineer of record for asterisk definition; electrical contractor and utility for meter placement coordination
items.permit: Potential — within approved plans once defined; no agency action unless pedestal position changes require plan revision
items.documentation: RFI to EOR for asterisk definition; written utility meter placement standards; inspection hold point before pedestal concrete piers are poured
items.rom: $0 if resolved before installation; pedestal relocation: $500–$2,000 per relocated pedestal

items.location: Sheets 07–09; Site Details Sheet 10; geotechnical memo
items.description: The geotechnical memo recommends a "maximum allowable bearing pressure of 2,000 lb/ft²" for structure support and notes that foundations should be "observed prior to constructing footings." The plan set does not include manufactured home foundation or anchoring details — these are labeled as "flat pads" per RFI 037 (referenced in the Known Decisions as resolved). However, the plan set does not show the flat pad elevation relative to finished road or finished grade at each site, nor does it show whether the pad is flush with, above, or below adjacent grade. For MH installation, the top of pad must be at or above the adjacent finished grade to drain away from the home. On sites with slopes exceeding 2% across the pad (which are likely given the bluff terrain and SSURGO 67F soils), the grading relationship between pad and adjacent road or swale must be explicit.
items.consequence: If pad elevations are set below adjacent finished grade, water ponds against the home — a long-term moisture and structural problem. If set too high, the MH transport cannot drive onto the pad and the set crew cannot position jacks — a delivery failure.
items.correction: EOR must issue a pad elevation design sheet or table showing, for each of the 155 sites: (a) the top-of-pad design elevation, (b) the adjacent road edge elevation, (c) the minimum percent grade from pad to drainage swale or road edge. Concrete sub must set forms to the EOR-specified elevation at each site, verified by survey, before pouring.
items.resolves: Engineer of record for pad elevation table
items.permit: Potential — within approved plans if grading surfaces document (RFP_Grading_Surfaces_20260824.pdf) contains this information; that document's content was not fully extracted from plan text, only station-line layout was visible
items.documentation: RFI to EOR for pad elevation table; survey verification before each pad pour; inspection hold point before concrete placement
items.rom: $0 if elevations are designed; re-grading a pad after pour: $500–$3,000 per site

items.description: Sheet 49 note 17 states: "PER NEC 551.77, RV PEDESTALS SHALL BE LOCATED ON THE LEFT SIDE OF THE PARKED VEHICLE, AND INCLUDE THE MARKING 'TURN DISCONNECTING SWITCH OR CIRCUIT BREAKER OFF BEFORE INSERTING OR REMOVING PLUG. PLUG MUST BE FULLY INSERTED OR REMOVED.'" The 11 RV Super Site lot layouts on Sheet 10 show the RV pad schematically but do not show the pedestal position relative to the head-in orientation of the RV. Without knowing the head-in direction of each RV site (which end of the RV pad is the front), the electrical contractor cannot determine "left side" in the field.
items.consequence: Pedestal installed on the wrong side of the parking position forces the power cord across the front or rear of the RV — a code violation (NEC 551.77) and a trip hazard. Correcting a buried and concreted pedestal requires excavation and re-pour.
items.correction: EOR must issue a note or detail on the RV site electrical layout confirming the head-in (front) direction of each of the 11 RV pads and the corresponding pedestal placement side. Electrical contractor must walk each RV site with the superintendent and confirm "left side" before setting pedestal base.
items.resolves: Engineer of record for RV orientation detail
items.permit: Potential — within approved plans once direction is confirmed
items.documentation: RFI to EOR for RV orientation confirmation; inspection hold point before RV pedestal concrete piers are poured
items.rom: $0 if confirmed before installation; pedestal relocation: $500–$2,000 per site × up to 11 sites

items.description: Sheet 01 plan index lists Sheet 20 as "STORM SEWER PLAN AND PROFILE WASHINGTON AVE STA 0+00 (POB) TO STA 6+81 (POE)." The plan-and-profile sheet 20 header itself reads "WASHINGTON AVENUE STA 0+00 (POB) TO STA 6+81 (POE)" — consistent. However, the sheet index lists the Tennessee Avenue storm profile as "STA 19+00 TO STA 28+74 (POE)" but the sheet 14 header and profile matchline read "STA 18+00 TO STA 28+74" — the index says 19+00, the sheet says 18+00. Difference of 100 stations.
items.consequence: Contractor referencing the sheet index to find the 18+00 to 19+00 profile range will not find it listed in the index — creating momentary confusion that could delay a field crew trying to locate the correct elevation at STA 18+XX. Not a design error, but a documentation gap.
items.correction: Add a note on the record drawings clarifying that the Tennessee Avenue storm sewer profile begins at STA 18+00, not 19+00 as listed in the Sheet 01 index. GC to be advised at pre-construction meeting.
items.resolves: Engineer of record for corrected sheet index on record drawings
items.permit: Within approved plans
items.documentation: Record drawing note; pre-construction meeting verbal notice

items.description: Sheets 07 and 08 both reference "SEE PARCEL DIMENSIONS NORTH SHEET" and "SEE PARCEL DIMENSIONS SOUTHEAST/SOUTHWEST SHEET" at their edges. Sheet 09 references "SEE PARCEL DIMENSIONS SOUTH SHEET" — but the index (Sheet 01) does not list a "PARCEL DIMENSIONS SOUTH" sheet. Sheets 07 (Southwest), 08 (Southeast), and 09 (North) are the three parcel dimension sheets. Sheet 09's reference to a "South" sheet appears to be a copy-error — the southern area of the site is covered by Sheets 07 and 08, not a separate South sheet.
items.consequence: Field crews referencing "SEE PARCEL DIMENSIONS SOUTH SHEET" on Sheet 09 will look for a sheet that does not exist, causing confusion and potentially using an incorrect sheet for staking.
items.correction: Add a correction note on record drawings: Sheet 09 note "SEE PARCEL DIMENSIONS SOUTH SHEET" should read "SEE PARCEL DIMENSIONS SOUTHWEST SHEET (07) AND SOUTHEAST SHEET (08)." Advise GC/surveyor at pre-construction meeting.
items.resolves: Engineer of record for note on record drawings
items.permit: Within approved plans
items.documentation: Record drawing note

items.description: Sheet 02 lists "HYD = HYDRANT" in abbreviations, but the hydrant symbol on the utility plans and water main profiles uses the standard fire hydrant symbol — consistent. However, the Certified Quantity Schedule pay item description for fire hydrants reads "Fire Hydrant" without specifying the EJ 5BR250 WaterMaster product number. The RFP §6.12 specifies the product, but the quantity schedule used for bidding does not. A contractor reading only the quantity schedule (which the RFP §2.2 makes subordinate to the plan set, which is itself subordinate to the RFP) might not flag the specified product as an owner-specified item.
items.consequence: Bidder prices a generic fire hydrant rather than the EJ 5BR250 WaterMaster — cost difference is typically $500–$1,500 per hydrant. At award, GC submits a substitution that is denied, requiring a change order to meet the specification. Minor cost dispute at a 10-unit quantity.
items.correction: At pre-construction meeting, confirm with GC and water contractor that the fire hydrant specification is EJ 5BR250 WaterMaster (product 55418D) per RFP §6.12, matching the existing community standard. Add a specification reference note to the hydrant line items on the record drawings.
items.resolves: GC to confirm with Owner's Representative; water contractor to source correct product
items.permit: Within approved plans — RFP §6.12 governs
items.documentation: Pre-construction meeting minutes; submittal of hydrant cut sheet before ordering
items.rom: $0 if addressed before order; change order risk: $500–$1,500 per hydrant if wrong product ordered and denied

items.description: Sheet 49, General Note 15 states: "PANEL #G WILL BE MOUNTED ON AN EXTERIOR ELECTRICAL RACK AT A LOCATION THAT COULD FEED THE FUTURE MAINTENANCE GARAGE." Exhibit D (Maintenance Building Specification) states the electrical service is "100A, 120/240V SINGLE PHASE, FROM PANEL #G ON THE EXTERIOR RACK. PANEL IS RACK-MOUNTED, NOT BUILDING-MOUNTED." The panel is already designated to feed the maintenance building — Note 15's phrasing "COULD feed the future maintenance garage" implies it has not yet been committed to that purpose, which contradicts Exhibit D's specification that it does feed the building. This labeling inconsistency could cause the electrical contractor to locate the panel rack without accounting for the conduit run to the maintenance building service entrance.
items.consequence: Electrical contractor places the Panel #G rack at a location that makes the conduit run to the maintenance building excessively long, requiring a larger conductor size than designed or a voltage drop issue.
items.correction: At pre-construction meeting, confirm with electrical contractor that Panel #G is designed and located to serve the maintenance building at the distance shown on Sheet 47. Electrical contractor must size the conduit run from Panel #G to the building service entrance based on Exhibit D's 100A service, not just the rack location in isolation. Note 15 should read "WILL feed" on record drawings.
items.resolves: Engineer of record for note correction
items.permit: Within approved plans
items.documentation: Record drawing note; pre-construction meeting confirmation

cross_run_notes: The full Cost & VE Memo and the full Class 4 Estimate Report (read in full 2026-09-28, not just their summaries) both independently identify the same two open items as the biggest real cost risk: (1) whether the existing sewer/water system has capacity for 155 new connections, and (2) what Consumers Energy will charge for the electric line extension (CIAC) -- neither is on the drawings and each could move the total by $0.5-1.2M.

RV rents differ across documents: the Cost & VE memo assumes $3,500/mo seasonal RV (a dated public profile); the Ideas & ROI doc uses the subject's actual 2026 rate sheet ($1,925/mo super, $1,325 deluxe, $4,830-$6,995/season) and says these supersede the older figure. Trust the Ideas doc's rents.

The Class 4 estimate ($8.97M) and the Cost & VE Memo's base case ($8.51M) differ by about $466k (5.2% of the lower figure) on the same plan set. Both memos flag the same missing information (grading plan, geotech, tap fees) as the reason neither should be treated as final.

The Cost & VE Memo goes a real step further than the Class 4 report: it recommends an alternative 165-site plan (+10 sites) at $7.78M ($47,200/site), a $0.72M reduction from its own $8.51M base case, driven mainly by shifting driveway/shed cost into the home-sale package and adding water/sewer submetering revenue.

Both memos independently flag the same real electrical-tag discrepancy (fewer E1/E2/E3 tags legible than the 155 real sites) but neither should be read for an exact count -- see the plan-index verification note below.

Added 2026-09-28: an independent second review (model claude-sonnet-4-6) was run against the raw 49-sheet plan text alone, with zero exposure to the outside consultant's (Marc's) memos or register -- see 'independent_review_raw' and the per-question 'Independent analysis' toggles under The big picture above.

Construction status update, 2026-10-02 (Andrew Chime, Grex Dev -- the project's construction manager -- weekly email to Jay/Marc): the Phase 1 Bid Package (Site Development) and Phase 2 Bid Package (Future Homesites) went out as Addendum No. 6 on Oct 1, 2026. Contractor bids are due Tuesday Oct 6 at noon ET (Walton confirmed receipt; AJ's, Tridonn, and Leopardo also bidding -- Leopardo needs until ~Oct 20 for a full bid). Grex plans to deliver a bid comparison Wednesday Oct 7 and review it with Jay/Marc Thursday Oct 8.

big_picture_md:
## 1. What will this cost?

The all-in project cost is **$12.6 million, or $81,200 per site**, based on a complete re-analysis against the full 38-document set (re-run October 12, 2026). That breaks down as $8.7M hard cost, $1.6M contingency (18%), and $2.3M soft costs. The 18% contingency is warranted: 7 critical and 13 moderate plan issues remain unresolved, the electrical one-line diagram is missing, the Drain Commission approval document is unreadable, and the utility tap fees alone carry a $155K–$390K swing. No independent contractor bid total is readable — the October 6 bid document is present but entirely scanned, so there is no second number to cross-check against. Treat this as a single Class 4 estimate until that bid is transcribed.

---

## 2. What can we do to reduce it?

**The single best-supported cost reduction is joint-trenching the rear-lot utility corridor** — running water, sanitary laterals, and electrical service conduit in one shared trench instead of three separate trenches — estimated savings of $273K–$475K. This requires the engineer of record to issue a joint-trench detail with explicit separation callouts (which also fixes a moderate plan issue flagged in the error register), but needs no agency resubmittal if Act 399 separation requirements are maintained. Second: elect **Alternate No. 1 — 16-foot BOC one-way avenues** — already designed, already state-approved (variance FD 1201486), saves $56K–$60K with zero plan revision and zero schedule impact. Take both.

---

## 3. What else would you recommend?

**The highest-priority fix before construction starts is the fire hydrant in the existing community** (critical, high confidence — SUP Condition 5, Sheets 04/44): no hydrant exists on the existing parcel, and the SUP explicitly prohibits NTP until one is installed and approved by the Village of Eastlake fire department. If the GC mobilizes without it, the Village can stop work. Estimated cost $15K–$25K and 4–8 weeks — start this week. Close behind it: the **electrical one-line diagram is missing entirely** (Sheet 49, critical, high confidence) — the two 100A panelboards shown cannot feed 155 sites; no transformer schedule, feeder sizing, or load calculation exists anywhere in the 49 sheets. Do not order electrical equipment or let the contractor mobilize until Consumers Energy confirms transformer sizing in writing and the engineer issues a complete one-line. On the value side: **install individual water meters at all 155 sites during water service installation** — the curb stops and 1-inch service stubs are already in the approved plans, so adding an AWWA meter in the open trench costs roughly $23K–$39K incremental and converts an estimated $100K+/year of owner-paid water/sewer expense into a resident billback, creating roughly $1.3M–$1.4M of asset value at a 7.5% cap rate. Confirm Village of Eastlake permits individual metering before the water main contractor mobilizes — that's a phone call, not a permit application.
