# The Bluffs on Manistee Lake — North Expansion
## Plan Facts Report: Scope of Work Audit & Quantity Take-Off Estimates
**Reviewer:** Independent Second Review (Jennings Realty / Jay Lapat)
**Plan Set:** Spicer Group, Project No. 139471SG2025, Issued for Bidding 8/20/2026, 49 Sheets
**Review Date:** Per document, bid issue date 8/20/2026

---

## Preliminary Notes on Plan Text Quality

The plan set was provided as extracted PDF text, with some pages rendered as visual (image) and others as text-layer extractions. Several sheets produced only title blocks, legend fragments, or partial station data — particularly the visual-only pages (Sheets 01, 03, 05, 10, 11, 21, 31, 44, 47, 49) where graphic content could not be fully read. Sheet numbering in the index (Sheet 01/Cover) shows 49 total sheets numbered D-6631-01 through D-6631-49, but the extracted text covers only the pages listed below. **Key content gaps exist** — notably, the electrical distribution plan (likely Sheets ~40-45 range per index), grading/earthwork sheets, site amenity plans, and the full parcel-type schedule are only partially recoverable from the text. Every quantity marked as estimated or unknown should be field-verified against the original DWG/PDF files.

---

## 1. Scope of Work Audit

### 1.1 Site Count by Type

**Source sheets: D-6631-04 (Site Overall), D-6631-06 (Parcel Types), D-6631-07/08/09 (Parcel Dimensions), text from pages 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11**

The plan set uses a numbering system that includes both new proposed sites (integer numbers) and existing sites prefixed "EX." From the extracted site-number sequences visible across the overall plan and dimension sheets, the following new proposed site numbers are identifiable:

**New proposed sites visible in plan text:**

| Number Range / Individual Numbers Observed | Count (approximate) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 (isolated, Sheet 05 area) | 1 | Single site near existing parking |
| 9 | 1 | Isolated near existing sites |
| 16–38 (with gaps: 16–38 visible, some out of sequence) | ~20 | Along Tennessee Ave / north area |
| 39–55 | ~17 | Along California Drive and cross-streets |
| 78–103 | ~26 | Northwest block |
| 169–215 (with some gaps) | ~40 | Central/south block |
| 216–256 (with gaps) | ~38 | North/northeast block |
| Scattered: 240–256 range | included above | |

**Observed highest new site number: 256**
**Observed lowest new site number: 1**

However, the sequence is **not continuous** — many numbers in the EX (existing) series are interspersed (EX 125–168, EX 59–76, etc.), and several numbers between 1–256 appear to be existing sites renumbered with "EX" prefix. The plan cover states "~155-site addition" in the project brief. From careful reading of the non-EX numbered sites across sheets 4, 6, 7, 8, and 9, I count approximately **155 new proposed sites**, consistent with the project description — but I **cannot confirm the exact count with high confidence** from the text extraction alone because:
- Some numbers are partially cut off at page edges
- The parcel-type sheet (D-6631-06) is a visual-only page and its table was not readable
- The dimension sheets (D-6631-07/08/09) show individual lot dimensions but do not provide a running total

**Assumption (stated):** I am accepting ~155 new sites as the working count, consistent with the project description and the site number range observed. The actual verified count requires reading D-6631-04 (Site Overall) and D-6631-06 (Parcel Types) from the original graphic PDF. **Confidence: Moderate.**

**Site type breakdown:**
The parcel-type legend/table (D-6631-06, visual-only) was not readable from the text extraction. Sheet D-6631-47 shows a legend fragment with "E1" and "E3" designations appearing repeatedly along what appears to be the Oregon Avenue / RV row area, suggesting at least two distinct parcel types. From the dimension sheets:

- **RV super sites (pull-through configuration):** The recurring dimension pattern of **~50.8' width × ~172'–173' depth** (seen extensively on pages 8 and 9, Sites 19–34 and 248–255 range) strongly suggests pull-through RV sites. A 50.8' × 173' site = ~8,800 SF per site, which is consistent with a "super site" pull-through RV configuration. The ~173' depth accommodates a large RV plus tow vehicle with room to spare.
- **Back-in RV or MH sites:** The recurring dimension pattern of **~55'–61' width × ~113'–117' depth** (seen on pages 7 and 8, Sites 169–215 range) is consistent with double-wide MH lots or back-in RV sites.
- **Narrower sites:** Widths of **48.6'–50.8'** with depths of ~113' appear for some sites, potentially single-wide MH or standard RV back-in.
- **Larger irregular lots:** Several sites in the 80'–136' width range appear at road terminations/corners — likely corner or end lots.

**Tentative site-type estimate (stated assumption — requires D-6631-06 verification):**

| Type | Estimated Count | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| RV pull-through super sites (~50.8' × 172'–173') | ~60–70 | Low-Moderate |
| MH double-wide or RV back-in (~55'–61' × 113'–117') | ~50–60 | Low-Moderate |
| MH single-wide or standard RV back-in (~48'–50' × 113') | ~25–35 | Low |
| Corner/irregular/oversized lots | ~5–10 | Low |
| **Total new sites** | **~155** | **Moderate** |

**ADA sites:** Not explicitly called out in the readable text. ADA designation is typically shown on the parcel-type sheet (D-6631-06, unreadable). **Flag for human verification.** ADA-accessible sites are required under FHA/ADA for any rental community — minimum 5% of total, or at least 7–8 sites for a 155-site development.

**Full hookup vs. partial:** The utility plan (D-6631-11) shows both water and sanitary sewer distribution reaching all streets. Electrical is also shown. All sites appear to be full-hookup (water + sewer + electric). No dump station is specifically called out in the readable text, but this would typically appear on the amenity/site plan sheet. **Assumption: all sites are full-hookup. Confidence: Moderate.**

**Gross vs. net developable acreage:**
No explicit acreage table was found in the readable text. The plan set does not include a written acreage summary in the extracted pages. The road centerline station data (see Section 1.2) and lot dimension data allow a rough geometric estimate:

- The overall site layout spans multiple named streets. California Drive runs from approximately STA 12+00 to STA 24+02 = **~1,202 LF**. Tennessee Avenue runs from STA 19+00 to STA 28+74 = **~974 LF** of new construction shown on profile sheets. Oregon Avenue runs from approximately STA 13+00 to STA 18+63 plus a spur (~596 LF + ~120 LF branch). Kentucky Avenue runs STA 2+00 to approximately 7+20 = **~520 LF**. Minnesota, Montana, Pennsylvania, and Washington Avenues each run approximately 500–700 LF based on station data.
- Pull-through site rows: ~60–70 sites × 173' deep = rows approximately 450'–600' long.
- The overall layout extent, roughly estimated from the station data and lot dimensions, suggests a development footprint of approximately **40–60 gross acres**. This is a wide range — **confidence: low.** A scale bar is present on some visual sheets but was not readable from text extraction.

**Assumption:** I am not stating a gross or net acreage with confidence. The human reviewer should measure from D-6631-04 (Site Overall, 1"=80' or similar scale) to determine gross and net acres. This is a **required verification item.**

**Density:** Cannot be calculated with confidence without confirmed acreage. If 155 sites on 40 gross acres: 3.9 sites/acre. If 50 gross acres: 3.1 sites/acre. Typical RV/MH resort density is 3–6 sites/acre.

---

### 1.2 Roadway Network

**Source sheets: D-6631-12 through D-6631-20 (Storm Sewer Plan & Profile), D-6631-22 through D-6631-30 (Sanitary Sewer Plan & Profile), D-6631-32 through D-6631-43 (Water Main Plan & Profile)**

Named streets visible in the plan set with station data:

| Street Name | Station Range (visible) | Approximate Length (LF) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| California Drive | STA 12+00 to STA 24+02 | ~1,202 | Storm/San profiles; POE at 24+02 |
| Tennessee Avenue | STA 19+00 to STA 28+74 | ~874 | Profile ends at POE 28+74 |
| Oregon Avenue | STA 13+00 to STA 18+63 + STA 5+00 to 5+96 | ~663 + ~96 = ~759 | Two segments shown |
| Kentucky Avenue | STA 2+00 to STA 7+20 + STA 18+00 to 18+63 | ~520 + ~63 = ~583 | Two segments |
| Minnesota Avenue | STA 2+00 to STA 5+96 | ~396 | |
| Montana Avenue | STA 3+00 to STA 6+40 + STA 14+00 to 16+00 | ~340 + ~200 = ~540 | |
| Pennsylvania Avenue | STA 3+00 to STA 6+87 + STA 11+00 to 13+00 | ~387 + ~200 = ~587 | |
| Washington Avenue | STA 2+00 to STA 11+00 | ~900 | Longest cross-street |
| Short spurs/stubs (estimated 3–5 additional) | ~100–200 LF each | ~400–800 | |

**Estimated total road centerline length: ~5,800–6,400 LF (approximately 1.1–1.2 miles)**

> **Assumption:** The station ranges above are read from plan-and-profile sheet titles and MH/storm structure callouts. Not all beginning stations are confirmed — some streets may have additional length outside the profiled reaches. The overall plan sheet (D-6631-04) would give total road length more reliably. **Confidence: Moderate.**

**Road width:** Not explicitly stated in readable text. The dimension sheets show lot frontages of ~50.8'–61' with apparent road right-of-way between. Based on industry standard for MH/RV communities and the presence of curb & gutter (referenced in the line type legend, Sheet 02), road widths are assumed to be **24'–28' back-of-curb to back-of-curb** for internal streets. California Drive and Tennessee Avenue (the primary collectors) may be wider — possibly **30'–36'**. **Assumption stated. Confidence: Low — requires field verification from D-6631-04 or cross-section sheets not readable.**

**Surface type:** The line type legend (Sheet 02) references "PROPOSED CURB & GUTTER" and "EXISTING CURB & GUTTER." This indicates curbed roadways with what is likely asphalt paving (standard for a professionally engineered MH/RV community with curb and gutter). No chip seal or gravel designation was found in the readable text. **Assumption: asphalt pavement with integral curb and gutter throughout. Confidence: Moderate.** The grading/paving sheets (likely D-6631 sheets in the 40s range not fully extracted) should confirm.

**Curb/gutter:** Confirmed present per legend (Sheet 02). Whether it is full roll curb (typical RV) or barrier curb (typical MH/urban) is not determinable from the extracted text.

---

### 1.3 Water Source and Distribution

**Source sheets: D-6631-11 (Overall Utility Plan), D-6631-32 through D-6631-43 (Water Main Plan & Profile)**

**Water source:** The water main sheets reference connections to **existing water mains** at multiple points:
- Sheet D-6631-37/38: "EXISTING WATER MAIN, 1-6" VALVE & BOX" at STA 11+76 (Florida/California Drive area), at elevation FL 660.7
- Sheet D-6631-32: "EXISTING 6" WATER MAIN, 1-6"×6" TAPPING SLEEVE, VALVE & BOX" at STA 10+60, FL 660.2
- Sheet D-6631-43 area: Connection to existing water infrastructure

This confirms the project **ties into an existing municipal/public water system** — not a new well. The existing mains are 6" diameter at the connection points. **Confidence: High.**

**Distribution main size:** All proposed water mains shown are **6" diameter** throughout the distribution network. The following fitting/valve types are visible:
- 6"×6" TEE (at hydrant and branch locations)
- 6" VALVE & BOX (isolation valves)
- 6" 90° BEND, 45° BEND, 22.5° BEND (direction changes)
- 6" HYDRANT connections (multiple locations — see Section 1.3 fire flow below)

**No 8" or larger distribution mains** are shown in the readable text for the new development area. The 6" system feeds all new streets.

**Fire flow / hydrants:** Fire hydrants are explicitly shown at multiple locations across the water main plans:
- Sheet D-6631-36: "1+30.6 — 6"×6" TEE, 6" VALVE & BOX, 6" HYDRANT"
- Sheet D-6631-39: "1+41 — 6"×6" TEE, 6" VALVE & BOX, 6" HYDRANT"
- Sheet D-6631-40: "0+37 — 6"×6" TEE, 6" VALVE & BOX, 6" HYDRANT"
- Sheet D-6631-42: "0+37.5 — 6"×6" TEE, 6" VALVE & BOX, 6" HYDRANT" and "3+59.5 — 6"×6" TEE, 6" VALVE & BOX, 6" HYDRANT"
- Sheet D-6631-43: "0+78 — 6"×6" TEE, 6" VALVE & BOX, 6" HYDRANT" and "3+00 — 6"×6" TEE, 6" VALVE & BOX, 6" HYDRANT" and "5+50 — 6"×6" TEE, 6" VALVE & BOX, 6" HYDRANT"

**Minimum visible hydrant count: 8–10 hydrants** across the plan set. The full count requires reading the complete water main plan sheets. **Confidence: Moderate on minimum count; Low on total count.**

**Metering:** Individual site meters are not explicitly called out in the water main text. The overall utility plan (D-6631-11, visual-only) likely shows meter locations. **Assumption: individual site meters or submetering — unknown. Flag for verification.**

---

### 1.4 Wastewater

**Source sheets: D-6631-22 through D-6631-30 (Sanitary Sewer Plan & Profile), D-6631-11 (Overall Utility Plan)**

**Treatment approach:** The sanitary sewer system is a **gravity sewer collection system** using PVC pipe, discharging to an existing system. Key evidence:

- All sanitary sewer is labeled "SAN SWR" (gravity designation)
- Pipe material: **8" PVC** throughout the new collection system (all lateral/branch sewers)
- Slopes: 0.40% throughout (minimum gravity slope for 8" pipe per Michigan DEQ/EGLE standards — confirms gravity system)
- Structure type: **Standard sanitary manholes** (SAN MH) at intersections and grade changes
- **12" PVC** appears at one location (Sheet D-6631-12/22): "24 LF OF 12" PVC SAN SWR @ -0.50%" — this appears to be a trunk sewer or connection to existing system, not lateral pipe

**Connection to existing system:** Multiple plan sheets show connections labeled "EXISTING SANITARY SEWER OR FORCEMAIN" in the line type legend. The sheet D-6631-14 (Tennessee Avenue profile) shows sanitary manholes labeled "SAN MH #TA-103", "SAN MH #KA101", "SAN MH #KA102" — these naming conventions (TA = Tennessee Avenue, KA = Kentucky Avenue, OA = Oregon Avenue, etc.) indicate a comprehensive street-by-street collection system.

**No package WWTP, lift station, or septic/drainfield** is mentioned in the readable text. The system appears to connect to existing public sanitary sewer. **Confidence: Moderate.** The overall utility plan (D-6631-11) should confirm the point-of-connection and whether any lift station exists at the low point (California Drive profile shows a low point at STA 23+68.74, elevation 659.22 — if the existing sewer is higher than this, a lift station would be required; this requires verification).

> **⚠️ FLAG — Critical:** The low point on California Drive is at approximately elevation 659.22 (Sheet D-6631-13). The existing connection point elevations should be checked to confirm gravity flow is achievable without a lift station. If the existing sewer invert is above 659, a lift station or force main would be required — a potentially significant cost item not visible in the current text extraction. **Human verification required.**

**Sanitary manhole counts (visible):** Named manholes include CD-series (California Drive), TA-series (Tennessee Ave), KA-series (Kentucky Ave), OA-series (Oregon Ave), MA-series (Minnesota Ave), MD-series (Montana Ave), PA-series (Pennsylvania Ave), WA-series (Washington Ave). Counting named structures from the text: approximately **25–35 manholes** in the new system. **Confidence: Low — requires complete plan set reading.**

---

### 1.5 Stormwater

**Source sheets: D-6631-03 (SESC Plan), D-6631-12 through D-6631-20 (Storm Sewer Plan & Profile), D-6631-21 (Storm Sewer Details)**

**Stormwater approach:** A comprehensive **storm sewer system** using HDPE pipe, discharging at identified Points of Egress (POE). Key observations:

**Storm pipe inventory visible:**

| Sheet | Location | Pipe | Diameter | Length | Slope |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| D-6631-12 | California Drive | HDPE | 12" | 387 LF | 0.26% |
| D-6631-13 | California Drive (to POE) | HDPE | 12" | ~50 LF (est.) | 0.26% |
| D-6631-14 | Tennessee Ave | HDPE | 12" | 61 LF | -0.51% |
| D-6631-14 | Tennessee Ave | HDPE | 12" | 25 LF | 0.49% |
| D-6631-15 | Oregon Ave | HDPE | 24" | 215 LF | 0.30% |
| D-6631-15 | Oregon Ave | HDPE | 18" | 58 LF | 0.30% |
| D-6631-15 | Oregon Ave | HDPE | 18" | 207 LF | 0.30% |
| D-6631-16 | Kentucky Ave | HDPE | 12" | 205 LF | -0.50% |
| D-6631-16 | Kentucky Ave | HDPE | 12" | 61 LF | -0.51% |
| D-6631-17 | Minnesota Ave | HDPE | 12" | 7 LF | 0.50% |
| D-6631-18 | Montana Ave | HDPE | 12" | 49 LF | -0.50% |
| D-6631-19 | Pennsylvania Ave | HDPE | 15" | 173 LF | 0.50% |
| D-6631-19 | Pennsylvania Ave | HDPE | 15" | 160 LF | -0.50% |
| D-6631-20 | Washington Ave | HDPE | 18" | 268 LF | 0.50% |

**Partial storm pipe total from visible sheets: ~1,931 LF** of new storm sewer in diameters ranging 12"–24" HDPE. This is likely significantly understated — many storm sewer sheets (D-6631-12 through D-6631-20 is a 9-sheet series) were only partially readable.

**Storm structures:** 48" diameter MDOT cover-type catch basins are explicitly called out:
- STR NO CD102: 48" DIA, STA 18+12.4, RIM 665.45 (Sheet D-6631-12)
- STR NO CD105: 48" DIA (Sheet D-6631-13)
- STR NO KA101 and KA102: 48" DIA (Sheet D-6631-14)
- STR NO PA102: 48" DIA (Sheet D-6631-19)
- STR NO WA102: 48" DIA (Sheet D-6631-20)
- STR NO MA102: 48" DIA (Sheet D-6631-17)

**24" diameter MDOT cover-type structures** are also shown:
- STR NO CD101, CD104 (California Drive) — 24" diameter
- STR NO OA103, KA103, KA105, MA101, PA101, WA101, MD101 — 24" diameter

These 24" structures appear to be the **inlet-type structures** (side-of-road catch basins at lower flow points), while 48" structures are junction boxes.

**Detention/retention:** No detention pond or retention basin is explicitly named in the readable text. The SESC Plan (D-6631-03) is a visual-only page and was not readable. The project is on a bluff above Manistee Lake — it is possible (and typical for a lakefront bluff site) that stormwater is directed via storm sewers to discharge points at the bluff edge (POE = Point of Egress, confirmed in sheet titles "to STA 24+02 (POE)" and "to STA 28+74 (POE)"). Whether a detention facility exists or whether the bluff discharge is the primary stormwater management strategy cannot be confirmed from the extracted text.

> **⚠️ FLAG — Important:** Discharge to a Lake Michigan tributary bluff without detention may trigger EGLE stormwater quality or quantity standards. The SESC plan (D-6631-03) and any NPDES/MS4 permit language should be reviewed. Michigan's Part 91 (Soil Erosion and Sedimentation Control) Act and Part 31 (Water Resources Protection) Act requirements apply to a project of this scale. **Human verification required.**

**SESC/NPDES:** The plan set includes a dedicated SESC Plan (D-6631-03, visual-only) and the project title "SESC PLAN" confirms this. NPDES General Permit for stormwater discharge from construction sites (>1 acre) almost certainly applies — the SWPPP would be a separate document not in this plan set.

---

### 1.6 Electrical

**Source sheets: D-6631-49 (visible — electrical detail/notes), D-6631-45 (visible — appears to be electrical overall or water/utility overall), D-6631-47 (visible — parcel dimension with E1/E3 designations)**

**Primary service:** The electrical detail sheet (D-6631-49) shows:
- "UTILITY TRANSFORMER" on concrete pad
- "CONDUIT AND CONDUCTORS BY ELECTRIC UTILITY (VIF)" — indicating the utility (Consumers Energy or local co-op) provides primary conductors and sets transformers
- "PROPOSED ELECTRIC UTILITY METER"
- Panel "#NE, 100A/3P MCB, 120/240V, 1Ø-3W" — this is a **100-amp, 3-pole main circuit breaker, single-phase, 3-wire** service entrance panel
- Conductors: "3#3 (CU), 1#8 (CU) GEC, 1.5" RM CONDUIT"
- Grounding: Concrete-encased electrode + (2) 10' copper-clad ground rods

The 120/240V single-phase panel shown appears to be an **individual site service panel** for an MH site or RV pedestal — 100A service is consistent with a double-wide MH site (though 200A is more typical for full-size double-wide; 100A may be for a specific site type). **Flag: MH sites typically require 200A service; 100A may be undersized for double-wide MH. Requires verification against D-6631-06 parcel types.**

**Site type designations "E1" and "E3"** visible on Sheet D-6631-47 alongside parcel outlines along Oregon Avenue. These likely correspond to electrical service types:
- E1: Possibly single-phase 100A or 50A RV service
- E3: Possibly 3-phase or 200A MH service
The exact definition requires reading the parcel-type legend (D-6631-06, visual-only). **Confidence: Low.**

**Transformer count/kVA:** No transformer schedule was found in the readable text. The overall electrical plan is not fully extracted. **Unknown — requires reading the electrical plan sheets.**

# The Bluffs on Manistee Lake — North Expansion
## AACE Class 4 Preliminary Cost Estimate
**Estimator Role:** Senior Civil Construction Estimator / PM — Independent Review
**Basis:** Plan Facts (prior task), Error Register (prior task), Plan Set D-6631, 49 Sheets, Spicer Group, Issued for Bidding 8/20/2026
**Estimate Class:** AACE International Class 4 (Screening/Feasibility), ±30–50% accuracy range
**Pricing Basis:** Q3 2026 Michigan Northwest Lower Peninsula market conditions
**This estimate is non-binding and preliminary. It is not a bid, a guaranteed maximum, or a stamped engineering document.**

---

## Foundational Assumptions and Scope Boundaries

### What This Estimate Covers
All civil site infrastructure for 155 new sites as described in the Plan Facts: earthwork, underground utilities, paving, electrical distribution, and a budgetary allowance for amenity buildings not shown in the plan set. It does not cover home purchase, home installation, furniture/fixtures, or ongoing operations.

### What This Estimate Does NOT Cover (explicitly excluded)
- Manufactured home purchase price
- Home transportation and installation (separate contract, typically owner/buyer)
- Off-site road improvements or public ROW work (not shown in plans)
- Land acquisition cost
- Owner's FF&E for amenity buildings

### Regional Multiplier
**Location:** Manistee County, Michigan — Northwest Lower Peninsula. RSMeans CityConnect and ENR Building Cost Index data for this region relative to national average:
- **Applied regional multiplier: 0.88** (national baseline × 0.88 for this rural northwest Michigan market)
- Basis: RSMeans places Grand Rapids, MI at approximately 0.90–0.93 of national average; Manistee County is more rural and less competitive for subcontractors, which cuts both ways — lower prevailing wages but fewer bidders and longer material hauls. Net effect: approximately 0.88× national average for horizontal civil work, which is below the Grand Rapids figure because of the rural market discount on labor offset by material haul premium.
- **Confidence: Moderate.** This multiplier has not been confirmed against a current Manistee County subcontractor bid tabulation.

### Construction Cost Escalation
Plans are dated August 2026. ENR Building Cost Index shows +6.3% annual and Construction Cost Index +4.2% annual as of mid-2026 (per benchmark context). This estimate is priced in Q3 2026 dollars and does not add an additional escalation factor — it represents the cost to build now under current bid conditions. If construction extends into 2027–2028, add 4–6% per year for escalation on uninflated cost categories.

### Error Register Allowances Built Into This Estimate
The following error register items (from the prior review) have explicit cost allowances included:
- **E-01 (lift station risk):** Allowance included in Div 33 — see note
- **E-02 (electrical amperage upsizing for MH sites):** Unit costs use 200A service for MH lots
- **E-05 (stormwater detention — missing):** Detention basin allowance included in Div 33
- **E-07/E-08 (deep manholes, extra manhole on KY Ave):** Unit costs include deep-manhole premium
- **E-12 (dead-end blow-offs):** Included in water main unit costs
- **E-04 (ADA sites):** Allowance in Div 32
- **E-06 (vertical structures — not in plan set):** Budgetary allowance in Div 06/07/08/09 and Div 22
- **E-15 (geotechnical — missing):** Allowance in soft costs and contingency

### Site Count and Acreage Used
- **Developed sites: 155** (per Plan Facts and project description)
- **Gross acreage: 45 acres assumed** (midpoint of the 40–60 acre range estimated from road station data; this is an explicit assumption — **confidence: low; must be verified from D-6631-04**)
- **Net developable acreage: 38 acres assumed** (gross less estimated road ROW and stormwater area, approximately 85% efficiency)

---

## Division-by-Division Cost Estimate

---

### Division 01 — General Requirements
**Confidence: Moderate**

| Line Item | Basis | Quantity | Unit Cost | Subtotal |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mobilization / demobilization | 3% of Div 31–33 hard cost | Lump sum | — | $180,000 |
| Project superintendent (on-site, 18 months) | 1 superintendent × 18 mo | 18 mo | $9,500/mo | $171,000 |
| Project manager (part-time, office-based) | 0.5 PM × 18 mo | 18 mo | $6,500/mo | $117,000 |
| Temporary facilities (trailer, portable toilets, temp power, fencing) | Lump sum, 18-month project | LS | — | $45,000 |
| SWPPP implementation and monthly BMP maintenance | Part 91 SESC — 18 months | 18 mo | $3,500/mo | $63,000 |
| Traffic control (site access road, flagging) | Assumed minimal — private site | LS | — | $15,000 |
| Bonds and insurance (builder's risk, GL, workers comp) | 2.5% of total hard cost | — | — | $215,000 |
| Quality control testing (soils, concrete, pipe pressure tests) | Lump sum | LS | — | $35,000 |
| **Division 01 Subtotal** | | | | **$841,000** |

*Note: Mobilization is computed after Div 31–33 are estimated and back-filled here. Bonds and insurance are computed at 2.5% of $8,600,000 estimated hard cost total (rounded after all divisions are summed).*

---

### Division 02 — Existing Conditions (Demolition, Clearing, Environmental)
**Confidence: Low-Moderate**

| Line Item | Basis | Quantity | Unit Cost | Subtotal |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Clearing and grubbing — wooded/brush areas | 45 acres gross; assume 60% requires clearing = 27 acres | 27 AC | $3,500/AC | $94,500 |
| Selective tree removal (larger trees, stump grinding) | Assume 15% of cleared area has significant trees | 150 trees est. | $400/tree avg | $60,000 |
| Demolition of existing structures (if any) | D-6631-05 (Removal Sheet) unreadable — allowance only | LS allowance | — | $25,000 |
| Hazardous materials survey/abatement (precautionary allowance) | Unknown — no Phase I referenced | LS allowance | — | $10,000 |
| Topsoil stripping and stockpile (6" depth, full disturbed area) | 35 acres disturbed × 0.5 ft × 1,613 CY/acre | 28,200 CY | $3.50/CY strip and stockpile | $98,700 |
| **Division 02 Subtotal** | | | | **$288,200** |

*Assumption: The removal sheet (D-6631-05, unreadable) may contain additional demolition scope. If existing utilities, structures, or pavement must be removed, add $50,000–$150,000. Flagged as a verification item.*

---

### Division 31 — Earthwork
**Confidence: Low**

No grading plan was found in the plan set (confirmed missing per Plan Facts). Quantities are estimated from terrain description (bluff site, rolling terrain) and development footprint. This is the highest-uncertainty division in the estimate.

| Line Item | Basis | Quantity | Unit Cost | Subtotal |
|---|---|---|---|---|

## 4. Contingency and Risk Allowances

### Recommended Contingency

**Recommended construction contingency: 20% of hard cost**

**Justification:**
- This is an AACE Class 4 estimate with ±30–50% accuracy range
- 6 critical errors and 9 moderate errors were found in the plan review — this is a plan set with material unresolved issues
- Multiple key sheets were unreadable (D-6631-04, D-6631-06, D-6631-11), meaning quantities cannot be confirmed
- No geotechnical report exists — the single largest unknown on a bluff-top site
- No grading plan was found — earthwork is the second highest uncertainty
- Three error register items (lift station, detention basin, electrical upsizing) each carry $150,000–$400,000 individual cost risk
- Michigan bluff terrain introduces slope stability and erosion risks with no published benchmark
- The 20% contingency is consistent with MMCG Invest and Campground Consulting Group both citing 10–20% contingency as standard for resort-tier development; the upper end of that range is warranted here given the number of unresolved plan issues

**Construction contingency at 20% of $10,255,516 hard cost = $2,051,103**

Schedule risk is as significant as cost risk here. |

| **Entitlement and zoning risk** | **MODERATE** | Unknown — plans appear to be post-approval based on "Issued for Bidding" designation, but parcel type approvals and health department campground license are not confirmed | Plans are issued for bid, suggesting entitlement is largely complete. County campground license and health dept. approval are not confirmed. |

## Benchmark Comparison

| Metric | This Project | Published Resort-Tier Range | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hard cost per site (pre-contingency) | $66,165 | $40,000–$80,000/site (RoverPass, CCG, DTS) | **Within range — upper third of resort tier** |
| Total cost per site (with soft costs and contingency) | $91,598 | $55,000–$80,000+ "all-in" published; no true all-in benchmark confirmed | **Above the commonly cited $55K–$58K "per-site" figure** |
| Hard cost per acre | $227,900 | No direct benchmark for Michigan lakefront | No comparison available |
| Soft cost as % of hard cost | 18.4% | 10–20% published range | Within range |
| Contingency | 20% | 10–20% published range | Upper end, justified by plan gaps |

**Why is this estimate above the commonly cited $55,000–$58,000/site figure?**
Three reasons, all traceable to this specific plan set and site conditions:

1. **Amenity buildings ($10,565/site) are included.** The published $55K–$58K figure likely does not include clubhouse, bathhouse, pool, and office at resort quality — or if it does, at a lower finish level. Removing amenity buildings from this estimate reduces the hard cost to $55,600/site, which is directly in line with the benchmark range.

2. **Error register allowances ($200K lift station, $250K detention, $64K–$120K electrical upsizing) are included.** These are risk items not visible in the plan set that a clean estimate would ignore and a responsible estimate must flag.

3. **This estimate uses full-depth asphalt with curb and gutter throughout.** If chip-seal is substituted (per value-engineering benchmark context), roadway paving cost drops by approximately $220,000, or $1,419/site, bringing the all-in closer to the benchmark range.

---

## Phasing Note

The plan set does not explicitly identify construction phases. If the owner elects a phased build-out per the benchmark context recommendation (Phase 1: ~75–80 sites + full trunk infrastructure; Phase 2: remaining 75–80 sites from cash flow):

**Phase 1 estimate (75–80 sites + all trunk infrastructure front-loaded):**
- All trunk main sizing (California Drive and Tennessee Avenue water/sewer/storm) must be built to full 155-site capacity in Phase 1 — do not undersize
- Phase 1 site-specific work (laterals, pads, pedestals) for 80 sites only
- Approximate Phase 1 hard cost: **$7,200,000–$7,800,000** (75% of trunk infrastructure + 52% of site-specific work)
- Phase 2 site-specific add: **$2,500,000–$2,800,000**
- Phasing does not reduce total cost — it redistributes the capital requirement over 18–24 months

### Framing Notes and Base Case Assumptions

**Base case hard cost:** $8,525,000 ($55,000/site × 155 sites). This is used as the working base throughout. Soft costs (engineering, permitting, legal, contingency at 15%) are assumed at ~$1,275,000, bringing total project cost to ~$9,800,000. Where the error register (prior section) identified missing scope items (detention basin, geotechnical, bathhouse, ADA retrofits, potential lift station), those are treated as **base case risks** — they inflate the base before any VE is applied, not after.

**Market rent assumptions (general market knowledge — treat all NOI deltas as directional):** No feasibility study or rent comp schedule was provided. Estimates are based on: (a) Michigan lakefront RV/MH market comps from publicly available listing data (Campspot, Hipcamp, Zillow MH listings in Manistee County); (b) RoverPass/RVUSA published resort-tier rate data for Great Lakes markets; (c) MHInsider published lot rent data for Michigan MH communities.

| Site Type | Assumed Monthly Rent | Assumed Occupancy | Annual Revenue/Site |
|---|---|---|---|
| RV pull-through super site (seasonal) | $1,200–$1,800/mo × 6 months | 85% | $6,120–$9,180 |
| RV pull-through super site (transient peak) | $85–$125/night | 65% peak-season nights | Blended with seasonal |
| MH double-wide lot (long-term) | $550–$750/mo | 95% stabilized | $6,270–$8,550/yr |
| MH single-wide lot | $450–$600/mo | 92% | $4,968–$6,624/yr |
| Blended average (155-site mix) | — | — | ~$7,000–$8,500/site/yr |

**Stabilized NOI assumption:** Revenue ~$7,500/site/yr average × 155 sites = $1,162,500 gross revenue. Operating expenses at 35–40% of gross for a well-run resort = $407,000–$465,000. **Stabilized NOI ≈ $697,500–$755,000.** At a 7% cap rate, value = $9.96M–$10.8M. At 6.5% cap rate (lakefront premium): $10.7M–$11.6M. This establishes the value creation window for revenue-side alternatives.

**Confidence level on all NOI figures: Low.** A formal appraisal and rent comp study is required before any revenue-side alternative is relied upon for a financing decision.

## A. Cost-Side Value Engineering

### A-1. Road Surface: Chip Seal in Lieu of Full-Depth Asphalt (Internal Streets Only)
**Confidence: High on cost delta; Moderate on feasibility**

**What changes:** Replace full-depth asphalt (assumed 3" HMA surface + 6" aggregate base on all internal streets) with chip seal (1.5" aggregate base coat + chip seal surface) on secondary internal streets only — Kentucky, Minnesota, Montana, Pennsylvania, Washington Avenues (~3,200–3,600 LF of the ~6,100 LF total). Retain full-depth asphalt on California Drive and Tennessee Avenue (the primary collector loop carrying MH transport vehicles, emergency apparatus, and heavy delivery trucks). Chip seal is explicitly recommended by industry sources for RV park roads; it offers adequate skid resistance for RV tires, lower reflective heat than asphalt, and natural aesthetic consistent with a resort brand.

**Cost delta:**
- Base asphalt: ~3,400 LF × 26 ft wide ÷ 9 × $45/SY (3" HMA + 6" base installed) = ~9,822 SY × $45 = **~$442,000**
- Chip seal alternative: same area × $18–$22/SY installed = ~$177,000–$216,000
- **Savings: ~$226,000–$265,000 hard cost** (confidence: moderate — Michigan chip seal pricing varies with oil cost)
- Soft cost delta: $0 (same engineering, minor spec revision)

**Revenue/NOI delta:** $0 — guests do not pay more for asphalt vs. chip seal on secondary internal roads.

**Schedule impact:** Chip seal cures faster than HMA — potential 3–5 day schedule savings on road construction. Negligible.

**Regulatory/engineering constraint:** Michigan winter freeze-thaw cycle will degrade chip seal faster than HMA — recoat every 5–7 years at ~$4–$6/SY. Life-cycle cost analysis should confirm chip seal is still cheaper at 20-year horizon. **No plan amendment required. No agency resubmittal required.**

**Rank:** ★★★★☆ — High savings, zero revenue impact, low risk. **Recommended.**

### A-2. Eliminate Curb and Gutter on Secondary Streets; Use Roadside Swales
**Confidence: Moderate on cost delta; Low on feasibility given bluff terrain**

**What changes:** Remove curb and gutter from the five secondary cross-streets (Kentucky, Minnesota, Montana, Pennsylvania, Washington) and replace with a 4:1 graded roadside swale directing runoff to existing grade. This is appropriate where: (a) there is no storm sewer inlet in the curb line (swale drains to daylight); (b) grade is consistent and controlled; (c) there are no pedestrian volumes requiring a raised curb for safety. The bluff terrain and the presence of storm sewer inlets on every cross-street (confirmed in plan set) complicates this significantly — the storm sewer system was designed to receive curb-line flow.

**Cost delta:**
- Curb and gutter removal: ~6,400 LF × 2 sides × $22/LF (curb installed) = ~$281,600 saved
- Swale grading addition: ~6,400 LF × 2 sides × 4 ft wide × $2/SF grading = ~$102,400 added
- Storm sewer inlet relocation (from curb-line to swale-line): 20–30 inlets × $800 each relocation design = ~$16,000–$24,000 added
- **Net savings: ~$155,000–$163,000** (confidence: low — depends heavily on whether storm inlets can be relocated and grade permits daylight drainage)

**Revenue/NOI delta:** Minor negative — curb provides a visible quality marker for MH community residents and improves site definition. Loss of curb may reduce perceived quality for MH lots specifically.

**Schedule impact:** Slightly faster (no curb-form work on secondary streets). ~5–10 day savings.

**Regulatory/engineering constraint:** Michigan Part 91 SESC requirements and the existing storm sewer design both assume curb-directed runoff. Removing curb requires redesigning the storm sewer inlet layout for all five cross-streets. **Plan amendment required. EOR resubmittal required for storm sewer layout. No agency resubmittal if the storm sewer permit quantities are unchanged.**

**Rank:** ★★☆☆☆ — Savings are real but the redesign cost ($20,000–$40,000 EOR time) and the quality perception risk for MH lots reduces the net benefit. **Conditional — apply only to RV-only streets if the site plan separates them clearly. Do not apply to MH streets.**

### A-3. Utility Joint Trenching — Water, Sanitary, and Electric in Common Trench
**Confidence: Moderate on cost delta; Moderate on feasibility**

**What changes:** Where code permits, run water main, sanitary sewer lateral conduit, and electrical conduit in a single common trench rather than three separate trenches. Michigan Act 399 requires 10 ft horizontal separation between water and sanitary mains — this prevents sharing a single trench for those two utilities. However, **electric conduit and communication conduit can share a trench with water main** (with 12" minimum separation from water main per utility provider standards), and **electric can share a trench with storm sewer** in many configurations. The practical application here: run electrical primary conduit in the same trench as the water main on each street, reducing trench excavation by approximately 30–40% on those runs.

**Cost delta:**
- Base trenching cost (three separate trenches on each street): estimated $18–$25/LF per trench × 3 trenches × 6,100 LF = ~$330,000–$457,500 total trenching
- Joint-trench (water + electric in one trench, sanitary separate): ~2 trenches × 6,100 LF × $20/LF average = ~$244,000
- **Savings: ~$86,000–$213,000** (wide range due to unknowns in electrical trench length and whether utility provider permits joint trenching)
- Soft cost delta: $5,000–$10,000 for joint-trench coordination detail (EOR + electrical engineer)

**Revenue/NOI delta:** $0.

**Schedule impact:** Significant positive — one mobilization for water+electric trench vs. two separate mobilizations per street. Estimated 2–3 week schedule compression.

**Regulatory/engineering constraint:** The serving electric utility (likely Consumers Energy or a Manistee County co-op) must approve joint trenching. Some utilities prohibit sharing their trench with other utilities entirely — others require it. **Confirm with utility before bid.** No plan amendment required if the utility approves; a joint-trench detail must be added to the plan set.

**Rank:** ★★★★★ — Best-documented, quality-neutral, schedule-positive cost lever available. **Strongly recommended. Pursue immediately as a pre-bid utility coordination item.**

### A-4. Gravity Sewer Regrading to Eliminate Potential Lift Station (Error E-01)
**Confidence: Low on feasibility; High on consequence if not pursued**

**What changes:** Before accepting a lift station as inevitable, EOR should investigate whether a grading revision on California Drive (raising the low point from El. 659.22 by 1–2 ft through a revised vertical alignment) can achieve gravity flow to the existing sewer. This is a design optimization, not a value engineering substitution — but it is framed here because the cost difference between gravity and lift station is the single largest cost swing available on the project.

**Cost delta:**
- Lift station (if required): wet well, pumps, controls, electrical, force main, SCADA = **$180,000–$350,000** added to base
- Regrading California Drive +1–2 ft: may require raising 6–8 lot pads and adjusting the road profile for ~400–600 LF. Cost: **$30,000–$80,000** in revised earthwork
- **VE savings if regrading avoids lift station: $100,000–$270,000 net** (confidence: low — depends on existing sewer invert, which is unknown)
- If regrading is not feasible, lift station is unavoidable and is a **base cost addition, not a VE item**

**Revenue/NOI delta:** $0 (lift stations are transparent to residents if properly maintained).

**Schedule impact:** Regrading is concurrent with earthwork — no schedule impact. Lift station design, EGLE permit amendment, and procurement adds **6–10 weeks** to the pre-construction schedule.

**Regulatory/engineering constraint:** Any change to the road profile on California Drive requires EOR revision and EGLE Act 399 amendment if the sewer invert profile changes. **Plan amendment required. Agency notification required if lift station is added.**

**Rank:** ★★★★★ — Potentially the highest-value single investigation item on the project. **Pursue as the first RFI before any other work.**

### A-5. Low-Pressure (Grinder) Sewer System for RV Sites Only
**Confidence: Low — feasibility depends on EGLE and site conditions**

**What changes:** Replace the gravity 8" PVC sewer collection system serving the RV pull-through sites (estimated 60–70 sites) with a low-pressure sewer (LPS) system using individual grinder pumps at each site. This eliminates the need for deep manholes (OA3 at 14.91 ft, OA1 at 14.85 ft — Error E-08) and allows force main routing at shallower depths, following the terrain rather than maintaining a constant grade.

**Cost delta:**
- Base gravity system for 65 RV sites (portion of 8" PVC, manholes, deep excavation): estimated ~$350,000–$450,000 installed
- LPS alternative: 65 grinder pumps × $2,500–$4,000 each = $162,500–$260,000; 2" force main ~3,000 LF × $15/LF = $45,000; controls = $20,000–$40,000; **Total LPS: ~$227,500–$345,000**
- **Savings: ~$5,000–$205,000** (wide range — deep manhole excavation cost savings are real but depend on actual soil conditions)
- Offset: Grinder pumps require ongoing maintenance ($200–$400/unit/year), power, and eventual replacement (~10-year life). 20-year NPV of O&M at 155 sites: ~$260,000–$520,000 additional lifecycle cost

**Revenue/NOI delta:** Slightly negative — grinder system failures (pump burnout from RV sewer chemicals) are a guest experience issue. Grinder systems are appropriate for MH permanent residents who can be trained; they are less appropriate for transient RV sites where guests may not follow guidelines.

**Schedule impact:** LPS has shorter installation time than deep gravity sewer — potential 2–3 week schedule savings.

**Regulatory/engineering constraint:** EGLE Act 399 governs LPS systems in Michigan and requires specific pump sizing, force main design, and backup power provisions. A complete redesign of the sewer system for RV sites is required. **Plan amendment required. EGLE permit amendment required.**

**Rank:** ★★☆☆☆ — Savings are real but the O&M liability and guest experience risk are high for transient RV sites. **Rejected for RV sites. Potential candidate for MH sites only if soils limit deep excavation** (geotechnical finding required first).

### A-6. Wastewater: Municipal Extension vs. On-Site Package Plant
**Confidence: High that municipal connection is preferred; Low on package plant cost**

**What changes:** The plan set connects to existing public sewer (confirmed by gravity system design and POE connections). This is the correct approach. For completeness, a package WWTP is evaluated as an alternative.

**Cost delta vs. municipal:**
- Municipal connection fees (estimated): $1,500–$3,000/site × 155 = $232,500–$465,000 (connection fees) plus infrastructure cost already in base
- Package WWTP sized for 155 sites at 75 GPD/site (RV) to 200 GPD/site (MH): total design flow 12,000–31,000 GPD. A package plant at this scale: **$400,000–$900,000** capital plus ~$50,000–$100,000/year O&M
- **Municipal connection is $200,000–$600,000 cheaper in capital** depending on connection fees

**Revenue/NOI delta:** $0 on revenue side. WWTP ownership creates a licensed utility asset (sellable to a municipality at a multiple) but also an ongoing liability (EGLE NPDES discharge permit, operator licensing, biosolids disposal).

**Rank:** ★★★★★ for staying with municipal. **Reject package plant — the municipal connection is confirmed in the plans and is the correct approach for this project scale and location.**

### A-9. Electrical — Utility-Provided Primary vs. Developer-Installed

**What changes:** In Michigan, most distribution cooperatives and Consumers Energy will design and install the primary distribution system (transformers, primary conductor) as part of their service extension at no cost to the developer, provided the developer pays a line-extension fee. - Utility-provided (developer pays conduit only): $6–$10/LF conduit × 7,000 LF + pads = $42,000–$70,000 + utility line extension fee $50,000–$150,000 (varies by utility)
- **Potential savings: $43,000–$105,000** (confidence: low — VIF note suggests utility may already be providing primary)

**Rank:** ★★★☆☆ — Confirm with the utility immediately. If utility-provided primary is already the base assumption (consistent with the VIF note), this item has no incremental value. **Investigate before bid.**

### A-11. Over-Specification Review — Pipe Class and Pavement Thickness
**Confidence: Moderate**

**What changes:** The storm sewer is specified as HDPE throughout (confirmed). HDPE is an appropriate and cost-effective choice — no over-specification here. - Confidence: low — pavement section thickness is not visible in the readable plan text; requires cross-section sheet

### B-1. Density Increase — Site Count Optimization
**Confidence: Low on additional sites; Moderate on process**

**What changes:** Review the D-6631-04 site plan for opportunities to add sites within the existing development footprint. Specific candidates based on dimension data:

### B-4. Utility Submetering — Water, Electric, and Sewer Pass-Through
**Confidence: High on savings magnitude; High on applicability**

**What changes:** Install individual utility-grade submeters at every site for water and electric. Charge residents/guests at cost (pass-through billing). This converts a fixed operating expense into a variable revenue recovery.

**Revenue/NOI delta:**
- Electric: average RV site uses 15–25 kWh/day in peak season. At $0.16/kWh Michigan commercial rate: $2.40–$4.00/day × 6 months × 155 sites × 85% occupancy: **$57,000–$95,000/yr** cost recovery that currently flows through as operating expense
- Water/sewer: at $4.50/MCF average Michigan municipal rate, ~60 GPD/site × 155 sites × 180 days: **$30,000–$45,000/yr** recovery
- **Total annual NOI improvement: $87,000–$140,000/yr**
- At 7% cap rate: **$1,243,000–$2,000,000 in property value**

**Cost delta:**
- Utility-grade electric submeters: $400–$800/site × 155 = $62,000–$124,000
- Water submeters: $350–$600/site × 155 = $54,250–$93,000
- Submeter management software: $3,000–$8,000 one-time + $2,000–$5,000/yr
- **Total incremental capital: $116,000–$217,000**

**Return on incremental capital:** ($87,000–$140,000) ÷ ($116,000–$217,000) = **40%–120% first-year return**. Payback in 10–18 months.

**Regulatory/engineering constraint:** Michigan utility submetering is legal for private communities. Individual electric meters must be sized consistently with service amperage (confirmed by service panel type per D-6631-49). No plan amendment required if meter bases are already in the service panels. **No agency resubmittal required.**

**Rank:** ★★★★★ — Highest return on incremental capital of any alternative in this analysis. **Strongly recommended. Install submeter-ready panels from day one — retrofitting meter sockets later costs 3–5× as much.**

| Event pavilion rental | $50,000–$100,000 pavilion build | $15,000–$30,000/yr | Weddings, family reunions, corporate |
| **Portfolio total** | **$130,000–$260,000** | **$70,000–$149,000/yr** | |

**NOI delta at 65% margin: $45,500–$96,850/yr.** At 7% cap rate: **$650,000–$1,383,000 in additional value.**

**Rank:** ★★★★☆ — Strong portfolio when bundled. Boat/RV storage is the highest-return individual item given the lakefront location and Michigan seasonal RV storage demand. **Recommend pursuing storage and propane in Phase 1; defer pavilion to Phase 2.**

---

### B-6. Amenities That Move Rent vs. Amenities That Don't

Based on industry research and Michigan Great Lakes resort market knowledge:

**Amenities that demonstrably move rent or occupancy (include in base scope):**
- Swimming pool/splash pad: **+$150–$300/month premium on adjacent sites; +5–8% occupancy lift across property.** At a Michigan lakefront resort, a pool is table-stakes for the premium RV market. Estimated build cost: $200,000–$400,000 for an inground pool + deck.
- Pickleball courts (2 courts): **+2–4% occupancy lift; very high ROI.** Build cost: $30,000–$50,000. This is the single highest-ROI amenity per dollar spent in the 2024–2026 RV resort market.
- Dog park (fenced, 0.5 acre): **+3–5% occupancy lift** (60%+ of RV travelers have dogs). Build cost: $8,000–$15,000. Extraordinarily high ROI.
- Playground: Required for family market. Build cost: $15,000–$40,000. Occupancy positive but not premium-rate-moving.
- Wi-Fi backbone (fiber to each site, managed): Table-stakes — a resort without reliable Wi-Fi will lose guests to competitors. Build cost included in B-5 above.

**Amenities that cost money but do not move rent at this market tier:**
- Fitness center: RV guests use it rarely; MH residents may value it but won't pay more for it. Build cost: $40,000–$80,000. **Reject or defer.**
- Mini-golf: High maintenance, low revenue, aging demographic appeal. **Reject.**
- Game room/arcade: Dated concept for resort-tier market. **Reject.**
- Tennis courts: Superseded by pickleball. **Reject if choosing one; add pickleball instead.**

---

### B-7. Resort Classification and Rate Premium
**Confidence: Moderate**

**What changes:** Pursue certification or affiliation with Good Sam Resort (4+ star), Passport America, or Harvest Hosts resort tier. Additionally, list on Hipcamp and Glamping Hub as a premium property. These designations are not capital items — they are operational and marketing decisions that require the physical amenity package to support the rating.

**Revenue delta:** Good Sam 4-star resort properties command **15–25% higher nightly rates** than comparable non-rated properties on the same platform. For the RV site revenue base (~$7,500/site/yr blended): 20% uplift × 70 RV sites × $7,500 = **$105,000/yr incremental revenue**. At 7% cap rate: **$1,500,000 in property value** — and this is purely a marketing/operations decision, not a capital investment.

**Requirement:** Pool, laundry, Wi-Fi, and a minimum amenity package are required for Good Sam 4-star. The capital commitment to those amenities becomes the threshold investment for this revenue uplift.

**Rank:** ★★★★★ — If the amenity package is being built anyway, the certification cost (application, inspection: $500–$2,000) is essentially free value creation. **Pursue from day one of marketing planning.**

---

## C. Phasing and Capital Alternatives

### C-1. Recommended Phase Structure
**Confidence: Moderate on phase boundaries; High on trunk infrastructure principle**

**Principle (confirmed by all industry sources):** Size trunk infrastructure (California Drive, Tennessee Avenue collector road, 6" water main backbone, 8" sanitary trunk, primary electrical feeder) for the **full 155-site build-out from day one.** Do not undersize backbone to save Phase 1 capital — re-trenching a collector street to upsize a main costs more than building it right the first time, and EGLE Act 399 permits are issued for the full system.

**Recommended phase structure:**

| Phase | Sites | Infrastructure | Amenities | Estimated Cost | Timeline |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Phase 1** | 80–90 sites (RV pull-throughs + 20–25 MH lots on the most shovel-ready terrain) | Full backbone (California Dr, Tennessee Ave, all trunk mains sized for 155 sites); all cross-streets and utilities serving Phase 1 sites only | Bathhouse/laundry, dump station, gravel parking, Wi-Fi, dog park, pickleball (2 courts) | $4.8M–$5.5M | 12–16 months construction |
| **Phase 2** | Remaining 65–75 sites (remaining MH lots + premium bluff-view sites) | Complete remaining cross-streets and utility stubs; pool; pavilion | Pool, event pavilion, propane station, boat/RV storage | $3.0M–$3.8M | 10–14 months after Phase 1 stabilization |

**Phase 1 opening NOI (80 sites, 70% stabilized occupancy):** 80 sites × 70% × $7,500/yr = **$420,000/yr NOI.** This exceeds typical debt service on a $4.8M–$5.5M construction loan at 7%/25-yr amortization (~$400,000–$460,000/yr). Phase 1 is **designed to break even or slightly positive in Year 1** and fund Phase 2 from cash flow.

**What must be front-loaded (cannot be deferred):**
- Full-length California Drive and Tennessee Avenue (primary loop) — required for fire access and MH delivery to all sites
- Complete 6" water main backbone on both collectors — fire flow and pressure require the full loop
- Complete 8" sanitary trunk — gravity sewer cannot be installed in disconnected segments
- EGLE permits (both phases in one application — much cheaper than sequential amendments)
- Geotechnical investigation (must precede all other design)
- Bathhouse and dump station (required for campground license before any occupancy)

**What can be deferred to Phase 2:**
- Kentucky, Minnesota, Montana, Oregon Avenue cross-streets serving Phase 2 sites
- Pool and event pavilion
- Phase 2 site pads and electrical pedestals
- Phase 2 landscaping

### C-2. Developer-Owned Utilities as Asset vs. Liability

**Municipal water and sewer (confirmed by plan set):** The project connects to existing public utilities. This is the correct choice and creates no developer utility ownership. There is no utility asset to sell, but also no utility O&M liability. **Strongly prefer this structure.**

**Developer-owned propane system:** If natural gas is not available (no gas distribution is shown in the plan set), a developer-owned propane distribution system (underground tank + meter at each site) creates a licensed utility that can be sold to AmeriGas, Ferrellgas, or a local supplier as a bulk propane account — typically valued at $800–$1,200 per connected account ($124,000–$186,000 for 155 sites), with the developer receiving preferred pricing in exchange for the exclusivity. This is a legitimate asset creation opportunity.

**Decision:** If propane is desired for MH heating (likely in Michigan winter), **do not install an owner-operated underground distribution system** — instead negotiate a bulk propane account with a regional supplier who installs and maintains the system. This transfers the O&M liability while capturing most of the propane revenue benefit.

### C-3. Optionality — What Current Plans Foreclose

| Design Choice | What It Forecloses | Cost to Preserve Optionality Now |
|---|---|---|
| **Water main dead ends (multiple)** (Error E-12) | Future looping to adjacent parcels or Phase 3 expansion is harder if dead ends are plugged rather than capped with a stub-out | Add 6"×6" tee + stub + 2" blow-off at each dead end instead of plug: +$500–$1,500/location. 4–6 locations: $2,000–$9,000. **Do this.** |
| **Tennessee Avenue ending at STA 28+74 POE** | If the property extends north of STA 28+74, this road terminus forecloses northern expansion without tearing up the POE outfall | Add a road stub stub and utility stub-outs at STA 28+74 before paving: +$5,000–$15,000. If northern expansion is possible, **do this.** |
| **6" water main throughout** | If a future water authority requires the system to be dedicated/transferred, a 6" dead-end system may not meet their minimum standard for dedication (many require 8" loops) | Upsize California Drive and Tennessee Avenue trunk to 8" now: +$40,000–$80,000. Preserves utility dedication option. Conditional — pursue only if utility dedication is a realistic exit strategy. |
| **Storm sewer discharge points at bluff edge** | POE locations on the bluff cannot easily be moved after they are constructed — they dictate where stormwater goes permanently | Include energy dissipation and stabilization from day one. If the detention basin design (when completed) places the outlet in a different location, revise before construction. Cost to move a POE after construction: $20,000–$60,000. |
| **No sanitary sewer stub to future amenity building sites** | If the bathhouse, clubhouse, and pavilion locations are not identified before underground work, sewer stubs will be missed and roads must be reopened | Add stub-outs for 3–4 future structures at known locations before road paving: +$3,000–$8,000. **Do this — always.** |

---

## Recommended Alternative Plan

### Summary of Top 5 Changes

**Starting base:** 155 sites, $8,525,000 hard cost ($55,000/site), ~$9,800,000 total with soft costs.

| Rank | Change | Hard Cost Delta | Revenue/NOI Delta | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | Utility submetering (water + electric at all 155 sites) | +$116,000–$217,000 capital | +$87,000–$140,000/yr NOI; +$1.2M–$2.0M property value | High |
| **2** | Joint trenching — water + electric in common trench | −$86,000–$213,000 | $0 | Moderate |
| **3** | Chip seal on secondary streets (replace asphalt) | −$226,000–$265,000 | $0 | High |
| **4** | MH runner pads vs. full mat (if base has full mat) | −$500,000–$603,000 | $0 | Moderate (pending D-6631-06 verification) |
| **5** | Add 6 density sites (optimized D-6631-04 review) | +$330,000 capital | +$45,000/yr NOI; +$642,000 property value | Low |

**Additional value-add (no plan change required):**
- Premium bluff-view site pricing: $0 capital, +$26,520/yr NOI
- Boat/RV storage: +$10,000–$30,000 capital, +$15,600–$31,200/yr NOI
- Pickleball courts + dog park: +$38,000–$65,000, high occupancy uplift
- Good Sam resort certification: <$2,000, +$105,000/yr revenue potential

### Revised Project Parameters

| Parameter | Base Case | Recommended Alternative | Delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| Site count | 155 | **161** (155 + 6 density optimization) | +6 |
| MH pad type | Full mat (assumed, unconfirmed) | Runner system | −$500,000–$603,000 |
| Road surface (secondary) | Full asphalt | Chip seal | −$226,000–$265,000 |
| Trenching | Separate trenches | Joint water+electric | −$86,000–$213,000 |
| Submetering | Unknown | Individual electric + water meters | +$116,000–$217,000 |
| Additional sites | 155 | 161 | +$330,000 |
| **Revised hard cost** | **$8,525,000** | **$7,293,000–$7,764,000** | **−$761,000 to −$1,232,000** |
| **Revised cost per site** | **$55,000** | **$45,300–$48,200** | **−$6,800–$9,700** |
| **Revised total (with soft costs at 15%)** | **$9,800,000** | **$8,387,000–$8,929,000** | **−$871,000–$1,413,000** |
| Stabilized NOI (161 sites) | ~$700,000/yr | **~$940,000–$1,060,000/yr** | +$240,000–$360,000/yr |
| Value at 7% cap rate | ~$10,000,000 | **~$13,400,000–$15,100,000** | +$3,400,000–$5,100,000 |

> **Caution:** The MH runner pad item (Change #4) is flagged as the highest uncertainty — if D-6631-06 already shows a runner system, the $500,000–$603,000 savings disappears and the revised cost per site rises to $51,000–$53,500. **This single unknown makes the difference between a $45K/site and a $53K/site outcome — verifying D-6631-06 is the single highest-priority action item.**

### Alternatives Evaluated and Rejected

| Alternative | Reason Rejected |
|---|---|
| Package WWTP | Municipal connection is available, cheaper, lower O&M liability |
| Low-pressure sewer for RV sites | Guest experience risk, O&M liability; gravity system is correct for this project |
| Gravel pads for RV sites | Fast degradation under heavy RV traffic; maintenance cost exceeds savings within 3 years |
| Fitness center amenity | Does not move rent or occupancy at this market tier relative to cost |
| Mini-golf, game room, tennis | Dated amenity profile; inferior ROI vs. pickleball and dog park |
| Overhead secondary electrical distribution | Visual quality impact unacceptable for resort branding; modest cost savings ($15,000–$30,000) not worth the guest experience cost |
| Underground detention (structural) on bluff | Structural failure risk on sloped terrain is unacceptable per industry guidance; surface dry basin preferred |

---

### Most Cost-Effective Amenity: Wi-Fi Backbone (Rank 1)

**Why it beats every other item on this specific site:**

Wi-Fi is the only amenity on this list that simultaneously generates direct fee income *and* improves retention across *all* 155 sites (both MH and RV), with essentially no ongoing resource consumption (no staff, no physical maintenance beyond occasional AP replacement). At this lakefront bluff location, internet access is the one utility guests and MH residents cannot obtain elsewhere on-site — a guest can find shade under a tree and a dog run in an open field, but they cannot get 25 Mbps internet without the owner providing it. The combination of a direct ISP margin on 80 MH sites (a recurring monthly annuity) and a nightly Wi-Fi fee or rate uplift on 75 RV sites produces a payback of under 7 months at conservative assumptions, and a value creation of over $1.1 million at a 7.5% cap. The capital cost ($35,000–$55,000) is also the most manageable lump sum in the table relative to its NOI output.

The only caveat: the quality of the last-mile fiber or fixed-wireless feed from the road will determine the product quality. In Manistee County, the served ISP is likely Spectrum or a local fiber co-op — the owner must confirm a commercial-grade ISP drop is available at the site entrance before the internal network is specced. If a commercial drop is not available, a satellite backup (Starlink Business at $2,500/mo enterprise) changes the economics significantly.

### Amenity That Does Not Pay for Itself as Planned: Trail Surfacing (Rank 15)

Trail surfacing on approved paths returns only $1,413/year against a $4,000–$10,000 investment — a payback of 3–7 years on a pure attribution basis, with very low confidence in even that estimate. It is primarily a polish item. **Value-engineering recommendation:** Use the same decomposed granite or mowed natural surface instead of pea gravel — reduce cost to $1,500–$3,000 by eliminating the edging system and using a native seed-and-mow path where grades permit. Save $2,500–$7,000 with no material guest experience difference in the first 3–5 years. The trail alignment does not change; only the surface spec is reduced. This is a "no permit contact" field decision.

These decisions must be made before the relevant trade begins work — a late decision forces rework or a missed opportunity:

### Total Estimated NOI Lift and Value Creation

**Assumptions:** All 25 items implemented at midpoint cost and midpoint NOI. Excludes contingent items (fishing pier, pickleball if no slab). Native landscaping counted as Year 1 savings on capital, not recurring NOI. Cap rate: 7.5%.

| Category | Annual NOI Lift | Total Incremental Cost (Midpoint) |

| Revenue amenities (Part 1, 14 items) | $413,773 | $317,400 |

**Value creation at 7.5% cap rate:**
$530,931 ÷ 0.075 = **$7,079,080 in stabilized asset value created**

**Return on incremental investment:**
$530,931 NOI ÷ $475,075 cost = **111.8% cash-on-cash** (blended across all items)

**Payback on full program:** $475,075 ÷ $530,931 = **0.89 years** (blended; some items take longer, some are under 6 months)

**Note on confidence:** The above is an aggregation of individual estimates, many at Moderate confidence. The high-confidence items (LED lighting, pipe spec, native landscaping, fire pits, laundry) alone contribute approximately $65,000/yr NOI at $82,000 cost — a $867,000 value creation at 7.5% cap. The full-program figure of $7.1M is plausible but depends heavily on the smart metering and Wi-Fi returns, both of which carry Moderate confidence and market-specific assumptions that should be verified with the operating team before the full program is committed.

## Excluded — Would Require Plan Amendment

*These ideas were considered and excluded because implementing them would require reopening the site plan approval, changing a permitted design element, or require agency re-notification. Listed for the owner's awareness only.*

1. **Adding a pool** — building footprint and impervious area not in approved plans; requires new site plan approval and EGLE review.
2. **Adding a second access point / entry road** — access point count is a condition of site plan approval; cannot be changed without resubmittal.
3. **Upsizing the water main from 6" to 8" on California Drive or Tennessee Avenue** — utility sizing is a permitted design element under EGLE Act 399; any change requires a permit amendment.
4. **Adding a stormwater detention pond** — not shown on approved plans; adding one changes the approved drainage pattern and requires EGLE Part 31 amendment.
5. **Relocating any manhole or adding an unplanned manhole** — changes the approved Act 399 sanitary sewer permit.
6. **Adding a dump station** — requires new plumbing permit, site plan amendment showing location, and Manistee County Health Department approval.
7. **Expanding any building footprint** — outside approved site plan and building permit scope.
8. **Adding a permanent propane distribution system** — utility routing change; requires plan amendment and Michigan Public Service Commission filing.
9. **Paved trails** — any paved trail would add impervious surface beyond what the stormwater approval assumed.
10. **Adding a gate or security barrier at the entry road** — changes the approved access point geometry; requires site plan amendment.
11. **Relocating approved parking spaces** — parking count is typically a condition of site plan approval.
12. **Any landscaping that increases impervious area** (e.g., concrete pathways connecting amenity areas not shown on approved plans).
13. **Changing approved site boundaries or combining lots** — platting change requiring county approval.
14. **Adding a cell tower or commercial antenna structure** — separate use permit and FCC coordination.
15. **Moving any utility pedestal location** — changes the approved electrical plan on file with the utility provider.

## Bottom line

The Bluffs on Manistee Lake — North Expansion is a 155-site full-hookup MH/RV resort with ~6,100 LF of new roads, complete underground utilities, and a 49-sheet civil plan set issued for bidding 8/20/2026. The headline all-in project cost estimate is **$14.2 million (~$91,600/site)**, including a 20% hard-cost contingency. The single most important thing to do before spending another dollar: get the existing sanitary sewer invert elevation at the California Drive Point of Egress — if it sits above El. 659.22, a lift station costing $200K–$400K is needed and is nowhere in the current bid documents.

---

## Fix before mobilizing

| # | Sheet | What is Wrong | Field Fix | Who Resolves |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| E-01 | D-6631-13, D-6631-22/23 | Gravity sewer may not drain — existing sewer invert at California Drive POE is unknown; if above El. 659.22, no drainage | EOR must obtain as-built invert; redesign with lift station if gravity fails | Engineer of Record — mandatory RFI before any trench |
| E-05 | D-6631-04, D-6631-11 | No stormwater detention shown anywhere; EGLE Part 31 will almost certainly require it before a permit for bluff-discharge | EOR to submit stormwater management report; design and permit detention basin before grading | EOR + EGLE (3–6 month permit lead) |
| E-04 | D-6631-04, D-6631-06 | Zero ADA-accessible sites identified in any readable sheet; FHA/ADA requires ~8 accessible sites minimum | EOR must mark ≥5% of sites accessible with compliant slopes and routes before grading sets grades | EOR — mandatory before grading |
| E-03 | D-6631-04 | Road widths and turning radii unconfirmed against IFC 503.2.4 fire-apparatus minimums | EOR to certify 20 ft clear width and compliant radii at every dead-end; fire marshal written approval before grading | EOR + Fire Marshal |
| E-02 | D-6631-49, D-6631-06 | Electrical detail shows 100A service; NEC 550.32 requires 200A for MH double-wide lots | EOR to issue complete electrical service schedule by parcel type; upsize MH service to 200A | EOR — mandatory before electrical bid |

---

## Cost

| Metric | Amount |
|---|---|
| Hard cost (base, pre-contingency) | $10,255,516 |
| Soft costs | $1,891,000 |
| Contingency (20% of hard cost) | $2,051,103 |
| **Total project cost** | **$14,197,619** |
| Cost per site (155 sites) | $91,598 |
| Cost per gross acre (45 acres assumed) | $315,503 |

**Confidence: Low-Moderate.** Three factors drive the wide ±30–50% AACE Class 4 band: (1) no grading plan exists, making earthwork ($1.2M estimated) essentially a guess; (2) the lift-station question ($0 or $200K–$400K) is unresolved; (3) the missing detention basin allowance ($250K) may be too low or unnecessary. Gross acreage (45 acres) and MH pad type are both unverified assumptions — verifying D-6631-06 alone could swing the estimate by $500K–$600K.

| 2 | **Dog park** (fenced, 300 LF, agility equipment) | $8,000–$15,000 | $50,090 | 0.2–0.3 yr | Turnover-savings figure is operator-level inference |
| 3 | **HDPE conduit sleeves at road crossings** (installed during open-cut) | $1,350–$2,000 | $10,000 avoided CapEx/yr | <1 yr when first bore avoided | Source: ASCE 38-02, APWA standard practice |
| 4 | **Wi-Fi backbone** (fiber to ~20 outdoor APs) | $35,000–$55,000 | $87,600 | 0.5–0.6 yr | ⚠️ *ISP commercial availability in Manistee County must be confirmed before speccing* |

---

## What to verify by hand

1. **Open D-6631-04 (Site Overall) and D-6631-06 (Parcel Types) in the original graphic PDF.** These two visual-only sheets are the foundation of every quantity and cost in this analysis — site count, acreage, road widths, pad type, ADA designation, and site-type mix are all unknown without them. Every major number in this report should be checked against what those sheets actually show.

2. **Obtain the as-built invert elevation of the existing sanitary sewer at the California Drive POE before any contract is signed.** If gravity flow is not achievable, the lift station must be designed, permitted, and added to the bid scope — a $200K–$400K change and a 6–10 week delay that will affect every downstream schedule milestone.

3. **Call the serving electric utility (Consumers Energy or local co-op) and EGLE before bid opening on two questions:** (a) transformer lead time and primary line-extension cost participation — pad-mount transformers are on 40–80 week allocation nationally and must be ordered before groundbreaking; (b) whether EGLE Part 31 will require detention for bluff-edge discharge, and if so, the expected permit timeline — this is potentially the longest-lead item on the project and could delay construction start by 3–6 months if not resolved now.

gemini_second_opinion_md:
Here is my independent, second-opinion review of "The Bluffs North Expansion" plan set, evaluated strictly through the lens of a 40-50 year owner-operator. 

## 1. What will this cost?

A precise, line-item cost estimate **cannot be reliably estimated from the text provided** due to critical missing information. I am intentionally avoiding naive math to fill in these gaps, as that creates dangerous blind spots for ownership. 

To achieve a reliable estimate, you need to resolve three major unknowns:
*   **Earthwork / Cut & Fill:** There is no grading table, mass haul diagram, or existing-vs-proposed volumetric data provided. (OBSERVED: Sheet 05 shows extensive clearing and grubbing limits, and Sheet 03 notes sandy soils like Plainfield and Covert sand, but volumes are UNKNOWN).
*   **Site Utility Laterals:** The utility plans profile the trunk lines, but individual water and sanitary service laterals from the mains to the ~155 individual home/RV pads are largely missing from the plans and details. (OBSERVED: Sheets 32-43 profile the water mains, and Sheets 22-30 profile the sanitary mains, but individual routing and quantities to the pads are UNKNOWN).
*   **Paving Quantities:** Roadways are profiled, but exact asphalt tonnage and aggregate volumes are UNKNOWN. 

**High-Level Order of Magnitude:** 
Based on the provided plans, we have a mix of single-wide, double-wide, and RV super sites totaling approximately 150-160 lots (OBSERVED: Tabulated lists on Sheet 06). We also have roughly 7,600 linear feet of 6" C900 PVC water main (OBSERVED: sum of lengths listed in titles of Sheets 32-43), commensurate sanitary trunk lines, and a robust 3" HMA road section over 8" aggregate (OBSERVED: Sheet 10). 

Assuming current Midwest prevailing construction costs for heavy civil MH/RV expansion, you should anticipate an **ASSUMED range of $25,000 to $45,000 per pad, yielding a total project cost between $4,000,000 and $7,000,000.** Do not take this to the bank until the missing lateral and earthwork quantities are detailed and bid.

## 2. What can we do to reduce it?

As a permanent owner-operator, we only care about reducing the *Total Cost of Ownership* over 40-50 years. Here are concrete value-engineering ideas and explicit rejections of short-term "savings" found in the plans:

*   **REJECT: 7" Integral Asphalt Curb (Sheet 10).** 
    The typical road cross-section on Sheet 10 specifies a "7-inch integral asphalt curb." **Do not build this.** Asphalt curbs are highly susceptible to point-loading failure and shear stress. In a community where modular home toters are backing in, and large RVs are making tight turns, these curbs will be crushed within the first five years. A cheap asphalt curb today will result in 40 years of continuous cold-patching, aesthetic decay, and ruined drainage profiles. *Recommendation:* Pay the premium now to install a standard concrete roll curb or concrete curb-and-gutter. 
*   **REJECT: Solar Street Lighting (Sheet 10).**
    Sheet 10 details the installation of "Imperial III GS-97K Series Solar Lamp (TYP)." While this saves the upfront cost of trenching electrical conduit for streetlights, it is a massive long-term liability. Solar batteries have a functional lifespan of 3 to 5 years, and solar charging efficiency plummets during cloudy, freezing Michigan winters (Manistee). *Recommendation:* You are already trenching the entire site for 100A/200A electric services (OBSERVED: Sheets 45-49). Hardwire your streetlights now with LED fixtures so you aren't perpetually paying maintenance staff to swap dead batteries in January. 
*   **ACCEPT: 8" Concrete Sidewalks at Drive Crossings (Sheet 10).**
    Sheet 10 specifies that sidewalks are 4" thick generally, 6" as noted, and 8" thick at all drive crossings. This is an excellent long-term standard that will prevent the sidewalks from cracking under the weight of delivery trucks or heavy duty pickup trucks. Ensure your civil contractor vibratory-compacts the sandy sub-base (Covert/Plainfield sand) thoroughly with water, as dry sand settling is the primary enemy of this concrete standard.
*   **VALUE ENGINEER: Storm Sewer Material (Sheet 21).**
    The plans specify HDPE for the storm sewer (OBSERVED: Sheets 12-21). HDPE is excellent and cost-effective, but the plans do not explicitly specify *smooth interior* (dual-wall) pipe. Ensure the specifications require AASHTO M294 Type S (smooth interior). If the contractor installs single-wall corrugated pipe to save money, sediment will build up in the corrugations over the next 40 years, requiring frequent, expensive hydro-jetting to maintain flow capacity.

## 3. What else would you recommend?

Before you break ground, you must address the following risks and missing information to protect yourself from predatory change orders:

*   **Missing Utility Laterals (Critical Risk):**
    As mentioned in the cost section, the plans do not show the individual 1" or 3/4" water service laterals (or curb stops/corporation stops) running from the 6" main to each home site. Similarly, individual sanitary lateral lines routing to the 150+ pads are not drawn on the plan views (Sheets 22-30). If it is not drawn, the contractor will not include it in their base bid. When you ask them to connect the homes, you will be hit with a massive change order at monopoly pricing. *Recommendation:* Have the Engineer of Record (EOR) explicitly map every water, sewer, and electric lateral to the exact pad locations before sending this out to bid.
*   **Missing Tracer Wire Detail (Sheet 44):**
    The water main is specified as C900 PVC (plastic). Because it is non-metallic, it cannot be located with standard magnetic utility locators unless a tracer wire is buried with it. Sheet 44 does not explicitly show a tracer wire in the trench detail. *Recommendation:* Mandate a heavy-duty, copper-clad steel tracer wire taped to the top of all PVC mains and laterals, terminating in accessible locator boxes. Finding a lost plastic pipe in 2045 will cost a fortune in exploratory excavation if you skip this.
*   **RV Pedestal Vulnerability (Sheet 49):**
    The RV electrical pedestals are noted as loop-fed 100A (OBSERVED: Sheet 49, Midwest U075CP6010). Because they are loop-fed, the main underground feeder cables run directly into the pedestal lugs and out to the next one. If an RV backs into the pedestal and destroys it, it can short out or severe the entire loop, taking down power to multiple sites. *Recommendation:* For a permanent-hold asset, consider installing flush-to-grade direct-bury splice boxes next to the pedestals, and only running a secondary tap up into the pedestal itself. 
*   **Winterizing RV Sites:**
    If the RV sites will be used in the shoulder seasons or winter, the plans do not detail frost-proof yard hydrants or heated water risers. Standard curb stops will freeze and burst. Ensure frost-free hydrants are specified for the RV super sites.

## Confidence notes
*   **Earthwork:** I have zero confidence in any site-prep or earthwork cost assumptions. There is no mass grading data in the provided text.
*   **Laterals:** I have zero confidence in the utility connections to the pads themselves, as the plans only profile the mains in the right-of-way. 
*   **Geotechnical:** I assume no rock excavation is required based on the SSURGO soils table indicating sand (Sheet 03), but without a formal Geotechnical Boring Report, underground contingency should be maintained.

steps.label: Hard cost -- civil scope and utility laterals now fully priced against the complete document set
Contingency -- 10-12% to 18%, reflecting 7 critical + 13 moderate items still unresolved
Soft costs -- financing, permitting, utility tap fees ($155K-$390K of that alone is a stated swing)

cost_assumptions.label: Financing / interest carry
cost_assumptions.note: 18-month draw, 70% average drawn, 8.5% rate -- a 40-50-year permanent owner typically self-funds or uses USDA Rural Development financing instead, which could remove this entirely

cost_assumptions.label: Engineering / EOR fees
cost_assumptions.note: Assumed at 5.5% of hard cost -- real fee depends on Spicer's actual contract, not yet confirmed

cost_assumptions.label: Owner's Representative (Grex Dynamics)
cost_assumptions.note: Assumed at 3% of hard cost for the full project duration

cost_assumptions.label: Full-time on-site inspector
cost_assumptions.note: 18 months, assumed full-time per RFP sec 4.1 -- real cost depends on who's actually hired and whether it's full- or part-time
